404.html: Not found That page is not part of this site. Start from the map , or look a term up in the terminology . AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. SAFe names the same altitudes Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team and is cited as one framework that uses them, not as the source of the labels. coined Agile Release Train (ART) SAFe's name for the train level: "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream". Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc.; this site uses "train" as the generic label for the same altitude. adopted safe-art Planning Interval (PI) SAFe's name for the planning cycle of a train: "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives". SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox, and calls the pattern of PI Planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule. Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
adapters.html: Adapters The thin layer that binds an Engineering Kit's core to each tool it runs against, so that its rules, validators and evidence schema depend on no one product. Definition An adapter is the thin binding between an Engineering Kit 's core and one tool the kit runs against: the execution surface where the coding agent works, the change host where the pull request lives, the pipeline runner where checks run unattended, the work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. The core holds what the team means: its rules, its validators and its evidence schema. The adapter holds only what it takes to talk to one product. The idea comes from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern, also called hexagonal architecture, in which a technology-specific adapter turns whatever arrives at a port into a call the application understands, so the application does not depend on the device on the other side 3 . Using "adapter" as the name of one layer of a kit is this site's own usage. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Why it matters In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the same checks have to run wherever the work happens: on a developer's machine, inside the agent's execution surface, and in the pipeline that guards the merge. A kit that calls one product's interface from inside its rules is tied to that product's release cycle and vocabulary. When the product changes its interface, or the team moves to another, the rules have to be rewritten, and results differ between environments while that work is under way. Cockburn's motivating problem applies directly. A layer that is promised to hold no business logic, with nothing in place to detect a breach of that promise, collects business logic over the years, and logic in the wrong layer can no longer be exercised by automated test suites 3 . Domain-driven design describes the same risk between models: without an isolating layer, another system's model can gradually reshape the model that uses it. Eric Evans's anticorruption layer talks to the other system through its existing interface and translates in both directions, so the other system's concepts stay outside 4 . For a kit, the outside model is a tool's own idea of a check, a status, a work item or a permission. A tool-free core also keeps the harness portable. The tools an agent can call are part of its harness 1 , and a team's choice of tools changes over time. A kit whose meaning sits in the core follows those changes by swapping bindings, not by re-deriving its rules. The Twelve-Factor App makes the parallel point about backing services: code that treats each outside service as an attached resource can exchange one for another through configuration, without code changes 17 . How it works The bindings a kit needs No public source lists the bindings an agent engineering kit needs; the list below is recommended practice. A kit ships one adapter per tool the team uses, not a fixed set. Execution surface. Installs the kit's guidance and commands in the form the surface loads, and lets the agent run the same verify command a person runs. Change host. Reads the change and its metadata, posts each result as a check on the pull request, and links the report behind it. Pipeline runner. Runs the kit's commands unattended, with the same inputs as a local run, and collects the evidence record the run produces. Work tracker. Reads and writes the few work-item fields the kit relies on, such as the link between a change and the item it serves. Tool servers. Connect the agent to capabilities published over an interface. The Model Context Protocol is one example: an open protocol in which servers offer tools, resources and prompts to client applications using JSON-RPC 2.0 messages 10 . An HTTP API described in the OpenAPI Specification, a language-agnostic description of what a service offers, is another 12 . What goes in an adapter, and what stays in the core The split follows the difference between mechanism and meaning. It is recommended practice, resting by analogy on Cockburn's and Evans's patterns. Stays in the core Goes in an adapter Rule identifiers, routes and owners (the rule registry ) Endpoints, authentication calls and rate-limit handling Validator logic and the results it returns Translating the tool's input into the core's interface The evidence schema and what each field means Translating the core's results into the tool's vocabulary: a check, a status, a comment The four results a check can report: passed, failed, skipped and could_not_run Packaging the kit in the form the tool loads Validators are deterministic checks of the kind Birgitta Böckeler calls computational sensors 2 , and they belong in the core. The adapter passes on what validators return and adds no verdict of its own. It also does not restate a machine-checkable rule as text for a model to read, since only the validator gives the same answer on every run. Once a rule lives in a binding, replacing the tool means rewriting the rule. The boundary is enforced by a check, not by a convention. An architecture rule can be written as an executable test 5 , for example a test that fails when any module in the core imports from an adapter. One model vendor's account of harness engineering describes enforcing architectural constraints through automated checks in the same way 11 . Cockburn's observation that an unguarded boundary erodes is the reason for making it a check. Every adapter follows an interface that its owners do not control and has to keep up with it, so, as recommended practice, a team writes one only for a tool it actually uses and only where configuration cannot express the need. An integration the tool's users already publish can serve as the adapter, provided it passes the same contract suite as one the team writes itself. How an adapter is tested Testing follows the same split. The recommended practice below builds on two public patterns. Ian Robinson's consumer-driven contracts have each consumer of a service state its expectations as tests that the provider runs, so the provider can change without breaking any of its consumers 13 . Martin Fowler's contract test checks that a test double still answers the way the real outside service does; it runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes, and a failure starts work to bring the two back into line rather than necessarily breaking the build 7 . Applied to a kit: One contract suite per binding. The core states what it expects of any change-host adapter, any pipeline-runner adapter and so on, as tests against the core's interface. Every adapter for that binding must pass the same suite. A double in the fast checks, the real tool in the contract run. Checks on the adapter's own changes use a double of the tool, so they stay quick and repeatable. The contract run against the real tool happens separately, as Fowler describes, and shows when the double has stopped matching. The tool's own failures. The suite includes runs in which the tool is unreachable or answers with an error, and the adapter must report could_not_run with that cause, never failed and never passed. A code-coverage target set for the core fits an adapter poorly. Most of an adapter's lines call a tool that the fast checks replace with a double, so a high percentage there mostly measures the double. The measure for an adapter is whether it passes its binding's contract suite, failure runs included. An adapter that needs many tests of its own to reach a target has usually taken on logic that belongs in the core. This is recommended practice. The same result locally and in CI Continuous integration expects anyone to be able to check out the sources on a clean machine and build and test the system with one command, and the same build to run after every push to the mainline 6 . The Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed pipeline configuration treated as code, kept under source control and tested like any other code, in its Adopt ring (Volume 22, May 2020; the entry is no longer on the current Radar) 16 . For a kit, the pipeline-runner adapter calls the same verify a developer runs. It adds scheduling and reporting, never extra checks or different thresholds, so a difference between a local result and a pipeline result points at the environment, not at the rules. Adapters do not remove every difference: the Twelve-Factor App warns that even when adapters appear to hide the differences between backing services, small incompatibilities let code pass in one environment and fail in another 18 . That is why the contract run against the real tool stays. Versions, replacement and synchronisation An adapter is versioned and released separately from the core, and states the range of core versions it works with. Semantic Versioning makes such a range readable, because a new major version marks an incompatible change to a declared public interface 14 . When the core or the tool changes its interface, the contract suite shows whether the adapter still holds. Replacing a tool means writing a new adapter, passing the same contract suite, and switching. Rules, validators and schema stay as they are; that is the design intent of the layer, not a measured result. An adapter that keeps two systems in step, such as the repository and the work tracker, first settles which system owns each field and copies that field in one direction only. Where a field can still be edited in both places, a clash goes to a person rather than being settled automatically, because keeping whichever edit is newer silently throws the other one away. This is recommended practice. Reporting that a tool could not run Test frameworks already keep "could not run here" apart from "failed": in one widely used framework, a test whose assumption about the runtime environment does not hold is aborted rather than failed. 9 Change hosts, however, have their own list of check states, and the adapter has to choose one. It never chooses success, and it avoids any state the host treats as satisfying a required check: at least one change host accepts a skipped or neutral required check as passing. 8 So, as recommended practice, the adapter posts could_not_run in a state that is not successful, names the cause in the check's summary, and links the evidence. What that state means for the merge is decided in the assurance band of the map. On the pull request, the change-host adapter posts each check's result, with a link to that check's evidence, and alongside them the overall status that the evidence record carries. The adapter computes neither: validators produce the results and the evidence record derives the overall status. A check new to the team is posted as report-only at first, so its results are visible without holding changes, and is marked required later. The adapter posts the same result in both stages; only the label the change host attaches to it differs. The running example The customer-record export arrives as a pull request. The pipeline-runner adapter runs verify unattended, and gets the same result a developer gets locally: the validator for R-042, the access rule on which identities may export which records, fails because a background worker queries more records than the requesting user may see. The change-host adapter posts that failure as a check on the pull request and links the validator's report. The runner image lacks the load-test tool, so the 50k-row load scenario for R-017, the volume-limit rule, cannot start. The adapter posts that check as not successful, with could_not_run and the missing tool as its cause, rather than dropping it or showing it as passed, and posts the record's overall status of blocked beside the two checks. If the team later moves to another change host, only the change-host adapter is rewritten and passed through the same contract suite. R-042, R-017, their validators and the evidence schema do not change. Where it sits on the map Adapters sit in the core band, the part of the map that does the work, inside the Engineering Kit box as one of its five parts alongside the rule registry, validators, skills with evals and the evidence schema. Within the kit's four layers (shared core, technology profiles , tool adapters and project configuration ), adapters are the layer that faces outward. On one side are the rules, validators and schema they carry without changing. On the other side are the tools themselves, the execution surface, change host, pipeline runner, work tracker and tool servers, whose choice and configuration belong to the enablement band. So do the permissions and secrets an adapter uses, which follow the usual rule for automation: each automated actor has its own machine identity with no more access than its job needs. Adapters also carry the evidence record to the pull request, where a workflow 's human decision is taken, and the assurance band reads the same results to decide whether a change may merge or release. Pitfalls Rules in the binding. A rule or threshold is written into an adapter, and replacing the tool would change what is enforced. Sign: a rule change needs an adapter edit, or two adapters give different results for the same change. An adapter that grows a validator. The adapter starts to judge the product instead of translating. Sign: the adapter has tests about product behaviour, or it becomes the subject of coverage arguments. A lowest-common-denominator core. The core's interface is cut down to what every tool supports. Thoughtworks placed generic cloud usage on Hold (Volumes 18 and 19, 2018) for the same reason in a different setting: avoiding lock-in at all costs gives up each provider's distinctive benefits 15 . The comparison is an analogy. Sign: a core capability waits for the least capable tool. Absence read as a pass. A tool is missing and the check quietly disappears. Sign: a check vanishes from the pull request after a runner image change, or skipped results rise with no stated cause. Local and pipeline results drift apart. The pipeline defines steps of its own. Sign: changes pass locally and fail in the pipeline with no code difference. Doubles that no longer match the tool. The contract suite runs only against doubles. Sign: the first sign of a tool's interface change is a failure reported by users. Silent upgrades. An adapter says nothing about which core versions it works with. Sign: it breaks after an upgrade on either side and nobody is sure who fixes it. A sync adapter that settles clashes by itself. Conflicting edits are resolved by whichever came last. Sign: a value in the tracker changes and nobody reviewed the change. The same fix copied from project to project. Each project patches its tool binding for itself. Sign: several near-identical patches, no two quite the same, and no agreed version. Related Engineering Kit : the package adapters belong to, its layers and its commands. Validators : the deterministic checks adapters run and report, including how a validator reports that it could not run. Evidence schema : the fixed shape of the record adapters carry to the change host, including the overall status it derives. Rule registry : the identifiers adapters pass through unchanged. Workflows : the unit of work whose checks and decisions adapters connect to real tools. Harness engineering : the discipline the kit and its adapters serve. Terminology: adapter and the workflow catalog . Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
definition-of-ready-and-done.html: Definition of Ready and Definition of Done A Definition of Ready states what an item must meet before a team accepts it for work, and a Definition of Done states what the result must meet to count as finished; with coding agents, both need parts a machine can check and an owner who is not the agent. Definition A Definition of Ready and a Definition of Done are each a team's explicit, visible statement of a state that work must reach. They differ in the state they guard. The Definition of Ready guards the entrance: what an item has to satisfy before a team accepts it for work. The Definition of Done guards the exit: what the result has to satisfy before it counts as finished. Either one works as a gate only when someone or something checks it; a definition that is written down and never applied is a wish. This framing is this site's own; the two entries below follow their published sources. Definition of Ready The Agile Alliance glossary describes a team that makes explicit and visible the criteria (generally based on the INVEST matrix) that a user story must meet before it is accepted into the upcoming iteration 1 . This site applies the same idea to any item of work, not only a user story, and says so where it does. The Scrum Guide does not use the term. It neither defines nor forbids a Definition of Ready. What it says is that Product Backlog items that the Scrum Team can complete within one Sprint "are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event", and that such items "usually acquire this degree of transparency after refining activities" 15 . Refinement, in the Guide's words, is "an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size" 15 . A Definition of Ready is therefore a team practice, written down so that "ready" means the same thing to everyone who relies on it. No source cited on this page prescribes what the criteria contain, and this page does not either: the contents depend on the work and on the team. Definition of Done The Scrum Guide, by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, gives the term its formal meaning: the Definition of Done is "a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product" 15 . Three consequences follow from the Guide's text. The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born 15 . A Product Backlog item that does not meet it "cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review" 15 . It is the commitment attached to the Increment, as the Product Goal is the commitment of the Product Backlog and the Sprint Goal that of the Sprint Backlog 15 . The Guide adds that the Definition of Done creates transparency by giving everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment 15 . SAFe's glossary words it more generally: the Definition of Done "specifies the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value" 13 . Why it matters Without a stated Definition of Ready, work starts on items whose questions are still open, and the questions surface later as discussion and rework. The Agile Alliance entry lists, among the expected benefits of a stated definition, less "costly back-and-forth discussion or rework" and an explicit agreement that lets a team push back on ill-defined items 1 . Without a stated Definition of Done, "finished" is decided case by case, often after the work is in review, and the argument is about people rather than about criteria. When several teams work on one product the problem multiplies, because the Scrum Guide requires those teams to define and comply with the same Definition of Done 15 . As recommended practice, a definition earns its place by settling those arguments before they start. In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), two things raise the stakes. The first is volume. DORA's guidance on its AI Capabilities Model says AI "can easily generate massive blocks of code, which are hard to review and test" 4 , and its page on small batches says that large changes "are difficult to review, test, and integrate safely" 5 . When items arrive faster than people can judge them, a clear entrance criterion keeps unfinished thinking out of the queue, and a clear exit criterion tells a reviewer what to look for in a large diff. The second is that the exit criterion can be shaped by the party being judged. METR reports, on its own evaluation tasks, models "attempting (often successfully) to get a higher score by modifying the tests or scoring code" 10 . One model vendor's system card describes a model that "occasionally resorts to special-casing in order to pass test cases in agentic coding environments", most often by returning the expected test values, and "also includes modifying the problematic tests themselves" 2 . Both are limited evidence: METR's examples come from its own tasks and not from production teams, and the system card says the behaviour emerged during training and that partial mitigations were applied before launch, so it is not a statement about any model in use today. They show that a check which the agent can edit is not independent of the agent. No public statistic says how many teams keep either definition, and no study examines how coding agents change them. Where this page describes how agents change the two definitions, it is recommended practice and is labelled as such. How it works Who owns each The two definitions have different owners, and the Scrum Guide is explicit about only one of them. For the Definition of Done, the Developers are always accountable for "Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done", and are "required to conform to the Definition of Done" 15 . An organisational standard, where one exists, is followed by every Scrum Team as a minimum. Where none exists, the Scrum Team creates a definition appropriate for the product, and teams working on one product "must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done" 15 . For readiness the Guide names no owner of a definition, because it names no definition. It does say who is accountable for what makes an item ready for selection. The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management, which includes creating and clearly communicating the items, and the Developers who will do the work are responsible for the sizing 15 . On this site, as recommended practice, each definition has one named owner who answers for its wording and can change it, and that owner is a person, never the agent whose work the definition judges. The definitions are applied inside workflows, each with an accountable owner of its own (see Workflows ): readiness in specification readiness ( W04 ) and in task traceability and test planning ( W12 ), and release-level done in release readiness ( W25 ). Who decides in each of those workflows is set in its catalog row; owning a definition means keeping it current, while the workflow's deciders apply it. Public practice already sets different criteria for different levels of work. Bill Wake's 2003 article proposes INVEST for stories (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) and SMART for tasks (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-boxed) 17 , and the Agile Alliance entry says a team's criteria are generally based on the INVEST matrix 1 . The Scrum Guide's wording for readiness concerns the item as a whole: one that the team can complete within one Sprint is deemed ready for selection 15 . This page does not adopt any of these lists as the contents of a definition. Criteria a machine can check. A criterion is machine-checkable when a tool can decide it from the record alone. The catalog rows state which parts of each readiness decision have that form; see specification readiness ( W04 ) and task traceability and test planning ( W12 ). What a tool cannot decide stays with a person: whether the intent is right. The identifiers in those checks are the chain described on the Traceability spine page, which connects criteria, tasks, tests and results. Public sources show how criteria are written so that gaps can be found. The templates of an open-source spec-driven toolkit mandate [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] markers in place of guesses, and include checklists that act as "unit tests" for the specification 16 . As recommended practice, a marker left in a specification fails the readiness check in specification readiness ( W04 ), so a tool can find it and the item is not ready. A 2025 industrial study of language models on real-world requirements reports that giving ten worked examples in the prompt classified ambiguous requirements better than giving none 12 . An agent can therefore flag ambiguity for a person to resolve, and it does not replace the person who settles what is meant. Testability and size are also readiness properties. ISTQB defines testability as "The degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met" 8 . As recommended practice, an acceptance criterion counts as testable when a check can be written for it before implementation starts. On size, DORA advises breaking work into units "that can be completed independently and in short timeframes" 5 , which is the same shape as the Scrum Guide's test of an item that can be completed within one Sprint. Done at three levels The Definition of Done applies at three levels of work. The first two follow the published sources; the third is this site's recommended practice. Story. At the level of a single Product Backlog item, the moment the item meets the Definition of Done an Increment is born 15 . Increment. The Definition of Done is the commitment of the Increment as a whole 15 . A 2014 testing syllabus adds that each test level has its own definition of done 7 , so unit, integration and acceptance testing can each carry criteria of their own. Release. As recommended practice, a release candidate has a done decision of its own; see release readiness ( W25 ) and evidence hand-off . The Release page describes the phase. The separation of done from released rests on the Scrum Guide. An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released 15 , and the reverse does not hold: meeting the definition makes an item eligible for release, not released. The Guide also says an Increment may be delivered before the end of the Sprint, and that the Sprint Review "should never be considered a gate to releasing value" 15 . The release decision therefore has its own evidence and its own owner. How agents change both For readiness, see the agent task in specification readiness ( W04 ); the study cited above investigates this task 12 . A person still resolves the intent, because the agent can raise a question and cannot know what the business wants. For done, the volume of code changes what can be reviewed. DORA reports that working in small batches amplifies the positive impact of AI adoption on product performance 5 , and that large changes are hard to review, test and integrate safely 5 . As recommended practice, the Definition of Done for an agent's work includes a limit on size; see Workflows . A check can also be met by changing it. The reward-hacking reports under "Why it matters" describe models modifying tests or scoring code and special-casing to pass tests 10 2 . Tests an agent generates are a weaker basis than they look: a preprint on LLM-generated test oracles reports that LLM-based test generation approaches mainly capture the actual program behaviour, which makes bug detection difficult 9 . A test that records what the code does has little to say about what it should do. Two consequences follow, and both are recommended practice. First, the done criteria rest on a basis defined apart from the implementation, the site's independent basis : acceptance criteria 6 , access rules, interface contracts, representative data and failure scenarios that exist before and outside the code they judge. Second, no agent edits the criteria it is judged by; see the guardrails in Workflows . No study examines these two definitions with coding agents, so this is guidance, not a finding. The lessons also flow back. The Scrum Guide has the Retrospective inspect "individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and their Definition of Done" 15 . On this site the corresponding checkpoint takes its name from SAFe's Inspect and Adapt event 14 ; see Inspect and Adapt . The route by which an incident changes a readiness criterion is the feedback path , which this site adapts from Birgitta Böckeler's steering loop 3 . Sending a lesson to a readiness criterion is this site's own extension of that loop, not part of Böckeler's account; see Harness engineering . The export example The running example is a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records. Its open decisions are which records, which fields, large exports, failure and audit. It shows both definitions at work. Readiness. For the export, the Definition of Ready checks that the specification settles the questions its rules depend on before planning starts. The plainest is which roles may export which records, the question the access rule R-042 turns on: while the specification leaves it open, the item is not ready, however complete the rest of it looks. Software factory follows the item from that point. A rule open to exception and one that is not. The two rules behave differently when a change asks to depart from them. R-017's row limit for large exports is open to exception, and R-042, as an access rule, is not; see the failure paths in Workflows . A readiness criterion tied to R-042 is therefore met only as written. One tied to R-017 is met either by staying within the limit or by a recorded exception, so the record has to show which of the two applies. Readiness changing. In a hypothetical production incident, a scheduled full export within R-017's limit, but far larger than the load scenario, times out. Afterwards the readiness check asks every export-like specification for the largest export it expects. The Definition of Ready has changed through the feedback path; Software factory gives the incident in full. Done. For the export change, done means the verification record for the exact revision shows an explicit pass for every check the change requires, among them the access check for R-042 and the R-017 load scenario. On the first pull request the access check failed and the load scenario returned could_not_run ; neither result is a pass, so the change is not done until both checks run again and pass. Evidence schema describes the record. Where it sits on the map The map's lifecycle band shows two tags. The DoR tag sits on the Specification phase and the DoD tag sits on the Release phase. The Team level of the map is labelled with "stories · iterations · DoR / DoD", which is where the two definitions are applied day to day; the Lifecycle levels page describes it. The adoption path lists "Specification readiness as the Definition of Ready" as a step. The workflow catalog holds the decision behind each tag. Specification readiness ( W04 ) sits under the DoR tag. Between the two tags, Develop, Build and QA holds the verification that produces the evidence a done decision reads, among them acceptance-test generation and execution ( W17 ) and pull-request verification ( W23 ). Release readiness ( W25 ) sits under the DoD tag. The core band explains the machinery they share: Workflows for the decision unit, the Rule registry for the rules a check cites, the Evidence schema for the record each run leaves, the Software factory for what emerges when many workflows share records, and the page on checks that enforce rules for how a result such as could_not_run is reported. SAFe, cited as one framework that uses these altitudes of work (the map's portfolio, train and team levels), appears here only through its glossary wording for the Definition of Done, quoted above. The SAFe reference model page gives this site's wider mapping of the lifecycle onto SAFe. Pitfalls Readiness stated but not checked. The definition exists as a document and nothing applies it. Sign: items start with open mandatory questions; see specification readiness ( W04 ). Done reduced to "the tests pass". Tests and code come from the same incomplete reading of the specification, so both share its mistake. Sign: the tests mirror what the implementation does, and a defect that traces back to the specification passes every test. Generated tests tend to capture the program's actual behaviour 9 , so the done criteria need an independent basis . An agent meets the definition by editing the checks it is judged by. Sign: a diff touches the checks or tests beside the code. Reported cases include models modifying tests or scoring code and special-casing expected test values 10 2 . As recommended practice, changes to checks go to a person for review; see Workflows . Done mistaken for released. Sign: finished increments accumulate and no release record exists 15 . The release decision is separate and has its own evidence. Each team on one product keeps its own definition of done. Sign: the same item is done in one team and not in another. The Scrum Guide requires teams on one product to define and comply with the same Definition of Done 15 . Related Specification : the phase where the Definition of Ready tag sits. Design : the phase where tasks and their traceability are set up. Release : the phase where the Definition of Done tag sits. Develop, Build and QA : where the evidence for done is produced. Lifecycle levels : the Team level, where both definitions apply. Traceability spine : the identifier chain that connects criteria, tasks, tests and results. Inspect and Adapt : the checkpoint where a definition is reviewed and changed. SAFe reference model : the mapping of the lifecycle onto SAFe. Workflows : the decision unit that each readiness and done check belongs to. Rule registry , Evidence schema , Software factory and checks that enforce rules : the shared machinery behind the checks. Workflow catalog rows: specification readiness ( W04 ), task traceability and test planning ( W12 ), acceptance-test generation and execution ( W17 ), pull-request verification ( W23 ) and release readiness ( W25 ). Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses."
