Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
deploy-verification.html: Deploy verification The workflow that decides whether a revision now running in an environment stays there or the way back is taken, by comparing it with a control and with the service's objectives, and by treating a missing signal as a result of its own, never as health. Decision In the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), deploy verification is the workflow that settles one question for one revision in one environment: does the revision now running there stay, or is the way back taken? The workflow catalog states it in brief as deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ); this page sets out how the call is reached, what happens when it cannot be reached cleanly, what the run leaves behind and how a team can tell that the workflow works. "Healthy" is never judged in isolation. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as "a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation", in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the rest, the control 14 . The same chapter says it is important to "also use absolute measures, such as defined SLOs, to ensure the system is operating correctly" 14 . The decision therefore rests on two readings: the revision relative to a control running at the same time, and the service against its own objectives. Trigger A run starts when a deployment of a recorded revision begins in an environment (see Deploy for strategies and environments). Each environment is a run of its own. Google's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) book describes rollouts that start "in one cluster and expand exponentially until all clusters are updated" 13 ; as recommended practice, each step of such a staged rollout is judged before the next one begins, so a result from the first step is never carried silently to the last. A configuration change deployed on its own starts a run too. The SRE book counts as a push "Any change to a service's running software or its configuration" 12 , and the Twelve-Factor App describes config as "everything that is likely to vary between deploys" 15 . Because the evidence schema keeps the configuration revision apart from the change revision, a run started by configuration alone still names the code revision it left in place. Inputs The run reads what earlier work has already settled, and what it needs to compare against. The release record for the same revision. Release readiness settles it before deployment begins. The run reads that record instead of repeating its work and, as recommended practice, stops if the revision deployed is not the revision the record names. The configuration revision the deployment carries, recorded beside the change revision. The Twelve-Factor App notes that "Config varies substantially across deploys, code does not" 15 , which is why the two are read separately. The service's objectives. The SRE book defines a service level indicator (SLI) as "a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided" and a service level objective (SLO) as "a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI" 2 . The objectives supply the absolute side of the comparison. The control. In a canary, the control is the part of the service still running the previous revision over the same period 14 . Comparing the new revision with how the service behaved before the deployment is weaker: the workbook has a section headed "Before/After Evaluation Is Risky", with the example of a Monday release compared against weekend behaviour, where the change of day adds noise to the comparison 14 . The signals. The SRE book's four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation 12 . For canary metrics, the workbook says "We typically recommend using SLIs as a place to start thinking about canary metrics", asks for metrics that indicate problems and are representative and attributable, and keeps the set small, "perhaps no more than a dozen" in its own words 14 . The way back, and whether it is still open. In blue-green deployment the router is switched back 5 ; in a canary release users are rerouted "back to the old version" 6 . Fowler advises that "The trick is to separate the deployment of schema changes from application upgrades" 5 ; where that was not done, the previous revision may not run on the changed schema, and the way back is closed before the run starts. Agent task The agent's part in this workflow is set in its catalog row ( W26 ); this page adds how that part is bounded. This page draws on no study of agents in deployment verification, so what follows is recommended practice except where a source is named. The case for an agent is volume. Once a canary is live, the signals outnumber what a person on watch can follow, and an agent can lay out for that person where the canary and the control diverge and which of those differences the change could plausibly explain, using the workbook's idea of an attributable metric 14 . Its account enters the record as advice beside the check results. It never settles the outcome (see Deploy ). One operator's account describes agents in its incident management that "consolidate/summarize data", create handoff documents and draft postmortems (written records of an incident and its follow-up actions 9 ), and, separately, agents "to investigate incidents, and in some cases to autonomously mitigate issues" 8 . It is one organisation's description of incident work, not a study of deployment, and it reports no outcome figures. This page recommends no autonomous agent action on production. The agent reads the monitoring signals, the release record and the run's own record, and writes only its account. It does not start, pause or stop a rollout, does not take the way back, and cannot mark the deployment healthy. Checks The checks are what settles health the same way on every run. Which checks the workflow runs is in the catalog row; the points below describe how a check in this workflow is built. Canary against control, and against objectives The workbook calls canarying "effectively an A/B testing process" 14 . A check therefore compares the canary's metrics with the control's over the same window, and separately holds both to the service's objectives, rather than reading the canary alone. Thresholds come from objectives The SRE book calls SLIs and SLOs "crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems", and says that "The SLO violation rate can be compared against the error budget, with the gap used as an input to the process that decides when to roll out new releases" 2 . As recommended practice, each threshold a check applies is derived from an objective and stored in the configuration revision, which the evidence schema uses for rules and thresholds, so a later reader can see what the revision was held to. Attribution A difference seen during a canary is not always caused by the change. The workbook's example is an oversubscribed machine shared with the canary: a real problem that monitoring should catch, but not a canary failure if the change did not cause it 14 . The check reports the difference; whether the change caused it is weighed in the human decision. Rule IDs and result states Each check carries the identifier of the rule it enforces, where one exists, and reports a status from the fixed list on Evidence schema . A required signal that reports nothing is could_not_run , never health. At least one change host documents that a job skipped by a conditional reports "Success" 7 , which is why the state has to exist explicitly. A halt is a check, not a judgement As recommended practice, stopping on a threshold is a deterministic gate that answers the same way every run, not an agent's reading. Danilo Sato describes one such practice, the "cluster immune system" at IMVU, which monitors business metrics and rolls a release back automatically on a statistically significant regression 6 . Where a team automates a halt or a rollback, the trigger is a rule with a recorded threshold, and the named person still records the decision that follows. Guardrails Credentials. The agent holds read access to signals and records and no write access to production state. Least privilege applies to processes acting on behalf of users as well as to the users themselves 10 , and one operator's account relies on "consistent controls to prevent unwanted mutations of production state" 8 . The canary is bounded. By the workbook's definition it is partial and time-limited 14 , and the workbook says "We strongly advise running only one canary deployment at a time" 14 . As recommended practice, a run judges one revision, and a second deployment to the same environment waits until the first is decided. Stop conditions. These are recommended practice. No control to compare against. The run produces no result about the change, since canarying judges the canary against the control 14 . A required signal is missing. The result is could_not_run and the rollout does not proceed. The way back is closed , for example because a schema change shipped with the code that needs it 5 . The decision is then no longer whether to roll back, and it moves to incident handling ( W27 ). Human decision A named person decides, and the record carries that name and the reason, as recommended practice (see Deploy ). The catalog row records who holds the decision for this workflow ( W26 ). Public sources describe the work around it: the SRE book's on-call engineer, once a page is acknowledged, "is expected to triage the problem" and "work toward its resolution, possibly involving other team members and escalating as needed" 11 , and release engineers and site reliability engineers "work together to develop strategies for canarying changes" and share "rolling back features that demonstrate problems" 13 . On a bad canary the workbook's options are to "pause and roll back the deployment, or perhaps contact a human to help troubleshoot the issue" 14 . On what evidence. The check results, the canary-against-control comparison, the reading against objectives, and the agent's account, marked as advice. What the person may do. Halt or roll back at any time on their own judgement, even when every check has passed; proceed against the agent's account, with the reason recorded; decide whether a difference is attributable to the change. What the person may not do. Record the deployment as healthy while a required result is failed or could_not_run . As recommended practice, the deployment stays unconfirmed until the result exists or the way back is taken. Outputs and evidence The run leaves the revision either confirmed in place or returned to the previous one, and an evidence record in the shape the evidence schema fixes. The record names the change revision, the configuration revision and the environment, and, for a staged rollout, the step. It lists the expected checks before their results, each result with its rule identifier and status, the control and the window compared, the agent's account as advisory findings, and the decision with its decider and reason. As recommended practice, it also states what kinds of traffic the window covered, so a reader can see what the run did not observe. Its readers: The release decision , where exposing the change to users follows deployment ( Release ; see also deploy versus release ). Incident handling and its lessons. Incident remediation ( W27 ) and Incident feedback start from what was running. The traceability spine links an incident to the release that was running, and this record says which revision and configuration that was and what verification saw. This is the evidence hand-off in the downstream direction. The workflow's owner , who reads the records together to compute the measures below. The next run in the same environment , which reads the last confirmed record to know what the way back returns to (recommended practice). In the customer-record export , a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records, the verification record for the export change names the exact revision that went out, as the Deploy page describes. Failure paths The general shape of a failure path is on Workflows . The paths specific to this workflow: The canary does worse than the control. The rollout pauses and the way back is taken. In a canary release that means to "reroute users back to the old version until you have fixed the problem" 6 ; the workbook's words are "pause and roll back" 14 . The record keeps the failed results with the revision. The control moves too. Imperfect isolation means that "bad behavior of the canary deployment can also negatively impact the control", and the two can change together, so the comparison alone can show no difference while both are worse 14 . The reading against objectives then decides whether the service is within them. The result is recorded and not attributed to the change on the comparison alone. No control to compare against. The run records no result about the change, and the rollout does not proceed on it. As recommended practice, the named person who decides the deployment acts next, choosing whether a control is set up and the run repeated. A required signal is missing. The result is could_not_run and the rollout does not proceed. As recommended practice, whoever owns the monitoring is told; the gap is not a defect in the change. The way back is closed. Fixing forward or another response is decided in incident handling ( W27 ), not in this workflow. Fowler's advice on schema changes explains how it closes 5 . Environments differ by accident. The Twelve-Factor App warns that "tiny incompatibilities crop up, causing code that worked and passed tests in development or staging to fail in production" 16 . As recommended practice, a result from one environment is not carried to another, and the difference found is recorded. The deployment stalls part-way. As recommended practice, the record holds the partial state, which steps run which revision, and a named person decides whether to continue or go back. The method's limit. The workbook notes that performance defects often show only under heavy load, so a canary at a quiet time may not trigger them, and that "Some regressions may manifest only during events not included in the artificial load, leading to gaps in coverage" 14 . In the customer-record export, if the export were rolled out to a canary, the comparison would see ordinary export requests, and a scheduled full export might not run during the canary's window at all. Deploy verification judges the traffic that reached the canary, not what was never exercised. That is the limit the Deploy page records: in a hypothetical production incident, a scheduled full export, within the volume-limit rule R-017's limit but far larger than the 50k-row load scenario, times out, and no deployment check could have caught it, because that volume was never tested. Measures DORA's guide warns against setting its metrics as targets, and frames them as a way for one application or service to improve over time rather than a way to compare teams 3 . Each measure below is read against a baseline; this page sets no target or threshold. Change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time and deployment rework rate , as DORA names them 3 : the ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment; the time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention; and the ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production. Baseline: the same service's values before the workflow was in use. Share of runs judged with every required signal present , with could_not_run results counted by cause. Baseline: the first deployments under the workflow, since no earlier record exists. Recommended practice. Time from a regression appearing in the signals to a recorded decision. DORA lists time to detect among its measures of monitoring 4 . Baseline: the same interval in earlier incidents, where their records allow it. Recommended practice. Rollbacks that worked when used : the share of times the way back was taken and the service returned to its objectives without further action. Baseline: rollbacks before the workflow. Recommended practice. Signal quality. DORA also lists false positives and false negatives among those measures 4 ; here, halts that proved unnecessary, and deployments the run confirmed that later needed immediate intervention. Baseline: the first deployments under the workflow. Owner The workflow has one accountable owner, as every workflow does (see Workflows ), drawn from the people who run production (see Deploy ). As recommended practice, the owner changes the required signals, how thresholds are derived from objectives and the baselines, and each change is recorded as a new configuration revision. Related Release readiness : settles the record this workflow reads first. Incident feedback and incident remediation ( W27 ): read this workflow's record when something goes wrong later. Deploy , Release and Operate : the phases around it; strategies, environments and the deploy-versus-release distinction live on Deploy. Traceability spine : the link from release to incident. Workflows , Evidence schema , Validators 1 and Adapters : the Core pages behind the checks, the record and the bindings to the pipeline runner and monitoring. Workflow catalog: deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ), release readiness ( W25 ), data change execution ( W16 ) and incident remediation ( W27 ). Terminology: could_not_run , canary release and failure path . Warns against using different backing services in different environments even when adapters appear to hide the differences, because small incompatibilities let code pass tests in one environment and fail in another. ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. SAFe names the same altitudes Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team and is cited as one framework that uses them, not as the source of the labels. coined Agile Release Train (ART) SAFe's name for the train level: "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream". Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc.; this site uses "train" as the generic label for the same altitude. adopted safe-art Planning Interval (PI) SAFe's name for the planning cycle of a train: "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives". SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox, and calls the pattern of PI Planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule. Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
deploy.html: Deploy The phase that places a verified revision in an environment, confirms that it behaves there as intended and keeps a way back open, kept apart from the decision to release its behaviour to users. Purpose In the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), Deploy is the phase in which a revision that has already passed verification is placed in an environment and observed there. It answers whether that revision, running with its configuration in that environment, behaves as intended, and it keeps a way back open until the answer is settled. It produces a running revision and an evidence record of which revision went where, under which configuration, and what was seen afterwards. Deploying is not releasing. A revision can run in production while its new behaviour is still hidden from users; exposing it is a separate decision, taken in Release . The paragraph "Deploying versus releasing" below sets out the distinction with its sources, and the glossary entry deploy versus release states it in brief. Traditional practice Environments. A deployment pipeline breaks the build into stages, each giving more confidence, usually at the cost of extra time 7 . Continuous integration practice includes testing in a clone of the production environment 6 , and the Twelve-Factor App asks teams to keep development, staging and production as similar as possible 21 . The Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) treats continuous deployment as one aspect of its Continuous Delivery Pipeline 14 , one that "automates the migration of new functionality from a staging environment to production, where it is made available for release", with four activities: Deploy, Verify, Monitor and Respond 15 . Strategies. Three strategies have widely cited public descriptions. Blue-green deployment. Two production environments are kept as identical as possible, one of them live at any time, and the router is switched from one to the other 4 . Canary release. The change goes to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure 5 . Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as "a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation", in which the part receiving the change, the canary, is judged against the rest, the control 18 . Staged rollout across clusters. Google's Site Reliability Engineering book describes rollouts "to successive clusters over a period of several hours", or that start "in one cluster and expand exponentially until all clusters are updated" 17 . The same chapter says a rollout should fit the risk profile of the service 17 . Rollback. Rolling back returns an environment to what ran there before the deployment. Blue-green deployment and canary release each carry their own form of it: in blue-green deployment the router is switched back to the environment that was live before 4 , and in a canary release users are rerouted to the old version 5 . Google's SRE book counts rolling back features that demonstrate problems among the work release engineers and site reliability engineers share, beside canarying changes and pushing out new releases without interrupting services 17 . Data limits a rollback, because the previous revision may not run on a schema changed for the new one 4 ; the data changes paragraph below gives Martin Fowler's advice on that point. Configuration is the other limit: the Twelve-Factor App keeps it strictly separate from code 20 , so returning to an earlier code revision does not by itself return the configuration that ran with it. Configuration and secrets. The Twelve-Factor App calls for "strict separation of config from code", notes that "Config varies substantially across deploys, code does not", and stores config in the environment, including credentials and per-deploy values such as the canonical hostname 20 . The OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet says organisations need to centralise the storage, provisioning, auditing, rotation and management of secrets, under least privilege 13 . As recommended practice, a deployment records the configuration it ran with beside the code revision, as the evidence schema keeps a configuration revision apart from the change revision. Data changes. In his description of blue-green deployment, Fowler advises that "The trick is to separate the deployment of schema changes from application upgrades" 4 , and evolutionary database design keeps every database change as a migration script version controlled with the application code 8 . Running a migration is its own decision, in the Data change execution workflow. Deploying versus releasing. Several public sources separate the two words. SAFe says continuous deployment makes functionality "available for release" and that "it's optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing" 15 ; in its release on demand, "releases are decoupled from the work to deploy the functionality" 16 . The Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in its Adopt ring in November 2015 and April 2016; the entry is not on the current edition. The April 2016 entry recommends "strictly using the term Deployment when referring to the act of deploying a change to application components or infrastructure", says "The term Release should be used when a feature change is released to end users, with a business impact", and notes that feature toggles and dark launches let teams deploy more often without releasing features 19 . Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles on martinfowler.com, dated 9 October 2017, calls release toggles "the most common way to implement the Continuous Delivery principle of 'separating [feature] release from [code] deployment.'" 9 This page makes no claim about who drew the distinction first. This site's reading: deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment, and release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. AI-assisted practice No public study measures agents in deployment, so this section is recommended practice except where a source is named. The phase keeps the three roles every workflow uses: an agent prepares, deterministic checks settle what must not be wrong, and a person decides (see Workflows ). What moves to an agent. Once a revision runs, the signals multiply: health endpoints, error and latency measures, logs, and the difference between canary and control. An agent can read more of them than a person on watch and set out what changed, as input to a decision, not a verdict. Its task in this phase's workflow is set in the deployment and post-deploy verification row ( W26 ). What moves to a deterministic check. Whatever must not be wrong goes to a deterministic gate , a tool that answers the same way every run. SAFe lists Verify as the activity after Deploy 15 ; which checks this phase runs is set in the same catalog row. A required check that produced no result is could_not_run , a result of its own that, like a failure, prevents a positive overall status (see Evidence schema ), and silence from a health signal is never read as health. What stays with a person. The deployment decision stays with a named person, and the record carries that name; exposing the change to users belongs to Release . One operator's account of agentic AI in its site reliability work says it relies on "having consistent controls to prevent unwanted mutations of production state", and that an agentic approach "does not necessarily imply removing people from the process, specifically for higher-risk services and features" 11 . It is one organisation's description, not a study, and reports no figures. Workflows in this phase On the map, the bar under the Deploy box reads "deploy verification", which is the deployment and post-deploy verification workflow. The workflow catalog files that workflow and release readiness under its phase 6, "Release". Data change execution sits in catalog phase 3, "Develop", and incident remediation in catalog phase 7, "Operate & sustain"; both are rows from other phases that touch Deploy. Each catalog row holds the workflow's own definition; this page names and links them only. Deployment and post-deploy verification (see the Deploy verification page): the workflow that decides here. Release readiness (see the Release readiness page): settled for the same revision before deployment. Data change execution : schema migrations, apart from the application. Incident remediation : problems that surface after this phase. Gates and evidence Entry. The revision's evidence is current (see Workflows and Evidence schema ). Release readiness ( W25 ; see the Release readiness page) is settled for that same revision, and that row lists what it checks. As recommended practice, a deployment that is not ready does not start, and its record states what it is waiting for. Exit. The named person's decision is recorded with its reason, whichever way it goes. With a canary, "healthy" means judged against the control 18 , not judged alone. A could_not_run result is never a pass, so, as described above, the record cannot show the deployment as healthy while one stands. Order with release. The map draws Deploy before Release. Release readiness reads the evidence before deployment begins; exposing the change to users can come with deployment or after it, whenever a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout keeps the two apart (see Release ). Evidence. The phase leaves an evidence record in the shape the evidence schema fixes, which keeps the configuration revision apart from the change revision and holds the person's decision; the next decision reads that record, the evidence hand-off described on Workflows . In the customer-record export, a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records, the verification record for the export change is what release readiness reads, and it names the exact revision. The example also marks this phase's limit: in a hypothetical production incident, a scheduled full export, within R-017's volume limit but far larger than the 50k-row load scenario, times out. No deployment check could have caught it, because that volume was never tested. The incident, and the lesson it sends upstream along the feedback path , the site's extension of what Birgitta Böckeler calls the steering loop 1 , belong to Operate . Roles Public sources name few accountabilities here, so this section keeps to titles, which differ between organisations. The SRE book has release engineers and site reliability engineers sharing the rollout and rollback work described above 17 . The people who run production carry out the deployment and its way back. One accountable owner holds the deployment workflow, as every workflow has one (see Workflows ). A named person takes the deployment decision; the deployment and post-deploy verification row ( W26 ) records who. Exposure to users sits with Release . Pitfalls "Deployed" read as "released". New behaviour reaches users before anyone decided to expose it, though SAFe and the Radar keep the two apart 15 19 . Sign: users meet a feature before any release decision exists. A schema change shipped with the application that needs it. Fowler advises separating the two 4 ; shipped together, the old revision may not run on the new schema, and the way back closes. Sign: the only way back on record is a restore. Configuration in the code, or different by accident. Per-environment values are built in, or environments drift apart 20 21 . Sign: a change passes in staging and fails in production with no code difference. A canary with nothing to compare against. Canarying judges the canary against a control 18 ; read alone, a service-wide problem looks like a result about the change. Sign: the record holds no control measures. A missing health check read as healthy. At least one change host reports a job skipped by a condition as successful 10 , so silence passes for success unless could_not_run is its own state. Sign: fewer results than expected checks, and a positive status. An agent with standing write access to production. A wrong reading becomes a wrong action. Least privilege covers processes acting for users 12 , and one operator's account stresses controls against unwanted mutations of production state 11 . Sign: the agent's credential holds rights nobody granted for this deployment. Release toggles left in place. Hodgson describes teams that "view their Feature Toggles as inventory which comes with a carrying cost" and says release toggles "should generally not stick around much longer than a week or two" 9 . Sign: toggles unchanged long after the feature was exposed. Related Design , Develop, Build and QA , Release and Operate : the neighbouring phases. Workflows , Evidence schema and Software factory : the Core pages this phase draws on. Validators : the deterministic checks behind the gates, this site's adaptation of Birgitta Böckeler's computational sensors 2 . Adapters : the thin bindings to outside tools such as the pipeline runner, adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports-and-adapters pattern 3 . Deploy verification : whether a running revision stays or the way back is taken. Release readiness : whether a release candidate is fit to go out. Workflow catalog: deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ), release readiness ( W25 ), data change execution ( W16 ) and incident remediation ( W27 ). Terminology: could_not_run and feedback path . Sources Environments follow Martin Fowler 7 6 , the Twelve-Factor App 21 and SAFe 14 15 . Strategies and rollback draw on Fowler 4 , Danilo Sato 5 and Google's SRE workbook and book 18 17 ; configuration, secrets and data on the Twelve-Factor App 20 , OWASP 13 and Pramod Sadalage and Fowler 8 . Deploying versus releasing cites SAFe 16 , the Thoughtworks Radar 19 and Pete Hodgson 9 .
