Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
design-conformance.html: Design conformance The workflow that decides, before code is written, whether a planned technical approach is consistent with the architecture decisions, principles and constraints already on record for the system, and leaves a record that verification, release and incident review read later. Decision Is the technical approach proposed for this change consistent with the architecture decisions, principles and constraints already recorded for the system? The workflow answers that once for each revision of the plan. Its catalog entry is W08 , and the phase it closes is described on Design ; what else follows from the decision for the rest of the change is set out there and in the row. In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the plan is what an agent later builds from, so a departure that passes unnoticed here is repeated in code. The decision judges the plan, not an implementation: no code exists yet. Public practice already treats consistency with earlier decisions as something to check rather than to remember. Paula Paul and Rosemary Wang describe fitness functions as describing "how close an architecture is to achieving an architectural aim", giving continuous feedback for architectural conformance as development happens rather than after the fact 4 . Trigger A run starts when the author of a plan offers a revision of it for this decision, on a specification that has already passed Specification readiness . A plan written against a specification that has not passed carries that specification's open questions with it, so the run does not start without the readiness record ( Design ). Two later events start a fresh run, and both are this site's recommended practice. The first is a new revision of the plan; the earlier record stays with the earlier revision. The second is a change to a recorded decision the plan relies on. Michael Nygard's architecture decision records are not deleted when a decision is reversed: the old record is kept and marked superseded 9 . A plan that rests on a record later marked superseded is therefore resting on a decision the team no longer holds, and it is judged again. Inputs The run reads the plan revision itself and the records against which it is judged. The readiness record for the specification revision the plan answers, written by Specification readiness . The architecture decision records in force. Each records one significant decision with its context, status and consequences, and records are numbered without reuse 9 . The Thoughtworks Technology Radar recommends keeping them in source control beside the code 15 , which lets the run read the same set the code was built against. The rules the plan touches , read from their Rule registry entries, including how each rule is enforced ( Choosing a route ). The project configuration , which holds the project's own settings and the checks it has ( Engineering Kit ). The threat-model answers for the change. The Threat Modeling Manifesto frames threat modelling around four questions: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job? 14 OWASP's cheat sheet says threat modelling is ideally performed early, such as during the design phase, and that a threat model is maintained and refined alongside the system 10 . The plan is judged against the answers already given, not against a model written for the occasion. In the customer-record export , the site's hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records, the rule entries are R-042, the access rule on who may export which records, and R-017, the volume limit for large exports. Agent task The agent's part in this workflow is set in the catalog row W08 and is not repeated here. How the agent, the checks and people divide the work is set out under the three roles on the Workflows page. This page draws on no study of how well coding agents design, so what follows is recommended practice, as on Design . The agent prepares first versions of written design material for a person to accept or reject, and sets the plan beside the decision records and rule entries it reads, marking where the plan appears to depart from one. That comparison is advice. Birgitta Böckeler notes that language models "can partially address problems that require semantic judgment", but expensively and probabilistically, and that such checks catch problems sometimes, "but not reliably enough to reduce supervision" 1 . Independence has a public basis. NIST's Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF), task PW.2.1, asks that "1) a qualified person (or people) who were not involved with the design and/or 2) automated processes instantiated in the toolchain" review the software design to confirm that it meets all of the security requirements and addresses the identified risk information 8 . The bar is non-involvement, and the framework allows automated review in the toolchain. As this site's recommended practice, an agent that drafted the plan counts as involved in the design, so its comparison never stands in for the independent review. Checks A check here settles what a tool can decide from the plan and the records alone. It never settles whether the approach is the right one. A recorded decision, stated precisely, becomes a check. Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua introduced the architectural fitness function in Building Evolutionary Architectures 5 ; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar describes it as "an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristics", which may draw on unit tests, metrics and monitors 13 . A decision that has become such a check holds on every later change without being argued again. As recommended practice, when the run finds that a plan adds a decision of that kind, the decision is noted as a candidate for a fitness function on Validators 2 . One concern a tool can test at design time: interface contracts. In Ian Robinson's consumer-driven contracts , consumers' expectations of a service become tests that assert each expectation, so contracts are "described and enforced in a repeatable, automated fashion with each build" 11 . When a plan proposes a change to an interface, running those expectations against the proposed contract tells the provider, before anything is built, which consumer the change would break. Applying this at design time is recommended practice. Each result is one of four. A check ends passed, failed, skipped or could_not_run , the states defined under The could_not_run result . Only an explicit pass counts, and a check that never reports is not recorded as passed ( Evidence schema ). As an example, and as recommended practice: if the environment that runs consumers' contract tests 6 is unavailable, the contract check reports could_not_run. What no check settles. Whether an approach is right, given what it trades away, has no mechanical test ( Design ). That judgment belongs to the catalog's judgment-only Design and architecture review . Guardrails The agent's permissions follow the Workflows page. They rest on least privilege, which NIST's glossary gives as restricting the access privileges of users, or processes acting on behalf of users, to those needed for their assigned work 7 . The run also stops in three cases, each this site's recommended practice and each with the reason it cannot go on. The plan depends on a question the specification left open. The question goes back to the specification; it is not answered in the plan, for the reason the Specification page gives under its pitfall on ambiguity settled in code. The plan touches a rule that nothing checks. A gate proves only what its check inspects ( Rule registry ), so conformance to that rule cannot be shown by a result. The run stops and names the rule. The plan would change a check together with the code that check examines. Such a change goes to a person, as Validators describes. Human decision Who decides is set in the catalog row W08 and kept there. Where a person reviews the design, SSDF task PW.2.1, quoted under Agent task, asks for a qualified person not involved with the design 8 ; as recommended practice, the decider is therefore never the plan's author. Frameworks give the accountability different titles; in SAFe, for example, the System Architect is "responsible for defining and communicating a shared technical and architectural vision" 12 . The decider reads the plan revision, the decision records in force, the threat-model answers, the check results and the agent's comparison, which is marked as advice. That set is recommended practice. The decider may reject any departure the agent marked, or accept one the agent missed. A departure the decider accepts is not left implicit in the plan: it is recorded as a new decision record that supersedes the old one, which is how Nygard's practice handles a reversed decision 9 . When the people deciding disagree on a trade-off rather than on conformance, the question goes to the judgment-only Design and architecture review . Outputs and evidence The run leaves one record for the plan revision, in the shape the Evidence schema fixes: the check results, the agent's findings with the decision on each, the decider's name and conclusion, and any decision records the run produced. New and superseding architecture decision records sit beside the code, where later readers find them 15 . Who reads the record Pull-request verification reads it to judge code against the plan that was accepted, not against a plan as someone remembers it. Task traceability and test planning (catalog W12 ) builds its tasks from the accepted plan. Release readiness reads it when it checks that the evidence for a release candidate is complete ( Evidence schema ). Incident feedback opens it when a production miss is traced back, to see whether the plan foresaw the case and who accepted it. The workflow's owner reads the records together for the measures below. In the customer-record export On Design , the volume-limit rule R-017 is checked by a 50k-row load scenario rather than left to a sentence in the plan. This workflow adds a limit on what the decision can see. It judges the plan, so it cannot catch the background worker's broader query, which does not exist until code is written. That query is caught later, when the access validator for R-042 fails on the first pull request ( Develop, Build and QA ). The design record shows what the plan committed to; the verification record shows where the code departed from it. Failure paths The general failure paths every workflow shares are on Workflows . For this decision they take the following form, each with who acts next; the routing is recommended practice. A check fails. The plan does not pass as it stands. Next: the plan's author revises it, and the revision starts a new run. A check could not run. The record cannot reach a positive status, and the result is not read as a fault in the plan. Next: the owner of the tool or environment restores it, and the check runs again on the same revision. The agent stops. The run halts on one of the cases under Guardrails. Next: the specification's owner for an open question; the rule's owner for a rule that nothing checks; the owner of the check for a plan that would change it. Measures This page draws on no study of measuring design conformance, so each measure below is recommended practice, is read against a baseline and carries no target value. DORA advises setting a baseline for current performance and improving over time, and warns that metrics set as goals invite gaming 3 ; DORA says this of its own delivery metrics, and the site borrows it here by analogy. Design departures first found at pull-request review or later. Findings that code breaks a recorded decision, where the plan already showed the departure. Fitness function-driven development aims for feedback "as it happens, rather than after the fact" 4 , and a falling count shows the departure is being found earlier. Baseline: the same team's count before the workflow ran. Interface breaks found after merge. Changes that broke a consumer's stated expectation once merged. Baseline: the count before the workflow ran. Time from plan offered to recorded decision. Baseline: the first period in which the workflow runs, read so that a growing wait is noticed before people route around it. Owner One accountable owner answers for the workflow, distinct from the person who decides each run ( Workflows ). As recommended practice, the owner is the person accountable for the system's technical direction, who keeps the recorded decisions and principles current and changes what the workflow checks. Related Specification readiness : the workflow whose record this one reads. Pull-request verification : the workflow that judges code against the accepted plan. Release readiness and Incident feedback : later readers of the record. Design : the phase this workflow closes; Specification and Develop, Build and QA : the phases on either side. Core: Workflows , Rule registry , Validators , Engineering Kit , Evidence schema and Harness engineering . Workflow catalog: W08 , API contract design W09 , data model and migration plan W10 , security design review W11 , task traceability and test planning W12 and design and architecture review W24 . Sources Architecture decision records: Michael Nygard 9 and the Thoughtworks Technology Radar 15 . Fitness functions: Ford, Parsons and Kua 5 , the Thoughtworks Technology Radar 13 and Paul and Wang 4 . Interface contracts: Ian Robinson on consumer-driven contracts 11 . Threat modelling: the Threat Modeling Manifesto 14 and OWASP's Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet 10 . Independent design review: NIST SP 800-218, SSDF version 1.1 8 . Agents' semantic review: Birgitta Böckeler on harness engineering 1 . Least privilege: the NIST glossary 7 . Framework title for technical direction: Scaled Agile's System Architect page 12 . Baselines and targets: DORA's software delivery performance metrics 3 . Validators as computational sensors: Birgitta Böckeler on maintainability sensors 2 . Contract tests: Martin Fowler 6 . The re-run triggers, the agent's comparison, the design-time contract check and its example, the stop cases, the decider's evidence set, the failure routing, the measures and the owner are this site's recommended practice; no public source states them. Harness engineering for coding agent users — Birgitta Böckeler, Thoughtworks, published on martinfowler.com — 2026-04-02 · source Defines the harness as everything in an agent except the model, and introduces guides (feedforward) and sensors (feedback), computational vs inferential controls, the steering loop, harnessability, harness templates and three regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour), and discusses ambient affordances. ↩ ↩ Maintainability sensors for coding agents — Birgitta Böckeler, Thoughtworks, published on martinfowler.com — 2026-05 · source Worked examples of computational and inferential sensors on a real codebase. ↩ ↩ DORA's software delivery performance metrics — Nathen Harvey, DORA, published on dora.dev — last updated 2026-01-05 (as printed) · source Names five software delivery performance metrics in two groups: throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate). Failed deployment recovery time is a throughput metric on this page. The page https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys/ redirects here. Cited for DORA's software delivery performance metrics. Defines change fail rate as the ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment; failed deployment recovery time as the time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention; and deployment rework rate as the ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production. Advises setting a baseline for an application's current performance and improving over time, not competing against other teams or organizations; says the metrics are meant to be applied at the application or service level; lists 'Setting metrics as a goal' among its pitfalls and warns, citing Goodhart's law, that metrics set as goals invite gaming. ↩ ↩ Fitness function-driven development — Paula Paul, Rosemary Wang, Thoughtworks, published on thoughtworks.com (Insights) — 2019-01 · source Architecture goals expressed as executable tests, written first in the manner of test-driven development, giving continuous feedback on architectural conformance during development rather than after. What this site calls architecture gates. ↩ ↩ ↩ Building Evolutionary Architectures: Support Constant Change — Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, O'Reilly Media — 2017 · source Introduces architectural fitness functions, an objective integrity assessment of an architectural characteristic, implemented through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms; the term is borrowed from evolutionary computing. A second edition with Pramod Sadalage (2022) is subtitled Automated Software Governance. ↩ ↩ Contract Test — Martin Fowler, martinfowler.com (bliki) — 2011-01-12 · source Contract tests check that calls against a test double return the same results as the real external service would. They run separately from the regular pipeline, at the rhythm of changes to the external service, and a failure triggers work to restore consistency. Originally titled 'Integration Contract Test'. ↩ ↩ least privilege — National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST Computer Security Resource Center, Glossary — not printed · source Glossary entry giving four definitions with their sources. The NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 definition, taken from CNSSI 4009-2022, is the principle that a security architecture is designed so that each entity is granted the minimum system resources and authorizations it needs to perform its function. The SP 800-12 Rev. 1 definition, taken from CNSSI 4009, calls least privilege a security principle that a system should restrict the access privileges of users, or processes acting on behalf of users, to those needed for their assigned work. ↩ ↩ Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1: Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities — Murugiah Souppaya, Karen Scarfone, Donna Dodson, NIST Special Publication 800-218 — 2022-02 · source NIST SP 800-218 version 1.1, final (3 February 2022); practice and task identifiers checked in the PDF (https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218). Tasks relied on: PO.1.2 (identify and document all security requirements for organization-developed software to meet, and maintain the requirements over time); PO.3.3 (configure tools to generate artifacts of their support of secure development practices); PS.1.1 (store all forms of code according to least privilege); PS.3.1 (securely archive the files of each release); PS.3.2 (collect, safeguard, maintain and share provenance data); PW.1.1 (use forms of risk modeling, such as threat modeling, attack modeling or attack surface mapping); PW.2.1 (have a qualified person or people who were not involved with the design review the software design); PW.6.1 (use compilers, interpreters and build tools with security features); PW.7.1 and PW.7.2 (decide which code review or analysis to use, perform it in line with secure coding standards, and record and triage the issues found). Also the vulnerability-response practices RV.1 'Identify and Confirm Vulnerabilities on an Ongoing Basis', RV.2 'Assess, Prioritize, and Remediate Vulnerabilities' and RV.3 'Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes'. Version 1.2 (SP 800-218 Rev. 1) exists only as an initial public draft (published 2025-12-17, comments closed 2026-01-30); no final Rev. 1 was found on 2026-11-20, so version 1.1 is cited as the final. Practice PO.1: ensure that security requirements for software development are known at all times so that they can be taken into account throughout the SDLC and duplication of effort can be minimized because the requirements information can be collected once and shared. PS.3.2 examples include making provenance data available to the organization's operations and response teams to aid them in mitigating software vulnerabilities. RV.1.1: gather information from software acquirers, users and public sources on potential vulnerabilities, and investigate all credible reports. RV.3.1: analyze identified vulnerabilities to determine their root causes; RV.3.2: analyze the root causes over time to identify patterns; RV.3.4: review the SDLC process and update it if appropriate to prevent (or reduce the likelihood of) the root cause recurring. ↩ ↩ ↩ Documenting Architecture Decisions — Michael Nygard, Cognitect blog — 2011-11-15 · source Proposes architecture decision records: short, sequentially numbered records (title, context, decision, status, consequences) whose numbers are not reused; a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded. ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet — not printed (page footer credits 'Cheat Sheets Series Team'), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — not printed · source Breaks threat modeling into four basic steps: application decomposition, threat identification and ranking, mitigations, and review and validation, guided by the four Threat Modeling Manifesto questions. Tab title: 'Threat Modeling - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series'. ↩ ↩ Consumer-Driven Contracts: A Service Evolution Pattern — Ian Robinson, martinfowler.com — 2006-06-12 · source Describes provider contracts and consumer-driven contracts: consumers state their expectations of a service, the provider verifies them, and the service evolves without breaking its consumers. ↩ ↩ System Architect — not printed, Scaled Agile, Inc. — not printed in readable text · source Describes the role as responsible for defining and communicating a shared technical and architectural vision for the solutions developed by an Agile Release Train , by defining enablers, participating in solution definition and outlining non-functional requirements. ↩ ↩ Architectural fitness function — Thoughtworks Technology Advisory Board, Thoughtworks Technology Radar, Volumes 17 and 18 (archived entry) — 2017-11 and 2018-05 (Trial) · source Radar entry restating the Building Evolutionary Architectures definition of an architectural fitness function and noting it may encompass existing verification criteria such as unit tests, metrics and monitors. ↩ ↩ Threat Modeling Manifesto — Working group: Zoe Braiterman, Adam Shostack, Jonathan Marcil, Stephen de Vries, Irene Michlin, Kim Wuyts, Robert Hurlbut, Brook S.E. Schoenfield, Fraser Scott, Matthew Coles, Chris Romeo, Alyssa Miller, Izar Tarandach, Avi Douglen, Marc French, Threat Modeling Manifesto working group — not printed · source Authors in the order printed on the page. States that when the working group threat models, it asks four key questions: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job? No publication date is printed on the page or its linked PDF; licensed CC BY 4.0. ↩ ↩ Lightweight Architecture Decision Records — Thoughtworks, Thoughtworks Technology Radar, Volumes 17 and 18 (archived entry) — 2017-11 and 2018-05 (Adopt; earlier Trial in Volumes 15 and 16) · source Radar technique in the Adopt ring recommending that architecture decision records, with their context and consequences, be kept in source control alongside the code rather than in a wiki. ↩ ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. SAFe names the same altitudes Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team and is cited as one framework that uses them, not as the source of the labels. coined Agile Release Train (ART) SAFe's name for the train level: "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream". Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc.; this site uses "train" as the generic label for the same altitude. adopted safe-art Planning Interval (PI) SAFe's name for the planning cycle of a train: "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives". SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox, and calls the pattern of PI Planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule. Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
design.html: Design Design settles how a specified change is to be built and records the decisions and trade-offs behind that approach; an agent prepares first versions of the written design, while trade-off judgments stay with people. Purpose Design is the phase in which an accepted specification becomes a plan for building it. The phase chooses a technical approach, weighs what that approach trades away, and records the decisions taken so that a later reader can see what was chosen and why. Its central decision is design conformance ( W08 ), which the workflow catalog titles Plan and architecture conformance. In the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the plan is also what an agent builds from. Whatever the plan leaves open, an agent building from it decides on its own, so settling the approach in the plan is recommended practice. The site's account of risk tiers , which the phase works with, is under Risk tiers: same definition, different cost on the Workflows page. Traditional practice Without agents, people settle design in documents and review meetings. The practices that hold up best leave a record that a later reader can check. Trade-offs. The Software Engineering Institute's Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) is "a structured technique for understanding the tradeoffs inherent in the architectures of software-intensive systems" 17 ; its 2000 description includes a step in which scenarios are brainstormed and then prioritised by voting 18 . Recording decisions. Michael Nygard's architecture decision records capture one significant decision each, with its context, the decision, its status and its consequences. They are numbered in sequence, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited 10 . Security design. The Threat Modeling Manifesto's working group poses four questions: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job? 20 OWASP's cheat sheet breaks threat modeling into four basic steps: application decomposition, threat identification and ranking, mitigations, and review and validation 12 . NIST's Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF), version 1.1, asks teams to "use forms of risk modeling – such as threat modeling, attack modeling, or attack surface mapping" (task PW.1.1) 9 . Independent review. The same framework asks that a qualified person, or people, who were not involved with the design review the software design (task PW.2.1) 9 . Security requirements. SSDF task PO.1.2 asks that security requirements be identified and documented and maintained over time 9 . Design reads them as an input: the security design is the team's answer to them. Data design. Evolutionary database design represents every change to the database as a migration script, version-controlled together with the application code changes 7 . Fowler's description of blue-green deployment adds that the trick is to separate the deployment of schema changes from application upgrades 5 . Contracts. In Ian Robinson's consumer-driven contracts , the consumers of a service state their expectations, the provider is checked against them, and the service can then change without breaking its consumers 13 . Martin Fowler's contract tests check that a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for 6 . Agreeing an interface before either side builds against it is recommended practice rather than a cited standard. Proportion. Effort scales with risk. Risk-based testing bases the management, selection, prioritisation and use of test activities and resources on risk types and risk levels 8 . OWASP's Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) gives a published precedent for choosing a level of rigour by risk: an organisation should analyse its risks and decide what level it should be at, where level 1 holds the minimum requirements, level 2 is what most applications should strive for, and level 3 is for applications that need to demonstrate the highest levels of security 11 . Executable architecture. Architecture goals written as executable checks are fitness functions: objective assessments of how well a system keeps an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics and similar mechanisms 4 3 . They let a structural decision made at design time be checked on every later change. AI-assisted practice What changes first is who writes the first version. No public study was found that measures how well coding agents design, so this section describes recommended practice, not a finding. In that practice an agent prepares first versions of the phase's written material, such as candidate decision records, first answers to the threat-modeling questions and proposed interface or schema changes, each for a person to accept or reject. The agent's part in the central decision belongs to design conformance ( W08 ) and is not restated here; what follows is how the work divides among the site's three roles of agent, checks and people. Constraints on the drafting. Rules can bind the agent while it writes. One open-source spec-driven toolkit gives the agent a constitution of principles that includes a simplicity gate and an anti-abstraction gate, and states that the model "cannot proceed without either passing the gates or documenting justified exceptions" in a section that tracks complexity 19 . A departure then has to be argued in writing instead of entering the plan unnoticed. What moves to a deterministic check. A design decision that can be stated precisely can be checked by a machine on every later change instead of being remembered. Fitness functions turn an architectural goal into such a check 4 3 , and in consumer-driven contracts the consumers' stated expectations of an interface become tests the provider is run against 13 . As recommended practice, each design decision that can be written as a check is written as one, so that the decision holds whether or not an agent that later builds from the plan has read the reasoning behind it. In the customer-record export , the volume-limit rule R-017 is checked by a 50k-row load scenario rather than left to a sentence in the plan (see Validators ). What stays with a person. Whether an approach is right, given what it trades away, has no mechanical test. Birgitta Böckeler notes that inferential sensors, which use a model to judge the work, address semantic concerns only partially 1 , so an agent's review of a design is advice to the person who decides and never an approval (see Workflows ). The catalog keeps the trade-off decision as a judgment-only workflow, Design and architecture review , which stays with a person. As recommended practice, an agent that drafted a plan counts as involved in the design in the sense of SSDF task PW.2.1 9 , so it cannot serve as the independent reviewer of that plan. Workflows in this phase The workflow catalog uses its own phase names. The rows for this phase sit under the catalog's phase 2, "Plan & design": Plan and architecture conformance (see the Design conformance page): the phase's central decision, which the map draws as the bar labelled "design conformance". API contract design , Data model and migration plan and Security design review : specialist decisions within the phase. Task traceability and test planning : the last row of the catalog phase, where design meets the build. One further decision about design sits elsewhere in the catalog. Design and architecture review is filed under the catalog's phase 5, "Review". It is judgment-only and stays with a person. Gates and evidence Entry. Design starts from a specification that has passed its readiness decision, Specification readiness . The Specification page describes that phase and the readiness criteria behind it. A plan written against a specification that has not passed inherits its open questions. Exit. The phase ends with the design conformance decision ( W08 ; see the Design conformance page), taken by a named person; what that decision covers is set out in its catalog row. The exit leaves an evidence record in the common shape the Evidence schema sets. Decision records. A significant design decision leaves an architecture decision record; when a later change reverses it, the old record stays, marked superseded 10 . Review records. As recommended practice, the independent design review that the SSDF asks for 9 leaves an evidence record naming the reviewer, the conclusion and the revision of the plan reviewed. The Evidence schema fixes the fields; this page adds none. Roles Who owns the plan and who decides at each of the phase's gates is recorded in the catalog rows linked above, so the assignment is kept in one place. Each workflow has one accountable owner, and every decision is recorded under the name of the person who made it. Public frameworks set two accountabilities that bear on the phase. The SSDF asks that the design be reviewed by a qualified person, or people, who were not involved with it 9 , which keeps the author of a design and its reviewer apart. In SAFe, the system architect is "responsible for defining and communicating a shared technical and architectural vision for the solutions developed by an ART" 15 , that is, by an Agile Release Train 14 . Pitfalls The agent's summary taken as the design review. Sign: the review record holds the agent's summary and an approval, and nothing of the reviewer's own. See the pitfalls in Workflows . Complexity the change does not need. A plan adds layers, abstractions or options that no requirement asks for. The simplicity and anti-abstraction gates of the toolkit cited above, with justified exceptions written down, are one public answer 19 ; treating unrequested structure as a finding is recommended practice. Sign: a new abstraction with no recorded reason. A schema or interface change made without its safeguards. Sign: a schema change ships in the same deployment as the code that needs it, against the advice to deploy the two separately 5 ; a migration exists only as a manual step rather than as a versioned script beside the code 7 ; or a provider changes an interface without checking its consumers' stated expectations 13 . Decisions left unrecorded. Sign: the same design argument returns on later changes, and nobody can find why the current approach was chosen. A short decision record per significant choice, kept and superseded rather than edited 10 , is the recommended practice. Related Specification : the phase before Design, whose accepted specification is Design's input. Develop, Build and QA : the phase after Design, where the checks run. Definition of Ready and Definition of Done : the entrance and exit criteria around the phases. The Definition of Done is the Scrum Guide's formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product 16 . Workflows : the decision unit, the three roles and how risk tiers work. Rule registry : rules and their routes. Engineering Kit : the project configuration that holds which checks run. Harness engineering : computational and inferential controls. Validators : the deterministic checks that hold design decisions on later changes. Evidence schema : the fixed shape of every evidence record. Design conformance : whether a planned approach fits the decisions already on record. Workflow catalog rows W08 , W12 and W24 . Terminology: Risk tier . Sources Trade-off analysis: the SEI's 1998 ATAM report 17 and its 2000 report, cited for scenario prioritisation 18 . Decision records: Michael Nygard 10 . Security design and independent review: the Threat Modeling Manifesto 20 , OWASP's Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet 12 and NIST SP 800-218, SSDF version 1.1 9 . Data and contracts: Sadalage and Fowler on evolutionary database design 7 , Fowler on blue-green deployment 5 , Ian Robinson on consumer-driven contracts 13 and Fowler on contract tests 6 . Scaling effort to risk: the ISTQB glossary 8 and OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 11 . Fitness functions: Ford, Parsons and Kua 4 and Paul and Wang 3 . Agents and controls: an open-source spec-driven toolkit 19 and Birgitta Böckeler on harness engineering 1 . SAFe: Scaled Agile's System Architect page 15 and its Agile Release Train page 14 . Definition of Done: the 2020 Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland 16 . Validators: this site's adaptation of Birgitta Böckeler's computational sensors 2 . Harness engineering for coding agent users — Birgitta Böckeler, Thoughtworks, published on martinfowler.com — 2026-04-02 · source Defines the harness as everything in an agent except the model, and introduces guides (feedforward) and sensors (feedback), computational vs inferential controls, the steering loop, harnessability, harness templates and three regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour), and discusses ambient affordances. ↩ ↩ Maintainability sensors for coding agents — Birgitta Böckeler, Thoughtworks, published on martinfowler.com — 2026-05 · source Worked examples of computational and inferential sensors on a real codebase. ↩ Fitness function-driven development — Paula Paul, Rosemary Wang, Thoughtworks, published on thoughtworks.com (Insights) — 2019-01 · source Architecture goals expressed as executable tests, written first in the manner of test-driven development, giving continuous feedback on architectural conformance during development rather than after. What this site calls architecture gates. ↩ ↩ ↩ Building Evolutionary Architectures: Support Constant Change — Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, O'Reilly Media — 2017 · source Introduces architectural fitness functions , an objective integrity assessment of an architectural characteristic, implemented through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms; the term is borrowed from evolutionary computing. A second edition with Pramod Sadalage (2022) is subtitled Automated Software Governance. ↩ ↩ ↩ Blue Green Deployment — Martin Fowler, martinfowler.com (bliki) — 1 March 2010 (page also records an update on 2015-06-05 adding the database paragraph) · source Describes two production environments kept as identical as possible, one of them live at any time; the switch is made at the router, and rollback is switching it back. On databases, says the trick is to separate the deployment of schema changes from application upgrades. ↩ ↩ ↩ Contract Test — Martin Fowler, martinfowler.com (bliki) — 2011-01-12 · source Contract tests check that calls against a test double return the same results as the real external service would. They run separately from the regular pipeline, at the rhythm of changes to the external service, and a failure triggers work to restore consistency.
