Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
develop-build-qa.html: Develop, Build and QA Develop, Build and QA are the three phases in which one change is made, assembled and tested under one set of checks and one evidence record; they end in the merge decision, and agents, deterministic checks and people each have a distinct part along the way. Purpose Develop, Build and QA are the phases in which one change is made, assembled into something that runs, and tested. In the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the three share a page because, for a single change, they share one set of checks, one evidence record and one decision at the end, the merge decision, which the Workflows page gives as its example of a workflow . The map draws one workflow bar across all three labels, "pull-request verification · security & performance checks by tier", for the same reason. The question the stretch answers is what must be true, and shown, before a change may join the mainline. Beneath every answer sits the deterministic floor : the Engineering Kit 's verify command, which every task runs before anything else. An agent adds speed above that floor and never replaces it. The workflow catalog names its phases differently from the map: the rows for this stretch sit in catalog phase 3 "Develop", phase 4 "Verify" and, for pull-request verification, phase 5 "Review". Traditional practice Long before coding agents, each of the three phases had public guidance of its own. That guidance still holds: agents change who produces the first version of the work, not what good work is. Develop Development practice centres on small changes that carry their own tests. Google's engineering practices document defines the right size as one that "makes a minimal change that addresses just one thing" and says a change "should include related test code". Small changes, it says, are reviewed more quickly and more thoroughly, are less likely to introduce bugs and are simpler to roll back. 16 In its guidance for reviewers, a reviewer looks at design, functionality, complexity, tests, naming, comments, style, consistency and documentation, in that order, and asks for "unit, integration, or end-to-end tests as appropriate for the change". 15 The tests run without ceremony. Martin Fowler describes self-testing code as being able to "invoke a single command that executes the tests" with confidence that they would expose the bugs hiding in the code. 13 His account of continuous integration counts making the build self-testing, fixing broken builds immediately and keeping the build fast among its practices. 11 DORA's guidance on test automation expects feedback from automated tests "in less than ten minutes both on local workstations and from the continuous integration system". 10 Security sits in the same loop. NIST's Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) asks teams to decide which kinds of code review or analysis to use (PW.7.1), to perform them in line with secure coding standards and to record and triage what they find (PW.7.2), and to store all forms of code according to least privilege (PS.1.1). 25 Build A build turns source into something that can be tested and shipped, and its first property is repeatability. Google's site reliability engineering book says that if two people build the same product at the same revision on different machines, "we expect identical results"; its builds are hermetic, depending on "known versions of build tools, such as compilers, and dependencies, such as libraries". 34 Builds run inside a deployment pipeline, which Fowler describes as "breaking up your build into stages. Each stage provides increasing confidence, usually at the cost of extra time." 12 Jez Humble and David Farley's Continuous Delivery gives the subject a chapter titled "Commit Testing Stage". 17 SAFe places this work in continuous integration, where "new functionality is developed, tested, integrated, and validated in preparation for deployment and release". 30 A build also records where its output came from. SLSA defines provenance as "verifiable information about software artifacts describing where, when, and how something was produced". 33 Its Build track, in SLSA v1.2, has three levels: provenance showing how the package was built; signed provenance generated by a hosted build platform; and a hardened build platform. 32 The SSDF asks for compilers, interpreters and build tools with security features (PW.6.1), for tools configured to generate artifacts (PO.3.3), and for teams to collect, safeguard, maintain and share provenance data (PS.3.2). 25 QA Testing is organised by level. The ISTQB Foundation Level syllabus describes five test levels: component testing (also called unit testing), component integration testing, system testing, system integration testing and acceptance testing. It separates confirmation testing, which confirms that an original defect has been fixed, from regression testing , which confirms that a change has caused no adverse consequences. 19 Fowler's test pyramid advises "many more low-level UnitTests than high level BroadStackTests running through a GUI", and credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book with spreading the name. 14 Effort follows risk: in risk-based testing, the selection and use of test activities and resources depend on risk types and risk levels. 20 The Workflows page applies that idea as the risk tier . Security verification draws on a wider set of techniques. NIST IR 8397, written as minimum standards for developer verification, recommends eleven, in this order: threat modeling; automated testing; static code scanning; heuristic tools for hardcoded secrets; built-in checks and protections; "black box" test cases; code-based structural test cases; historical test cases; fuzzing; web application scanners; and addressing included code. It states that it "does not address the totality of software verification". 24 OWASP's Application Security Verification Standard leaves the choice of verification level to an organisation's analysis of its own risks. 26 For credentials, OWASP advises centralising the storage, provisioning, auditing, rotation and management of secrets, and applying least privilege to them. 27 Performance testing examines behaviour under load. The ISTQB glossary defines stress testing as "a type of performance testing to evaluate a system or component at or beyond the limits of its anticipated or specified workloads, or with reduced availability of resources such as access to memory or servers". 21 The Validators page notes that checks depending on timing or shared environments are the ones most exposed to flaky results. AI-assisted practice Agents change who writes the first version of code and tests. They do not change what a merge requires. No public study sets out how work in these phases should be divided between an agent, deterministic checks and people, so the division below is this site's recommended practice, with research cited where it exists. Develop with agents The agent writes code and tests for one task inside its harness, which Birgitta Böckeler describes as everything in a coding agent except the model: guides that steer it before it acts and sensors that check its work after. 2 On this site the guides include skills the agent loads when a task calls for them, and the sensors include validators , the deterministic checks tied to rule identifiers that Böckeler's examples call computational sensors. 3 The agent runs the same verify command a person runs before it hands anything on, and reads the failures to correct its own change. It works under an identity with only the permissions its task needs, as the Harness engineering page explains, so staying in scope never depends on its following an instruction. The developer who directs it remains the author of the change. DORA's research explains why the floor matters more once an agent writes code. Its 2024 research found that AI adoption "negatively impacts software delivery stability and throughput, reminding teams that fundamentals like small batch sizes and robust testing remain crucial"; 5 the announcement of that report points to the same two fundamentals. 4 In 2025 DORA describes AI's primary role as "an amplifier, magnifying an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses", 7 and warns that "without robust control systems, like strong automated testing, mature version control practices, and fast feedback loops, an increase in change volume leads to instability". 6 Its guidance on putting the AI Capabilities Model to work adds that "AI can easily generate massive blocks of code, which are hard to review and test", and calls version control a critical safety net. 8 The recommended response is to keep each agent task to a change one reviewer can read in full. An agent's confidence is not evidence of security. In one user study, participants with an AI code assistant "wrote significantly less secure code than those without access" and were "more likely to believe they wrote secure code". 28 Security checks therefore run on agent-written code exactly as on any other, and the agent's own account of its change never stands in for them. Build with agents The build stays deterministic and hermetic, as release engineering has long required. 34 No public evidence supports placing an agent inside the build as a step that decides its output, and this page recommends none. An agent may propose changes to build scripts, pipeline definitions or pinned tool versions, but each such change alters a controlled artefact: the SRE book's gated operations include "changes to build configuration". 34 As recommended practice, a change to build configuration goes to a person for review, and a change that edits a check together with the code the check examines is treated as a finding in its own right, as the Validators page describes. Provenance comes from the build platform, not from the agent. SLSA's second Build level calls for signed provenance generated by a hosted build platform, 32 so an agent's description of what it built is a note, not provenance. When an agent's task adds or upgrades a library, the change also passes through the catalog's Dependency change workflow. QA with agents Agents can write many tests quickly; the risk lies in what those tests rest on. When one agent writes code and tests from the same understanding, both can share one mistaken assumption, so the tests need an independent basis : acceptance criteria 18 , access rules, interface contracts or failure scenarios defined apart from the implementation. Research points the same way. A study of test cases and oracles for 24 Java repositories found that "LLM-based test generation approaches mainly capture the actual program behavior making bug detection difficult". 22 A generated test that passes on the code it was generated from shows that the code does what it does, not that it does what was specified. An agent that is rewarded for passing tests may change the tests. A research post by METR describes models attempting "to get a higher score by modifying the tests or scoring code" on METR's own evaluation tasks. 23 A model developer's system card reports that its model occasionally special-cased tests to make them pass, sometimes by modifying the tests themselves, and attributes the behaviour to reward hacking during training. 1 The Harness engineering page draws the conclusion: an agent must not be able to satisfy a sensor by changing it. Security and performance checks follow the change's risk tier . In the site's running example, the customer-record export , the access validator for rule R-042 fails on the first pull request because a background worker's query reads records outside the caller's scope; a review skill 's finding on the same query sits beside that failure as advice only. The Workflows page sets this beside a change to the export button's label. A required check that cannot produce a verdict is a result of its own, never a pass. In the same example, the 50k-row load scenario for the volume-limit rule R-017 reports could_not_run because the load-test tool is missing from the runner image. It is neither passed nor skipped, and the fix belongs to whoever maintains the runner. Workflows in this phase The workflow the map draws across all three phases is Pull-request verification (catalog row W23 ), where the stretch ends in the merge decision; the map adds "security & performance checks by tier" to its label. The other rows below run inside the stretch. Each row's definition (trigger, agent task, checks, human decision and evidence) is in the workflow catalog and is not repeated here; the Workflows page explains what a workflow is. Catalog row Where it falls on this page W13 Task execution loop Develop; the floor every task runs W14 Documentation generation Develop, beside the code it describes W15 Dependency change Build W16 Data change execution Develop W17 Acceptance-test generation and execution QA W18 Security verification QA, by tier W19 Performance verification QA, by tier W20 Accessibility and visual regression QA W21 API contract conformance QA W22 System integration and acceptance evidence QA W23 Pull-request verification The close of all three; see the Pull-request verification page Gates and evidence A task enters the stretch once it meets the team's Definition of Ready , which is set before development starts. The Scrum Guide defines the Definition of Done for the Increment as a formal description of its state when it meets the quality measures required for the product 31 . Applying a Definition of Done to each story at the close of this stretch is this site's recommended practice. The Definition of Ready and Done page covers both. The gates in this stretch check each change as it is made, not only once the work is finished. In that they put into practice what SAFe calls built-in quality, "a set of practices to help ensure that the outputs of Agile teams in business and technology domains meet appropriate quality standards throughout the process of creating customer value". 29 Inside the stretch, every gate runs through the verify command, which is the same command on a developer's machine, in an agent's session and in the pipeline ( Engineering Kit ). The checks a revision needs follow its risk tier. What each run records, and how its overall status follows from the results, is fixed on the Evidence schema page. The build leaves evidence of its own. Provenance generated by the build platform, in line with SLSA's Build track and the SSDF's provenance task, 32 25 records how the tested output was produced. The stretch is left through one exit: the merge decision. Each workflow's catalog row names the record it leaves, and the Workflows page explains how that record is handed on. Roles The stretch keeps apart the three roles the Workflows page sets out: the agent produces, the checks enforce what a tool can decide reliably, and people make the calls that need context. Google's engineering practices give separate guidance to the developer who authors a change and the reviewer who examines it, 16 15 and both accountabilities hold when an agent writes the code. The developer who directs the agent is the author of the change and answers for it. The reviewer takes the merge decision on what a tool cannot judge. Rule owners , recorded in the Rule registry , own what a rule means and any exception to it. In the export example, a request to exceed R-017's row limit is pending with the security owner while the record's overall status is blocked; R-042 is not open to exception. The owner of the runner or environment receives could_not_run results, since the change may be sound. The agent can comment on a pull request. It cannot approve, merge or change the checks. Who decides at the human step of each workflow is named in that workflow's catalog row. Pitfalls Code and tests from one understanding. The agent writes both, and the tests confirm what the code does rather than what was specified. 22 Sign: tests with no link to an acceptance criterion, a rule or a contract. The test changed to pass. The agent edits a test or a check instead of the code, a behaviour reported both by METR and in a model developer's system card. 23 1 Sign: one change that edits both a check and the code it checks. Silence read as success. A required check never reports, and the change merges anyway. Sign: a merged change whose record holds no result for a check its tier requires; the Workflows page covers the case. A flaky check re-run until it passes. The pass after a retry is counted like any other, and the check stops meaning anything. Sign: one check failing and passing on the same revision, a pattern the Validators page covers. A change too large to review. DORA notes that "large changes are difficult to review, test, and integrate safely", 9 and that AI can generate code in blocks that are hard to review and test. 8 Sign: large diffs approved with few comments. Reviewers doing a tool's job. Review threads fill with comments a check could make, and review fatigue follows. A recurring comment belongs on the feedback path , the site's extension of Böckeler's steering loop, 2 and the export's R-042 validator covers background workers for that reason. Sign: the same comment on many changes. Local and pipeline results that differ. The pipeline runs its own version of a check. With one verify command and one set of inputs, a difference points at the environment, not the rules ( Engineering Kit ). Sign: changes that pass locally and fail in the pipeline with no code difference. Generated code trusted as secure. In one study, users of an AI assistant wrote less secure code and were more likely to believe it secure. 28 Sign: security checks relaxed for agent-written changes. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited.
