Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. SAFe names the same altitudes Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team and is cited as one framework that uses them, not as the source of the labels. coined Agile Release Train (ART) SAFe's name for the train level: "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream". Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc.; this site uses "train" as the generic label for the same altitude. adopted safe-art Planning Interval (PI) SAFe's name for the planning cycle of a train: "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives". SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox, and calls the pattern of PI Planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule. Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
intake-and-triage.html: Intake and triage The workflow that decides whether an arriving request, report or lesson is taken on now, as it stands or broken into smaller items, with an agent's first reading offered as input and the decision recorded under a person's name. Decision Is this arriving item taken on now, and if so in what form: as it stands, or broken into smaller items first? Intake and triage is the workflow that answers that question in an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), once for every item that reaches a team's backlog. "Triage" carries its ordinary meaning here: sorting what arrives by kind and urgency. How an admitted item then ranks against the rest is a separate call, the ordering of a backlog the Scrum Guide describes as "an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product" 8 . The catalog row Intake and classification states the decision in the catalog's own terms; this page adds how a run proceeds, how it fails, what it records and how a team can tell whether it works. The decision is not limited to new features. For a reported defect, the ISTQB glossary defines defect management as "the process of recognizing, recording, classifying, investigating, fixing and disposing of defects" 6 . Read against that sequence, this workflow does the classifying: the report has been recorded, and nobody has started to investigate it yet. Trigger A run starts when an item arrives in the backlog. Items arrive from more than one direction, and public guidance stands behind each of the main ones. DORA asks whether a team actively and regularly gathers feedback from users and acts on it 2 ; in this site's catalog, those signals are handled by Usage and feedback intake . NIST's Secure Software Development Framework recommends gathering information from software acquirers, users and public sources on potential vulnerabilities and investigating all credible reports 7 , which the catalog covers in Vulnerability response . Lessons from production come back through the Incident feedback workflow. An item already admitted gets a fresh run when its content changes materially, because the earlier decision was taken about a different item; this is recommended practice. An incident that is still in progress is not a trigger at all. It belongs to incident handling, as the Guardrails section below explains. Inputs A run reads five things: The item as written , including who raised it and whose need it says it serves. The backlog it would join. Because the backlog is ordered 8 , the run can show the decider where the item would sit and which items already there look like it. Earlier items it may repeat , open or closed. Searching them before admission is recommended practice; no public source sets a method. The rules its subject touches , looked up in the rule registry , so that an item that reaches a rule with an owner is visible as such before anyone sizes it. The work already in progress. DORA's guidance on work in process limits is: "Don't allow more WIP in any given part of the process than you have people to work on tasks" 5 . DORA does not single out intake, but admission is the first point at which a team can hold to such a limit, so showing the current load beside the item is recommended practice. Agent task This section is recommended practice; it is not drawn from a study of agents at intake. The agent reads the item as written and offers a first reading, which a person then accepts, changes or rejects. What that reading contains is set out in the catalog row Intake and classification and is not repeated here. In the record it is marked as the agent's, so nobody later mistakes it for the decision. In the customer-record export , the hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records, the agent's reading notes that the request touches customer data and the access rule R-042. The agent's limits follow the accountabilities the Scrum Guide sets out 8 : It does not order items, because ordering is part of the Product Owner's accountability for Product Backlog management. It does not size items, because "The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing". It does not admit, reject, close or merge items, and it does not set a risk tier on its own authority. These limits are recommended practice: each is a decision the record attributes to a person, and an agent that took one would leave a decision on record that nobody made. The user need gets a person's attention for a researched reason. DORA reports that "in the absence of a user-centric focus, AI adoption can have a negative impact on team performance" 1 . An agent's text reads equally well whether or not anyone needs what it describes, so, as recommended practice, a person confirms the need rather than the agent. Checks The checks in this workflow decide only what a tool can tell from the record alone: whether the item is complete and well formed, never whether it is worth doing (see the Idea phase page). The particular checks are named in the catalog row; this page describes how they behave. A check that the item names the user or stakeholder whose need it serves is a form check. It confirms that a name is present; whether the need is real stays with the person deciding, for the reason DORA gives above 1 . Each check reports one of the result states fixed by the Evidence schema : passed, failed, skipped or could_not_run . The last is a status of its own, kept apart from a failure so that an unavailable tool and a real defect each get the right response, and, like a failure, it blocks a positive overall status. If the rule registry cannot be reached, for example, the run cannot list the rules an item touches. As recommended practice, the item then waits rather than being admitted on a guess about which rules apply. Guardrails How a workflow 's agent is limited in general is set out on the Workflows page. Intake adds bounds of its own: A time limit on the reading. If the agent has not produced its reading within a set time, the item goes to the decider without one. This is recommended practice; no public source sets the limit. Stop on a live incident. An item that describes something failing in production now leaves backlog triage for incident handling (see Operate ). There, in the SRE book's account, the on-call engineer is "expected to triage the problem" and "work toward its resolution" 9 : an urgent, different use of the same word. Stop on data that should not be there. If an item carries data that should not sit in a backlog, the agent stops and flags the item to a person instead of reading further. This is recommended practice. Human decision The Scrum Guide places this decision. The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management, which includes creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items and ordering them; the Product Owner "may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable" 8 . Sizing stays with the Developers who will do the work 8 . The catalog row Intake and classification names who decides in the catalog's terms. As recommended practice, the decider works from four things: the item, the agent's reading marked as such, the result of each check and the rules the item touches, all in the shape the Evidence schema fixes. The decider may: overrule any part of the agent's reading , with the reason recorded; split the item before admitting it , which the Scrum Guide's description of refinement as "the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items" supports 8 ; defer it , with the reason recorded. In the export example, the person who orders the backlog accepts the request with the open questions the Idea page lists recorded as open, for Specification readiness to settle. Outputs and evidence The run leaves one evidence record , the shape every workflow on this site writes. For intake, that record holds the decision under the decider's name, the agent's reading as an advisory finding, each check's result and the reason wherever the decider overruled the reading. The admitted item links to it, so anyone who opens the item can see why it was taken on. Four readers depend on the record the run leaves: Specification readiness starts from it instead of reopening the intake decision, the practice this site calls evidence hand-off . The train and portfolio levels read it when admitted items roll up into larger pieces of work (see Lifecycle levels ). The traceability spine takes it as the requirement end of the chain, where each requirement needs a named origin. The workflow's owner reads the records together to compute the measures below; this use is recommended practice. Failure paths The general responses to a failed check, a check that could not run and a rejected agent finding are on the Workflows page. At intake, as recommended practice, the two check results work as follows. When a check fails, for example because the item does not name whose need it serves, the item goes back to whoever raised it with the failure stated, and that person acts next. When a check reports could_not_run , as when the rule registry cannot be reached, the item waits rather than being admitted, and the owner of the unavailable tool acts next; the Evidence schema keeps that result apart from both a pass and a failure. When the agent stops for one of the reasons the Guardrails section defines, the next actor is named in the same way, as recommended practice. If the reading times out, the decider proceeds without it. If the item describes a live incident, the on-call engineer or incident owner acts next, through incident handling on the Operate page. If the item carries data that should not sit in a backlog, whoever owns the backlog's data handling acts next. Measures DORA warns against turning delivery metrics into targets, and treats them as a way for one team to improve over time rather than to compare teams 3 . Each measure below is therefore compared with the team's own earlier figure, never with a target. The specific measures are recommended practice; only their grounding is sourced. Measure Baseline to compare against What a change suggests Time from an item's arrival to a recorded decision, with the number and age of items waiting The same figures for the backlog before the workflow ran DORA's guidance on work in process limits asks whether a team knows "the mean lead time and variability for our entire value stream (from idea to customer)" 5 ; this is the first stretch of that stream How often the kind of work or the tier set at intake is changed later, at readiness or design The rate in the first period under the workflow A rising rate points at intake reading too little; a rate of zero over a long period may mean nobody revisits the call Share of admitted items later split because they were too large The share before the workflow ran Items are reaching later phases at a size DORA's small-batch guidance argues against 4 Agreement between the agent's reading and the recorded decision The rate in the first period, read together with the time each decision took Very low agreement means the reading is not useful; near-total agreement with near-instant decisions means nobody is weighing it, the pitfall the Idea page names first Owner The workflow has one accountable owner, as every workflow on this site does (see Workflows ), who changes its checks, the agent's limits and what the record holds. The Scrum Guide places Product Backlog management with the Product Owner, who may delegate the work but remains accountable 8 . Making the same person accountable for this workflow keeps the decision and the way it is made in one pair of hands; that is recommended practice, and a team may assign the workflow elsewhere as long as one person owns it. Related Specification readiness : the next workflow, which reads the record this one leaves. Incident feedback : one of the workflows that sends items here. Idea : the phase this workflow sits in, including backlog ordering and size. Lifecycle levels : the portfolio, train and team levels, including ordering across a portfolio . Traceability spine : the chain from requirement to incident that starts with the items admitted here. Operate : where a live incident goes instead of the backlog. Core: Workflows , Rule registry and Evidence schema . Workflow catalog rows: Intake and classification , Security discovery and baseline , Spike , Vulnerability response and Usage and feedback intake . Terminology: Risk tier , could_not_run , Evidence hand-off and The export example . Sources Backlog ownership, ordering, delegation, refinement and sizing: the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland 8 . Defect management as a sequence: the ISTQB glossary 6 . Where items come from: DORA on customer feedback 2 and NIST's Secure Software Development Framework on vulnerability reports 7 . Flow and batch size: DORA on work in process limits 5 and on working in small batches 4 . User focus and AI adoption: the introduction of the DORA AI Capabilities Model 1 . Incident triage: the Google SRE book on being on call 9 . Metrics as signals, not targets: DORA's guide to software delivery performance metrics 3 . Introducing the DORA AI Capabilities Model: 7 keys to succeeding in AI-assisted software development — Kevin M. Storer; Derek DeBellis, Google Cloud Blog — 2025-09-23 · source Tab title 'Introducing DORA's inaugural AI Capabilities Model | Google Cloud Blog' (page metadata: 2025-09-22). Names seven capabilities in this order: clear and communicated AI stance; healthy data ecosystems; AI-accessible internal data; strong version control practices; working in small batches; user-centric focus; quality internal platforms. Says working in small batches is especially powerful in an AI-assisted environment and that, in the absence of a user-centric focus, AI adoption can have a negative impact on team performance. ↩ ↩ ↩ Customer feedback — DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment), Google, published on dora.dev — not printed · source Capability page; no date printed. Places customer feedback in a wider group of capabilities, with visibility of work in the value stream, working in small batches and team experimentation, that together represent a lean approach to product management and, applied together, help predict software delivery performance and organizational performance. Its diagnostic questions include 'Do you actively and regularly gather feedback from users and act on it?' ↩ ↩ DORA's software delivery performance metrics — Nathen Harvey, DORA, published on dora.dev — last updated 2026-01-05 (as printed) · source Names five software delivery performance metrics in two groups: throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate). Failed deployment recovery time is a throughput metric on this page. The page https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys/ redirects here. Cited for DORA's software delivery performance metrics. Defines change fail rate as the ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment; failed deployment recovery time as the time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention; and deployment rework rate as the ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production. Advises setting a baseline for an application's current performance and improving over time, not competing against other teams or organizations; says the metrics are meant to be applied at the application or service level; lists 'Setting metrics as a goal' among its pitfalls and warns, citing Goodhart's law, that metrics set as goals invite gaming. ↩ ↩ Working in small batches — DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment), Google, published on dora.dev — last updated 2025-12-08 (as printed) · source Capability page (tab title 'DORA | Capabilities: Working in small batches'; tagged core and AI). Advises breaking work into units that can be completed independently and in short timeframes, says working in small batches amplifies the positive impact of AI adoption on product performance, and says large changes are difficult to review, test and integrate safely. ↩ ↩ Work in process limits — DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment), Google, published on dora.dev — not printed · source Capability page (tab title 'DORA | Capabilities: Work in process limits'). Says research shows WIP limits help drive improvements in software delivery performance, particularly when combined with visual displays and feedback loops from monitoring. The page's own title is 'Work in process limits', not 'WIP limits'.
