The record lists no synonyms, see-also terms or source standard. ↩ ↩ Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1: Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities — Murugiah Souppaya, Karen Scarfone, Donna Dodson, NIST Special Publication 800-218 — 2022-02 · source NIST SP 800-218 version 1.1, final (3 February 2022); practice and task identifiers checked in the PDF (https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218). Tasks relied on: PO.1.2 (identify and document all security requirements for organization-developed software to meet, and maintain the requirements over time); PO.3.3 (configure tools to generate artifacts of their support of secure development practices); PS.1.1 (store all forms of code according to least privilege); PS.3.1 (securely archive the files of each release); PS.3.2 (collect, safeguard, maintain and share provenance data); PW.1.1 (use forms of risk modeling, such as threat modeling, attack modeling or attack surface mapping); PW.2.1 (have a qualified person or people who were not involved with the design review the software design); PW.6.1 (use compilers, interpreters and build tools with security features); PW.7.1 and PW.7.2 (decide which code review or analysis to use, perform it in line with secure coding standards, and record and triage the issues found). Also the vulnerability-response practices RV.1 'Identify and Confirm Vulnerabilities on an Ongoing Basis', RV.2 'Assess, Prioritize, and Remediate Vulnerabilities' and RV.3 'Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes'. Version 1.2 (SP 800-218 Rev. 1) exists only as an initial public draft (published 2025-12-17, comments closed 2026-01-30); no final Rev. 1 was found on 2026-11-20, so version 1.1 is cited as the final. Practice PO.1: ensure that security requirements for software development are known at all times so that they can be taken into account throughout the SDLC and duplication of effort can be minimized because the requirements information can be collected once and shared. PS.3.2 examples include making provenance data available to the organization's operations and response teams to aid them in mitigating software vulnerabilities. RV.1.1: gather information from software acquirers, users and public sources on potential vulnerabilities, and investigate all credible reports. RV.3.1: analyze identified vulnerabilities to determine their root causes; RV.3.2: analyze the root causes over time to identify patterns; RV.3.4: review the SDLC process and update it if appropriate to prevent (or reduce the likelihood of) the root cause recurring. ↩ ↩ The 2020 Scrum Guide — Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, ScrumGuides.org — November 2020 · source HTML port of the November 2020 Scrum Guide; the site's download page labels the English November 2020 edition the official current version. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. Defines the Definition of Done as a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product, and as the Increment's commitment, as the Product Goal and the Sprint Goal are the commitments of the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Says the moment a Product Backlog item meets it an Increment is born, and an item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review; an organisational Definition of Done is followed by all Scrum Teams as a minimum, otherwise the Scrum Team creates one appropriate for the product, and teams on one product must mutually define and comply with the same one; the Developers are accountable for instilling quality by adhering to it and are required to conform to it. Does not use the term Definition of Ready ; says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event. Describes refinement as an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order and size, with the Developers who will be doing the work responsible for the sizing, and makes the Product Owner accountable for effective Product Backlog management, including creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items and ordering them. Names transparency, inspection and adaptation as the empirical Scrum pillars and says inspection without adaptation is considered pointless. The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to increase quality and effectiveness and inspects individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the Definition of Done; impactful improvements may be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint. An Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint, and the Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value. Describes Product Backlog refinement as the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items; counts ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood among the Product Owner's accountabilities; says the Product Owner may delegate the responsibility to others but remains accountable, and that the entire organization must respect the Product Owner's decisions, which are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog. Says the emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work, and that low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk. ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ Being On-Call — Andrea Spadaccini (edited by Kavita Guliani), Google, Site Reliability Engineering (first edition, O'Reilly Media), chapter 11; sre.google — chapter page footer: Copyright 2017 Google, Inc. (the book's preface prints 2016 in its citation example) · source After a page is acknowledged the on-call engineer is expected to triage the problem and work toward its resolution, possibly involving other team members and escalating as needed; many teams have both a primary and a secondary on-call rotation. ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. SAFe names the same altitudes Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team and is cited as one framework that uses them, not as the source of the labels. coined Agile Release Train (ART) SAFe's name for the train level: "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream". Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc.; this site uses "train" as the generic label for the same altitude. adopted safe-art Planning Interval (PI) SAFe's name for the planning cycle of a train: "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives". SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox, and calls the pattern of PI Planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule. Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
lifecycle-levels.html: Lifecycle levels: portfolio, train and team One delivery lifecycle runs at three altitudes, a portfolio that decides what to fund, a train that decides what to plan and demonstrate, and a team that decides what to build and when it is ready and done, with intent and rules flowing down and evidence and lessons flowing up. Definition The lifecycle levels are three altitudes at which one delivery lifecycle is run: Portfolio, Train and Team. In the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), a portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget; a train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows; and a team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. The three labels are generic names this site coined for the altitudes. They are not a standard, and a reader who uses other words for the same decisions loses nothing by keeping them. The Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) uses the same altitudes under its own names, and it is cited here as one framework that does so, not as the origin of the labels. SAFe defines a Portfolio as "a set of value streams that delivers a continuous flow of valuable solutions to customers within a common funding and governance model" 22 . It defines an Agile Release Train (ART) as "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream" 9 , and an Agile Team as "a cross-functional group of typically ten or fewer individuals with all the skills necessary to define, build, test, and deliver value to their customer" 8 . The worked mapping from this site's labels to SAFe's terms, a reference model in the OASIS sense, 7 is on the SAFe reference model page. Why it matters A decision placed at the wrong level reaches the wrong people, with the wrong evidence and at the wrong time. A question about one story's edge case, taken to a portfolio review, takes the time of people who cannot answer it. A question about which initiative to fund, settled inside a team because the team happens to be the one asking, commits money nobody with authority over it has weighed. Both are cases of one workflow decision (see Workflows ) being owned at an altitude that does not match its size. Two flows hold the levels together, and each fails in a recognisable way. When intent and rules do not flow down, each level re-decides what a higher level has already settled, because it has no record of that decision and no shared rule to read. When evidence and lessons do not flow up, higher levels decide on status updates instead of records, and the same miss recurs in later work. The reasoning behind the first follows from how the rule registry is shared, as the Software factory page describes; the second follows from the lessons that never close described there. Both readings are recommended practice, drawn from how workflows hand work on, not a measured finding. Agents raise the stakes at every level. DORA notes that "AI can easily generate massive blocks of code, which are hard to review and test" 3 , and its 2025 report announcement says that AI "doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there" 2 . More output per day lands on levels that were already short of review time, and an unclear decision right is amplified along with it. This site found no public study that examines the three levels with agents, so the level-by-level advice on this page is recommended practice, labelled as such where it appears, and not a research finding. How it works Each level is described by what it decides, in SAFe's public wording where a definition exists. Two things then connect the levels: what flows down and up, and the size of the work item. The customer-record export then shows the flows in one story. Portfolio A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order, and the budget behind them. SAFe's definition of a Portfolio is given above 22 . Its budgeting follows from that definition: the available portfolio budget is "directly allocated to these value streams rather than the traditional approach of project-based funding" 20 , and Lean budgets are a financial governance approach that funds value streams instead of projects 19 . Lean budget guardrails "describe the policies and practices for budgeting, spending, and governance for a specific portfolio" 15 . SAFe describes strategic themes as portfolio-level business objectives that provide competitive differentiation and strategic advantage, and as what connects the enterprise strategy to a portfolio 24 . What a portfolio funds and orders is the epic, which SAFe calls "a significant solution development initiative" 11 . Ordering epics uses weighted shortest job first ( WSJF ). In SAFe, WSJF "is estimated as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration" 26 . Its inputs are relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and opportunity enablement, and job size 26 . Cost of Delay is the money or value lost by delaying or not doing a job for a time period, relative to other jobs 10 . SAFe's WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen's The Principles of Product Development Flow 26 . No public study covers portfolio decisions with agents, so what this page says about agents at this level is recommended practice. Here an agent prepares and people decide. An agent can gather the evidence records of earlier work that bear on a candidate initiative, so that a funding discussion reads records rather than status reports, but it does not fund, order or budget anything; those decisions stay with named people. Two catalog workflows sit closest to these decisions, Intake and classification (W01) and Usage and feedback intake (W30) , and their rows say what the agent and the people do in each. Train A train decides which features go into which planning cycle, and what the integrated demonstration shows. SAFe's definition of an ART is given above 9 . A Feature is "solution functionality that delivers business value, fulfills a stakeholder need, and is sized to be delivered by an Agile Release Train within a PI" 12 . The Planning Interval (PI) is "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives" 13 . SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox and calls the pattern of planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule 13 . PI Planning "aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision" 21 . The System Demo 25 "provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART" 14 . Team A team decides which stories it builds, in which iteration, and when an item is ready and done. In SAFe, a story "focuses on a specific behavior that can be developed in incremental steps", and keeping stories small means they can be completed in a single iteration 23 . An iteration is "a standard, fixed-duration timebox during which Agile Teams and ARTs individually and collectively deliver incremental customer value while working towards the PI objectives" 18 . In Iteration Planning, "the team defines, organizes, and commits to the work for the next iteration" 17 . Iteration Goals are "a high-level summary of the business and technical goals that an Agile Team agrees to accomplish in an Iteration" 14 . Readiness and done sit at this level. The Scrum Guide says Product Backlog items "that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event", and describes the Definition of Done as "a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product" 27 . The Guide does not use the term " Definition of Ready ". SAFe's glossary defines the Definition of Done as specifying "the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value" 14 . The page Definition of Ready and Definition of Done treats both terms. What flows down and up Two things flow down. Intent flows down as the work item narrows: a portfolio funds an initiative, a train plans the features cut from it, and a team builds the stories cut from those features. In SAFe's terms that intent starts with the strategic themes described above, which connect the enterprise strategy to a portfolio 24 . Keeping each story linked to its feature and each feature to its initiative, so that a team can see which funded intent its work serves and does not re-decide it, is recommended practice. Rules flow down as one rule registry shared by every level; see Software factory . Two things flow up. Evidence flows up as the evidence record ; see Evidence schema . Lessons flow up and back as the feedback path ; see Harness engineering . The Inspect and Adapt page covers the checkpoint where they are collected. In SAFe, improvement backlog items from Inspect and Adapt go into the ART Backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event 16 . Signals from users flow up too, from outside the delivery work itself. DORA places customer feedback in a wider group of capabilities, with visibility of work in the value stream, working in small batches and team experimentation, that together represent a lean approach to product management and, applied together, help predict software delivery and organisational performance 4 . In this site's workflow catalog, the workflow that handles those signals is Usage and feedback intake (W30) . The size of the work item at each level The item that travels the lifecycle is a different size at each altitude. An epic is "significant" in SAFe 11 . A feature is sized to be delivered by one train within one PI 12 . A story is kept small enough to complete in a single iteration 23 . These sizes are one framework's wording, and fit to the planning cycle is one test of size, not the only one. A second test applies at every level. DORA advises breaking work "into work units that can be completed independently and in short timeframes", and says that working in small batches amplifies the positive impact of AI adoption on product performance 5 . The same page notes that "large changes are difficult to review, test, and integrate safely" 5 . DORA's page on work in process limits adds a test for the amount in flight. It advises prioritising work, limiting how much people work on at once and focusing on completing a small number of high-priority tasks, and it says research shows that limits on work in process help drive improvements in software delivery performance, particularly when combined with visual displays and feedback loops from monitoring 6 . Neither DORA page addresses the three levels, so applying both tests at the portfolio, train and team levels, and not only to a team's own tasks, is recommended practice. The export example across the levels The customer-record export is a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records. Its open decisions are which records, which fields, how large exports behave, what happens on failure and what is audited. The example does not size the export, place it in a planning cycle or assign any decision to a level. It shows what travels between the levels. Intent comes down with the feature: its open decisions, such as which fields an export includes, are answered against the purpose the feature was approved for rather than re-decided at each step. Rules come down as registry entries: the access rule R-042 and the volume-limit rule R-017 live in the rule registry , and the workflows that handle the export read them from there. Evidence goes up as a record: the pull-request run records R-042 as failed and R-017 as could_not_run in its evidence record , and once the fixes land and the checks run again, release readiness reads the new record instead of asking again. Lessons go back after a scheduled full export times out in production: a readiness question asking every export-like specification for its largest export changes what later export-like features are asked ( Software factory ). Band 2 uses the generic labels from this page. The Operating model box in the enablement band, band 4, keeps SAFe's own words, such as Scrum or Kanban teams on an Agile Release Train and PI cadence, so the SAFe reference model page is the place to read one vocabulary against the other. The core band below the lifecycle band holds the workflows, rules and records that the levels share. Pitfalls Items never cut to the size of the planning cycle they enter. Work arrives larger than the cycle can hold. Sign: the same item carried from one cycle to the next. SAFe sizes a feature to be delivered within one PI and keeps stories small enough for a single iteration 12 23 , and DORA advises breaking work into units that can be completed independently and in short timeframes 5 . Reading repeated carry-over as a failure of sizing is recommended practice. Prioritising without a measure of the cost of waiting. Items are ordered by who asked, and no one estimates what a delay costs. Sign: priority decided by the order of requests. WSJF and Cost of Delay are one public way to measure it 26 10 ; that having no measure is a failure is recommended practice. Evidence stops at the team. Records are written where the work runs, and higher levels are given summaries of them. Sign: portfolio reviews read status updates, not records. The Workflows page names the same failure at workflow scale as hand-off by conversation; the portfolio-review sign is recommended practice. Lessons stay where they were learned. A lesson changes the work of the team that found it and goes no further. Sign: the same kind of miss in a later feature. The Software factory page calls this lessons that never close. Agent output outruns the level that must judge it. Generation is cheap and review is not. Sign: batches of generated change larger than a reviewer can read. DORA's warning about code that is hard to review and test 3 and its advice on small batches 5 apply at each level; Workflows lists a run too large to review.
