Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
pull-request-verification.html: Pull-request verification The workflow that decides whether one revision of a change may join the mainline, on check results recorded for that exact revision, with a named reviewer deciding and an agent's review as advice. Decision May this revision of the change join the mainline as it stands? The catalog states it as W23 . In the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), this is the call that closes the Develop, Build and QA stretch. Martin Fowler defines the mainline as the codeline a team considers "the current state of the team's code", and names the practice of peer-reviewing every commit before the mainline accepts it pre-integration review. 7 The call matters because continuous integration "can only work if the mainline is kept in a healthy state". 8 The bar is not perfection. Google's guidance for reviewers favours approving a change once it definitely improves the overall health of the code, even if it is not perfect, and never accepting one that definitely makes code health worse, outside an emergency. 13 The decision attaches to one revision, a single identified state of the change, because a result is evidence only for the code it examined ( Evidence schema ). Trigger A run starts when the author offers a change for merge at a named revision. The usual vehicle is a pull request, which Fowler describes as a mechanism built to combine feature branching with pre-integration review . 7 Each new revision pushed to the change starts a new run. The record of the earlier run stays with the earlier revision as history and is never carried onto the new one ( Evidence schema ). A change its author still marks as a draft, not yet ready for review, may run checks for the author's benefit, but it does not start the merge decision; this is recommended practice, since no public source sets it out. A mainline that moves after a run has finished does not restart that run by itself; the case is handled under Failure paths below. Inputs No public source lists what a merge decision should read, so the set below is this site's recommended practice, drawn from the pages that describe each input. The diff at the named revision. Google's guidance describes a reviewable change as one self-contained change that addresses one thing and includes the tests related to it. 11 Changed behaviour without a changed or added test is therefore something the reviewer can see at once. The readiness record written by Specification readiness , which gives the intent the change is judged against, so the merge decision does not ask the specification's questions again. The entries in the Rule registry for every rule the change touches. Validators and the review skill both cite rules by identifier, so the registry is what lets their results line up ( Rule registry ). The kit version and the project configuration , which the record names separately so a later reader knows which rules and thresholds applied ( Engineering Kit ). What the run checks against must be defined apart from the implementation. When one agent writes code and tests from one understanding, both can carry the same mistake; the term for the remedy is an independent basis , and Develop, Build and QA gives the research behind it. One precondition comes before everything else: each input exists and is current for this revision. If one is missing or describes an older state, the run stops and says which record it is waiting for, rather than reaching a decision on a guess ( Workflows ). Agent task The agent's task in this workflow is set out in W23 . The agent is a review skill : an agent that reads the change against the applicable rules and proposes findings. In Birgitta Böckeler's vocabulary it is an inferential control, of the kind AI code review belongs to, as opposed to a computational one such as a test or a linter. 2 3 Each finding carries the identifier of the rule it concerns and sits beside the validators ' results for the same rule, but no finding changes a check's status or the record's overall status ( Evidence schema ). Three limits hold, each as this site's recommended practice: It does not approve or merge. No party both produces a result and accepts it, the principle security controls call separation of duties. 17 It does not resolve its own findings. A person accepts or rejects each finding, and the decision is recorded under that person's name. It does not edit a test or a check in the change it reviews. METR describes models trying to raise their score by modifying tests or scoring code, 16 and a model developer's system card reports special-casing of tests, sometimes by changing the tests themselves. 1 Its advice is not verification. NIST's profile for generative AI lists automation bias and over-reliance among the risks of human-AI configuration; 18 Parasuraman and Manzey's review finds that people relying on an imperfect aid miss what it misses and follow it when it is wrong; 21 and in Perry and colleagues' study, users of an AI code assistant wrote less secure code and were more likely to believe it secure. 22 The Workflows page sets out what follows for the split between agent, checks and people. Checks The page describes how the set of checks is formed and reported; what each check does is on Validators and in the catalog's QA rows. Selected by tier. Which security and performance checks a revision runs follows from its risk tier , as Workflows explains. Public frameworks leave that choice to the team's own judgement of risk. The ISTQB glossary defines risk-based testing as an approach in which the selection and use of test activities rest on risk; 14 the SSDF asks the organisation to determine whether code review or code analysis is used, and whether and which kinds of executable testing are performed (PW.7.1, PW.8.1); 19 and the ASVS asks an organisation to analyse its risks and decide which verification level to aim for. 20 The checks themselves are the catalog's QA rows, W17 to W21 . Fixed before results. The list of checks expected for the revision is written into the record before any check reports ( Evidence schema ). One explicit pass. Every result takes one of four states, passed, failed, skipped or could_not_run , and only an explicit pass counts as a pass ( Engineering Kit ). The distinction matters on a change host: one host's documentation says a job skipped by a condition reports "Success", while a workflow skipped by path filtering leaves its checks pending and blocks the merge. 9 SARIF, the OASIS format for analysis results, offers a standard precedent by recording whether the tool's run itself succeeded, apart from its results. 24 Report-only or required. A check can report without holding the merge, or hold it. How a check moves from one to the other is on Validators . Guardrails How a workflow 's agent is limited, and its place among the three roles, is described on Workflows . The bounds below are specific to a merge run, and each is recommended practice. Checks and code apart. A change that edits a check or the build configuration together with the code that check examines stops for a person, as Develop, Build and QA describes. No write to the mainline. The run reads, checks and records. Merging is a separate act by a person once the decision is taken. Human decision A person takes the merge call on what a tool cannot judge, and the call is recorded under that person's name ( Evidence schema ). Google's guidance for reviewers gives the areas to look at, in this order: design, functionality, complexity, tests, naming, comments, style, consistency and documentation. 10 It also says how to judge: technical facts and data overrule opinions and personal preferences, and the style guide is the authority on style. 13 When author and reviewer disagree, Google's sequence is to seek consensus first, then to talk face to face or by video and record the outcome as a comment on the change, then to escalate to a broader team discussion or to a technical lead, maintainer or engineering manager, without letting the change stall. 13 Approval does not override a required check's result, and a departure from a rule is a matter for exception handling ( W33 ); this is recommended practice. DORA finds change approval best done through peer review during development, supplemented by automation, and finds heavyweight approval from outside the team harmful to delivery performance; it treats segregation of duties, approval by someone other than the author, as met by peer review. 5 When an agent wrote the code, the developer who directed it remains the author, so the reviewer is still someone else ( Develop, Build and QA ). Outputs and evidence The run leaves one verification record for the revision, in the shape the Evidence schema fixes: the expected checks and their results, the review skill's findings, the decisions with their deciders, and the derived overall status. Public practice expects findings to be kept, not only discussed: the SSDF asks teams to record and triage issues found by code review and analysis in their workflow or issue tracking system (PW.7.2). 19 Provenance of the built output comes from the build platform, not from whoever writes the record. SLSA's Build track calls for provenance generated by a hosted build platform, 26 and its requirements put that generation out of reach of the tenant whose build it runs. 25 Who reads the record Each later reader takes the record as it stands instead of asking again, the pattern this site calls the evidence hand-off . Release readiness reads the records for the revisions a release candidate contains. Deploy verification reads them indirectly, through the release record. The traceability spine takes two links from it: the revision named on the record ties each test result to the change, and the revisions a release contains tie the change to the release. Incident feedback opens it when a later miss is traced back to this run, to see what was checked and who decided. Inspect and Adapt 23 reads could_not_run results by cause and the report-only checks that may become required. The workflow's owner reads the records in aggregate for the measures below. In the customer-record export The customer-record export is the site's running example, a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records. On its first revision, the access validator for rule R-042 fails on the background worker's broader query, the review skill's finding on the same query sits beside it as advice, the 50k-row load scenario for the volume-limit rule R-017 returns could_not_run because the load-test tool is missing from the runner image, and a request to exceed R-017's row limit is pending with the security owner; the overall status is blocked ( Evidence schema ). What this workflow adds is the shape of what follows. The worker's query is narrowed in a second revision, which gets a record of its own while the first stays as history. The could_not_run goes to whoever owns the runner image, not to the change's author. The reviewer, and later release readiness, read the record for the revision that would merge, not a thread of comments. Failure paths The general failure paths of a workflow are on Workflows . The paths below are the ones a merge decision meets in particular, each with the party who acts next. A new revision arrives during review. The record of the old revision stays as history and a new run starts ( Evidence schema ). Next: the run for the new revision; the reviewer reads its record, not the old one. The mainline moves under the change. Even a clean merge can hide semantic conflicts, which is why the merged code is built and the mainline's commit suite run. 7 Every push to the mainline triggers a build of its head, and a failed integration build is fixed at once, generally by reverting the commit. 8 A verification result applies to the revision it verified; re-verifying the integrated result before merge is recommended practice. Next: the author updates the change, which starts a new run. A required check fails. The record cannot reach a positive status, and the change goes back to its author; the fix arrives as a new revision with a record of its own, as the narrowed worker query does in the example above (recommended practice). Next: the author. The change edits a check together with the code it checks. This is a finding in its own right ( Develop, Build and QA ). Next: a person who owns the check decides whether the edit stands. The diff is too large to review. The reviewer asks for a split; where that is not possible, Google's guidance is to comment on the overall design and send the change back. 12 Next: the author. A required check returns could_not_run. The record cannot reach a positive status, and the result goes to the owner of the runner or environment, since the change may be sound ( Engineering Kit , Adapters ). Next: that owner restores the tool or environment and the check runs again on the same revision. An input is missing or stale. The run stops and names the record it waits for (recommended practice). Next: the workflow that writes that record, for example Specification readiness . Author and reviewer cannot agree. Google's escalation sequence under Human decision applies. 13 Next: whoever the sequence reaches. Measures No public source gives target values for these measures, and this page gives none. DORA advises setting a baseline of current performance and improving on it over time, rather than competing with other teams. 4 Each measure below is compared with the same team's values before the workflow became required, or with the period named. Delivery performance. DORA's change lead time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate, 4 whose definitions belong to the assurance band of the map. Baseline: the team's values for a period before the workflow became required. Time to first review response. Google's guidance says one business day is the maximum time it should take to respond to a review request, and that a fast individual response matters more than how long the whole review takes. 12 DORA counts the time taken to approve code changes among its measures for trunk-based development, 6 and suggests tracking time spent waiting for approvals. 5 Fowler notes that pre-integration review usually adds significant friction to continuous integration, 8 which is why the wait is worth watching. Baseline: the same team before the workflow. could_not_run results per required check, by cause. A rising count for one cause points at an environment, not at the code (recommended practice). Baseline: the check's report-only period ( Validators ). Share of agent findings rejected, with their coded reasons. This is an input to the review skill's evaluations ( Skills with evals ), not a target (recommended practice). Baseline: the rejection share when the review skill was first introduced. Owner One accountable owner holds and changes the workflow itself, a role distinct from the reviewer who decides each run ( Workflows ). Lean practice offers the model: a value stream has an accountable manager who may not own the people and resources in it. 15 DORA names pitfalls of change approval that such an owner guards against; three of them are treating all changes equally, failing to apply continuous improvement, and responding to problems by adding more process. 5 Related Takes evidence from: Specification readiness and Design conformance . Hands evidence to: Release readiness , Deploy verification and Incident feedback . Phase: Develop, Build and QA . Core: Workflows , Evidence schema , Validators , Skills with evals , Rule registry , Engineering Kit and Adapters . Readers of the record: Traceability spine and Inspect and Adapt . Catalog rows: pull-request verification W23 ; the QA rows it gathers results from, W17 to W21 ; task execution loop W13 ; exception handling W33 . Terminology: review skill , could_not_run , risk tier , evidence record and pre-integration review . Sources Mainline, pre-integration review and integration: Martin Fowler on branching patterns and on continuous integration. 7 8 Code review practice: Google's engineering practices on the standard of code review, the speed of reviews, small changes and what to look for. 13 12 11 10 Change approval, trunk-based development and delivery metrics: DORA. 5 6 4 Harness vocabulary: Böckeler. 2 3 Over-reliance on automated judgment: NIST's generative AI profile, Parasuraman and Manzey, and Perry and colleagues. 18 21 22 Agents changing tests: METR and a model developer's system card. 16 1 Risk-based selection of checks: the ISTQB glossary, the NIST SSDF and the OWASP ASVS. 14 19 20 Results and provenance: SARIF, SLSA and one change host's documentation on skipped checks. 24 26 25 9 Separation of duties: NIST's security and privacy control catalogue. 17 Accountable ownership: the Lean Enterprise Institute on the value-stream manager. 15 Inspect and Adapt : Scaled Agile, Inc.'s page on the event. 23 The inputs set, the agent's limits, the guardrails, what approval does not override, the handling of a failed check, the stop on a missing input, re-verification after the mainline moves and the last two measures are this site's recommended practice; no public source states them. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing

Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. SAFe names the same altitudes Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team and is cited as one framework that uses them, not as the source of the labels. coined Agile Release Train (ART) SAFe's name for the train level: "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream". Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc.; this site uses "train" as the generic label for the same altitude. adopted safe-art Planning Interval (PI) SAFe's name for the planning cycle of a train: "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives". SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox, and calls the pattern of PI Planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule. Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
release-readiness.html: Release readiness The workflow that decides whether a release candidate, fixed at one revision, is fit to go out, by reading the records already written for that revision rather than asking again, and leaves the release record that deployment and any later incident review start from. Decision Release readiness is a workflow of the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work) that settles one question: may this release candidate, at this one revision, go out, on evidence already recorded for that revision? The workflow's definition is the release readiness row of the workflow catalog ( W25 ). This page sets out how a run reads its evidence, how it fails, which record it leaves and who reads that record, and how a team can tell whether the workflow works. Meeting the Definition of Done does not settle the question on its own. In the 2020 Scrum Guide, a Product Backlog item that does not meet the definition "cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review", and the moment an item meets it, an Increment is born 8 . Done makes an item eligible for release; it does not release it. The release-level definition is described under Definition of Done . Release readiness is settled for a revision before that revision's deployment begins, while exposure to users can come with the deployment or later, as the Deploy and Release pages explain. Trigger A run starts when a release candidate is named and fixed at one revision, which is the entry gate of the Release phase. Building a release from one revision has public precedent: Google's site reliability engineering book describes branching "from the mainline at a specific revision" and rebuilding an older release "at the same revision as the original build" 13 . Any change to the candidate's contents makes a new candidate and starts a new run. Semantic Versioning says that once a versioned package has been released, its contents "MUST NOT be modified" and any modification "MUST be released as a new version" 9 . Applying the same rule to a named candidate before it is released is this site's recommended practice, by analogy. The SRE book also describes fixes reaching a release branch as cherry picks, each of which can be approved or rejected for inclusion 13 ; an accepted cherry pick changes the contents, so it starts a new run. Inputs The run reads records that other workflows wrote, each named by the revision it describes. The inputs carry no order of their own. Verification records. One for every change in the candidate, written by Pull-request verification . The Traceability spine links change to release through the revisions of the changes the candidate contains. Upstream records. The specification readiness and design conformance records those changes rest on. Provenance. SLSA defines provenance as "verifiable information about software artifacts describing where, when, and how something was produced" 10 . NIST's Secure Software Development Framework asks producers to securely archive the files and supporting data, provenance data among them, retained for each software release, and to collect, safeguard, maintain and share provenance data for all components of each release (tasks PS.3.1 and PS.3.2) 7 . The release-level Definition of Done , as the Definition of Done section describes it. One rule governs every input: a record is evidence only for the revision it names. When a change moves to a new revision, its earlier record stays attached to the earlier revision ( evidence schema ), and the evidence it carried expires with that revision ( evidence hand-off ). A record for any other revision is history, not input. Agent task The task itself is set in the catalog row ( W25 ). Its plainest part is drafting release notes. Keep a Changelog's 2.0.0 edition says a language model "can draft one from a diff in seconds, which is useful as a starting point", draws the line as "machines can draft, but humans curate", and advises: "Then read the result before anyone else does." 6 The same edition says not to use a list of commits as a changelog, because a commit records a step in the source code while a changelog entry records a notable difference written for the people who use the software 6 ; the 1.1.0 edition calls commit-log diffs "full of noise" 5 . A draft also follows the changelog's own conventions: the 2.0.0 edition, for example, asks for an Unreleased section at the top, the release date of each version, and a yanked release listed rather than hidden 6 . How the Release phase treats such drafts is on the Release page. What the agent writes stays a draft until a person curates it. How a workflow keeps its agent apart from the checks and the decision is set out on the Workflows page. Checks Each property below is one that a tool settles the same way every time, before anyone decides. The properties carry no order. The catalog row keeps its own list of checks ( W25 ); these are the properties a team can expect a run to establish. Revision match. Every record the run reads names the candidate's revision. A record that names any other revision fails the property ( revisions and versions ). Provenance verified, not merely present. SLSA says "provenance doesn't do anything unless somebody inspects it", and calls that inspection verification. Its steps check the provenance's signature, that its subject matches the artefact's digest, its predicate type and the builder's level; then compare it with expectations such as builder identity, canonical source repository, build type and external parameters; and, optionally, check dependencies recursively 11 . SLSA places verification at upload, at download or in continuous monitoring 11 ; running it before the release decision is this site's application. The result can be kept as a record of its own: a SLSA verification summary attestation names the verifier, the policy, the input attestations and a result of passed or failed, so that a consumer can decide about an artefact without reviewing every attestation behind it 12 . Test completion on record. The ISTQB glossary defines test completion as the activity that makes testware available for later use, leaves test environments in a satisfactory condition and communicates the results of testing to relevant stakeholders 4 . The property is that this activity's outcome is recorded for the candidate's revision. Guardrails Read, do not rerun. The run reads records; it does not run upstream checks again. When a record is missing or names another revision, the workflow that owns that record runs again for the candidate's revision, and release readiness reads the new record. The SRE book offers a precedent for a recorded result per revision: its release process re-runs the unit tests on the release branch and creates an audit trail showing that all the tests passed 13 . Here the result comes from the owning workflow, and this workflow reads it. Stop conditions. As recommended practice, the run stops when the candidate's revision differs from the revision any record names, and when a rule not open to exception shows anything but a pass; in the running example, that is the access rule R-042. A stopped run states what it is waiting for and leaves the decision open. Access to release operations. The SRE book counts creating a new release and deploying a new release among the operations it gates by access control 13 ; the full list is on the Release page. Human decision The named person who owns the decision takes it. The catalog row ( W25 ) records who that is, and the Release page explains why a single named decision is recommended practice. That person reads the release record, the agent's drafts, marked as drafts, and any risk put forward for acceptance. How heavy the approval should be is a separate question. DORA finds that change approvals "are best implemented through peer review during the development process", that heavyweight external approval has "a negative impact on software delivery performance", and treats segregation of duties, under which "changes must be approved by someone other than the author", as a requirement peer review can meet 2 . Where a release also falls under an organisation's change control, the change control row ( W32 ) says who approves it. In the customer-record export , the running example of this site, the record for the export change's latest revision shows the request to exceed R-017's row limit as pending until the security owner decides. While it is pending, the overall status cannot be positive, so the release decision waits. A general option, not what the example records, is to ship the export as latent code behind a release toggle : Pete Hodgson describes release toggles as allowing "incomplete and un-tested codepaths to be shipped to production as latent code which may never be turned on" 3 . Exposing the export then becomes a later release decision that reads the same pending entry. Outputs and evidence The run leaves the release record: an evidence record in the shape the evidence schema fixes, for the candidate's revision, holding the decision and its reason. It is kept beside the archived files of the release and their provenance, which SSDF task PS.3.1 asks producers to retain for each release 7 . Public practice keeps similar records: the SRE book's change report and test audit trail 13 , and SLSA's verification summary attestation as a stored verification result 12 . The record has several readers, in no particular order: Deploy verification reads it for the same revision before deployment starts ( Deploy ). Incident feedback and any incident review read it to learn which release was running, the release-to-incident link of the traceability spine . In the running example, a scheduled full export, within R-017's limit but far larger than the 50k-row load scenario, times out in production; the review starts from the release record and reads back through the records it names. The traceability spine uses it as the link from change to release. Operations and response teams use the provenance kept beside it; SSDF gives the example of making provenance data available to an organisation's operations and response teams to help them mitigate vulnerabilities 7 . Assurance reads release records when it audits how releases were decided, as recommended practice. For people, the run also produces release notes, which a person has curated: "Changelogs are for humans, not machines." 5 6 Where the project uses Semantic Versioning, the version number follows it 9 ; Keep a Changelog 2.0.0 says a project does not have to use it 6 . Failure paths The general cases, each naming who acts next, are on the Workflows page. Release readiness adds its own. A record names an earlier revision. The workflow that owns the record runs again for the candidate's revision, and the decision waits. It is the Release page's pitfall of evidence for an earlier revision ( Release ). A required result is could_not_run. The run cannot reach a positive status ( could_not_run ), and the owner of the missing environment or tool acts, not the author of the change. In the running example, if the 50k-row load scenario for the candidate's revision reports could_not_run because the load-test tool is missing from the runner image, the runner image's owner restores the tool, the scenario runs again in the owning workflow, and release readiness reads the new result. Provenance is missing or fails verification. The candidate is not fit to go out, and the owner of the build platform acts; that routing is recommended practice. SLSA says "Any unrecognized externalParameters SHOULD cause verification to fail", and that detecting a failure achieves little unless a person or an automated system acts on it 11 . The notes draft is rejected or unread. A person curates the notes before they are published 6 ; a draft nobody has read does not go out. The candidate changes after the run starts. A new candidate needs a new run, by the Semantic Versioning analogy above 9 , and the record of the abandoned run stays as history. A version already out proves faulty. Semantic Versioning's FAQ, on a release that broke its own compatibility promise, says to fix the problem in a new release and that "it is unacceptable to modify versioned releases" 9 . Keep a Changelog lists a yanked release, "do not hide it" 6 . A new run starts for the candidate that carries the fix, and Incident feedback carries the lesson upstream. Measures DORA advises setting a baseline for an application's current performance, applies its metrics at the application or service level, and lists setting metrics as a goal among its pitfalls 1 . So each measure below is compared with a baseline for the same service, and none carries a target. Change fail rate and deployment rework rate. Two of DORA's software delivery performance metrics, in its instability group 1 . Baseline: the same service's values before the workflow was introduced. Time from candidate named to decision recorded, and its spread. DORA suggests measuring the time changes spend waiting for approval from external bodies, and, as approvals move closer to the work, the time spent waiting for local reviewers 2 . Baseline: earlier releases of the same service. Very short times can signal approval without reading, the rubber-stamp pitfall on the Release page. Releases that needed a step outside the workflow. DORA suggests tracking the percentage of changes that do or do not require a manual change to be promoted to production 2 . The release-level counterpart, recommended practice here, is the share of releases that needed a manual approval or a hand-assembled record. Baseline: the first releases run under the workflow. Decisions that asked for evidence outside the record. The share of decisions in which the decider had to ask in a message or a meeting for something the record should have held. Baseline: the first releases run under the workflow. Recommended practice; no public source measures it. Release records that match what was deployed. The share of release records whose revision is the revision deploy verification found running. Baseline: earlier releases. Recommended practice; a mismatch is the sign of the earlier-revision pitfall on the Release page. Owner The workflow has one accountable owner, as every workflow does ( Workflows ). As recommended practice, that owner decides what counts as current for a candidate and which records a release requires, and changes the workflow when its measures or failure paths show a gap. This is distinct from the Definition of Done. The Scrum Guide holds the Developers "always accountable for ... Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done", and says several Scrum Teams on one product "must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done" 8 . The definition says what done means; the workflow's owner decides how a release decision reads the evidence. Related Takes evidence from Pull-request verification , Specification readiness and Design conformance . Hands evidence to Deploy verification and Incident feedback . Phases: Release , where this decision sits, and Deploy , which reads it for the same revision. Definition of Ready and Definition of Done : the release-level definition this workflow reads. Traceability spine : the change-to-release and release-to-incident links the release record carries. Core: Evidence schema , Workflows , Rule registry and Software factory . Workflow catalog: release readiness ( W25 ), deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ), change control ( W32 ) and exception handling ( W33 ). Sources Done and release: the 2020 Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland 8 . Release engineering: Google's site reliability engineering book, chapter on release engineering 13 . Versions and notes: Semantic Versioning 9 and Keep a Changelog, editions 1.1.0 5 and 2.0.0 6 . Release records and provenance: the NIST Secure Software Development Framework 7 and SLSA on provenance 10 , verifying artifacts 11 and verification summary attestations 12 . Test completion: the ISTQB glossary 4 . Change approval and measures: DORA on streamlining change approval 2 and on software delivery performance metrics 1 . Release toggles: Pete Hodgson on feature toggles 3 . The stop conditions, running provenance verification at release, the routing of failed provenance, the handling of a run that cannot complete, the owner's remit and the last three measures are this site's recommended practice; no public source states them. DORA's software delivery performance metrics — Nathen Harvey, DORA, published on dora.dev — last updated 2026-01-05 (as printed) · source Names five software delivery performance metrics in two groups: throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate). Failed deployment recovery time is a throughput metric on this page. The page https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys/ redirects here. Cited for DORA's software delivery performance metrics. Defines change fail rate as the ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment; failed deployment recovery time as the time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention; and deployment rework rate as the ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production. Advises setting a baseline for an application's current performance and improving over time, not competing against other teams or organizations; says the metrics are meant to be applied at the application or service level; lists 'Setting metrics as a goal' among its pitfalls and warns, citing Goodhart's law, that metrics set as goals invite gaming. ↩ ↩ ↩ Streamlining change approval — DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment), Google, published on dora.dev (capability page; tab title 'DORA | Capabilities: Streamlining change approval') — 2025-10-30 (last updated, as printed) · source Says change approvals are best implemented through peer review during the development process, supplemented by automation to detect, prevent and correct bad changes early, and that heavyweight external approval processes have a negative impact on software delivery performance. Treats segregation of duties, a common regulatory requirement, as satisfiable by peer review and gives the change advisory board a strategic role. Does not discuss an external control that mandates approval by an outside party. Carries the 'core' tag; cites the 2019 State of DevOps Report. Quotes segregation of duties as 'changes must be approved by someone other than the author'. Names as a pitfall responding to problems by adding more process, which drives up lead times and batch sizes, and advises investing in making it quicker and safer to make changes. PS.3.2 examples include making provenance data available to the organization's operations and response teams to aid them in mitigating software vulnerabilities. Describes hermetic builds (the same revision built on different machines gives identical results; builds depend on known versions of build tools, such as compilers, and dependencies, such as libraries); gated operations (approving source code changes, specifying the actions to perform during a release, creating a new release, approving the initial integration proposal and subsequent cherry picks, deploying a new release, and changes to a project's build configuration); rollouts that fit the risk profile of a service, such as rolling out to successive clusters over a period of several hours or starting in one cluster and expanding exponentially until all clusters are updated; a canary as a few jobs in production after system tests; and release engineers and SREs working together on canarying changes, pushing out new releases without interrupting services and rolling back features that demonstrate problems. The chapter does not use the word 'incubation'. Also: releases branch from the mainline at a specific revision and never merge back; older releases are rebuilt at the same revision; bug fixes reach a release as cherry picks, each approved or rejected for inclusion; the release system produces a report of all changes in a release and re-runs unit tests on the release branch, creating an audit trail that they passed. ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers.
