It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
release.html: Release Release decides whether a candidate is fit to reach its users, on evidence recorded for its exact revision, and leaves a record of that decision; an agent prepares, checks confirm and a named person decides. Purpose Release is the phase of the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work) in which a team decides that a change is fit to reach its users, and records that decision. The decision rests on evidence gathered for one candidate at one exact revision. Deploying puts a revision into an environment and releasing exposes its behaviour to users; the two can happen at the same moment or apart, as the glossary entry deploy versus release and the Deploy page set out with their sources. The phase produces a record of the release decision that later work can read. Its exit is also where the release-level Definition of Done is met, which is why the map's DoD tag sits on the Release box. Traditional practice Without agents, release is a controlled step. Google's site reliability engineering book, in its chapter on release engineering, enforces policy through gated operations, among them approving source code changes, specifying the actions to perform during a release, creating a new release, approving the initial integration proposal and subsequent cherry picks, deploying a new release, and changing a project's build configuration 15 . The same chapter asks for hermetic builds : the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, because a build depends on known versions of its tools and dependencies, and that makes a release reproducible 15 . Who approves, and how, varies more. DORA's capability guidance holds that change approvals are "best implemented through peer review during the development process, supplemented by automation to detect, prevent, and correct bad changes early", and that heavyweight external approval processes have "a negative impact on software delivery performance" 4 . The same page names segregation of duties as a common regulatory requirement, treats peer review as a way to meet it, and keeps a strategic role for the change advisory board 4 . Release notes tell people what changed. Keep a Changelog, created and maintained by Olivier Lacan, starts from one principle, "Changelogs are for humans, not machines.", advises against dumping raw commit logs from version control into a changelog, says there should be an entry for every single version, and groups changes under six types: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security 8 . It asks a project to mention whether it follows Semantic Versioning rather than requiring it 8 . Under Semantic Versioning, the major version changes when a release makes incompatible API changes 13 . Exposure can be controlled apart from deployment. Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles distinguishes release, experiment, ops and permissioning toggles by how long each lives, and says release toggles allow "incomplete and un-tested codepaths to be shipped to production as latent code which may never be turned on" 6 . Martin Fowler describes dark launching as "taking a new or changed back-end behavior and calling it from existing users without the users being able to tell it's being called", and notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion 5 . Canary releases, which expose a change to a small share first, are covered on the Deploy page. In SAFe, release on demand "releases new functionality immediately or incrementally based on business and customer needs" 11 . DORA treats the ability behind all of this as a capability: continuous delivery is "the ability to release changes of all kinds on demand quickly, safely, and sustainably" 3 . The Definition of Done , the quality standard an Increment must meet in the 2020 Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, decides what may be released at all: a Product Backlog item that does not meet it "cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review" 12 . The Guide also says the Sprint Review "should never be considered a gate to releasing value", and that where an organisation sets a Definition of Done as a standard, all Scrum Teams follow it as a minimum 12 . Supply-chain practice adds records of the release itself. NIST's Secure Software Development Framework asks producers to securely archive the files of each release and to collect, safeguard, maintain and share its provenance data (practice PS.3, tasks PS.3.1 and PS.3.2) 10 . SLSA defines provenance as "verifiable information about software artifacts describing where, when, and how something was produced" 14 . Testing closes here too: the ISTQB glossary defines test completion, also called test closure, as the activity that makes testware available for later use, leaves test environments in a satisfactory condition and communicates the results of testing to relevant stakeholders 7 . The catalog row for release readiness ( W25 ) lists the other traditional activities it takes in. AI-assisted practice With coding agents, release keeps its purpose and changes who does the legwork. The work splits the way it does across this site: an agent prepares, deterministic checks confirm, and a person decides. What follows is recommended practice; no public study measures it. An agent suits the preparatory side of release, where text has to be written from many records and a first attempt is cheap to correct. Release notes are the plainest case. Keep a Changelog's 2.0.0 edition, which still holds that changelogs are for humans, accepts that a model can draft a changelog from a diff and draws the line as "machines can draft, but humans curate"; it advises reading a model-drafted changelog before anyone else does 9 . What the agent prepares for a candidate is set in the release readiness row ( W25 ). Checks take what a tool can decide the same way every time. The decision then reads evidence, the evidence hand-off described on the Workflows page. The checks that run before the decision are listed in the same catalog row. Everything an agent prepares at release is material for the decision, never part of it. The agent never fills a decision field in the evidence record , the same line the Software factory page draws across every workflow. The decision stays with the named person who owns it; this split is recommended practice, not a measured finding. The stakes rise with volume. DORA's 2025 research puts it this way: "Without robust control systems, like strong automated testing, mature version control practices, and fast feedback loops, an increase in change volume leads to instability" 2 . The record of a release decision is where a reader can see whether those controls ran for the candidate; that reading is recommended practice, not a DORA finding. In the running example, the customer-record export , the release decision reads the verification record for the export change's latest revision instead of asking again which checks ran. A request to exceed R-017's row limit appears there as pending until the security owner decides, and R-042, an access rule, is not open to exception. Workflows in this phase Release holds one decision workflow and borders another. On the map, the bar under the Release box reads "release readiness", the workflow of that name. In the workflow catalog , whose phase names differ from the map's, both sit in its phase 6, which the catalog also calls Release, and two cross-lifecycle rows reach into it. Release readiness (see the Release readiness page): the decision this phase exists to make. Deployment and post-deploy verification (see the Deploy verification page): the neighbouring decision, covered on the Deploy page. Change control : a cross-lifecycle row that a release can fall under. Exception handling : a cross-lifecycle row; a waiver sought at release goes through it. Each catalog row carries its workflow's own definition, and this page does not repeat it. The records these workflows leave follow the evidence schema , and the way one workflow reads another's records is set out on the Workflows page. Gates and evidence Release has one gate at entry and one at exit, and it leaves one record. Entry. A named candidate, fixed at one revision. Everything the phase examines is tied to that revision, as the Workflows page explains. Exit. The named person who owns the decision has made it, on evidence for that revision, and the record carries the decision. The exit is also where the release-level Definition of Done is met; the DoD tag on the map marks it, and what the definition contains and who owns it are set out under Definition of Done . When the candidate meets an interruption instead, such as a failed check or a requested exception, the response follows one of the failure paths on the Workflows page, each of which names who acts next; a requested exception goes through exception handling ( W33 ). Evidence. The exit leaves the release record, an evidence record in the shape the evidence schema fixes, kept beside the archived release files and their provenance. Its value shows later, because an incident review starts from it. In the running example, a scheduled full export within R-017's limit but far larger than the 50k-row load scenario times out in production; the review that follows reads back through these records, and the Operate page carries the incident from there. Roles Release has one decision, taken by the named person who owns it. That person reads the evidence and the agent's drafts, decides, and is named in the record. A single named decision is recommended practice; the release readiness row ( W25 ) records who holds it. Public sources set out narrower accountabilities. The Scrum Guide holds Developers "always accountable for ... Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done" 12 , so meeting the definition is their work before it is anyone's decision. DORA recommends implementing change approval through peer review during development, supplemented by automation, and keeps a strategic role for the change advisory board 4 . Where a release also falls under change control ( W32 ), that row says who approves it. This page does not split the release decision further than those sources do. The agent holds no role in the decision. It prepares material, its findings are advisory, and the identity it runs under has no permission to write a decision. Pitfalls Evidence for an earlier revision. The candidate moved on, but the decision reads results recorded for a previous revision. Sign: the revision named in the release record does not match the candidate that shipped. Release notes generated from the commit log. Keep a Changelog advises against dumping raw commit logs into a changelog 8 . Sign: notes that list commit messages instead of what changed for the reader. Agent drafts accepted unread. Notes written by an agent go out without a person reading them, the same failure as treating an agent's review as approval. Keep a Changelog's 2.0.0 edition advises reading a model-drafted changelog before anyone else does 9 . Sign: notes published minutes after the draft, with no edits. Release toggles that stay. Hodgson describes toggles as "inventory which comes with a carrying cost", asks teams to be proactive in removing flags that are no longer needed, and says release toggles "should generally not stick around much longer than a week or two", while allowing that a small number of long-lived kill switches remain 6 . Sign: release toggles older than the releases they were added for. Approval that is either a rubber stamp or a heavyweight outside gate. DORA finds heavyweight external approval harms delivery performance 4 ; an approval given without reading the evidence fails the other way. Sign: approvals that arrive in seconds, or releases that wait days for a meeting. The Definition of Done waived under time pressure. An item that does not meet the definition cannot be released, and an organisational standard is a minimum for every team 12 . A departure goes through exception handling ( W33 ), and a rule such as R-042 that is not open to exception is never waived. Sign: "done except for" in the release discussion. The Sprint Review used as the release gate. The Scrum Guide says the Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value 12 . Sign: finished increments held back until the end of the Sprint for no other reason. Related Deploy : the phase before exposure, and the difference between deploying and releasing. Operate : the phase after release, where incidents are handled. Develop, Build and QA : where the verification record that the release decision reads is produced. Definition of Ready and Definition of Done : what the DoD tag at this phase stands for. Traceability spine : the chain of linked artefacts that runs from requirement to incident. Workflows , Evidence schema , Rule registry and Software factory : the Core pages behind the records this phase reads. Validators : the deterministic checks whose results the record holds, this site's adaptation of Birgitta Böckeler's computational sensors 1 . Release readiness : whether a release candidate is fit to go out. Deploy verification : whether a running revision stays or the way back is taken. Workflow catalog rows: release readiness ( W25 ), deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ), change control ( W32 ) and exception handling ( W33 ). Sources Release engineering and change approval: Google's site reliability engineering book on release engineering 15 and DORA on streamlining change approval 4 and continuous delivery 3 . Release notes and versions: Keep a Changelog, editions 1.1.0 8 and 2.0.0 9 , and Semantic Versioning 13 . Exposure control: Pete Hodgson on feature toggles 6 , Martin Fowler on dark launching 5 and SAFe on release on demand 11 . Definition of Done and the Sprint Review: the 2020 Scrum Guide 12 . Release records and test closure: the NIST Secure Software Development Framework 10 , SLSA provenance 14 and the ISTQB glossary 7 . AI-assisted delivery: DORA's announcement of its 2025 report 2 . Validators as computational sensors: Birgitta Böckeler on sensors for coding agents 1 . The agent's preparatory role, the single named release decision and the reading of the release record as evidence that controls ran are this site's recommended practice; no public source states them. RV.3.1: analyze identified vulnerabilities to determine their root causes; RV.3.2: analyze the root causes over time to identify patterns; RV.3.4: review the SDLC process and update it if appropriate to prevent (or reduce the likelihood of) the root cause recurring. ↩ ↩ Release on Demand — not printed, Scaled Agile, Inc. — last updated 2025-02-25 (as printed) · source Release on demand is an aspect of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline that 'releases new functionality immediately or incrementally based on business and customer needs'; 'releases are decoupled from the work to deploy the functionality'. Defines the Definition of Done as a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product, and as the Increment's commitment, as the Product Goal and the Sprint Goal are the commitments of the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Does not use the term Definition of Ready ; says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event. Names transparency, inspection and adaptation as the empirical Scrum pillars and says inspection without adaptation is considered pointless. Says the emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work, and that low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk. ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 — Tom Preston-Werner, semver.org · source Versioning scheme in which MAJOR marks incompatible changes, MINOR backward-compatible additions and PATCH backward-compatible fixes, against a declared public API. The page says it was originally authored by Tom Preston-Werner and prints no date. Item 3: once a versioned package has been released, the contents of that version must not be modified, and any modifications must be released as a new version. The FAQ, on a release that broke the specification, says to fix the problem in a new release and that modifying versioned releases is unacceptable. ↩ ↩ Build: Provenance — not printed, SLSA (Linux Foundation) — SLSA v1.2, Status: Approved (no release date printed) · source Defines provenance as verifiable information about software artifacts describing where, when, and how something was produced, split into buildDefinition (buildType, externalParameters, internalParameters, resolvedDependencies) and runDetails (builder, metadata, byproducts). Identifies the format with the versioned predicate type https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1, requires consumers to ignore unrecognized fields, and keeps minor versions backwards compatible. ↩ ↩ Release Engineering — Dinah McNutt (edited by Betsy Beyer and Tim Harvey), Google, Site Reliability Engineering (book, first edition), O'Reilly Media; sre.google — chapter page footer: Copyright © 2017 Google, Inc.; the book's preface prints 'Copyright 2016 Google, Inc.' in its citation example · source Chapter 8 of the SRE book. Describes hermetic builds (the same revision built on different machines gives identical results; builds depend on known versions of build tools, such as compilers, and dependencies, such as libraries); gated operations (approving source code changes, specifying the actions to perform during a release, creating a new release, approving the initial integration proposal and subsequent cherry picks, deploying a new release, and changes to a project's build configuration); rollouts that fit the risk profile of a service, such as rolling out to successive clusters over a period of several hours or starting in one cluster and expanding exponentially until all clusters are updated; a canary as a few jobs in production after system tests; and release engineers and SREs working together on canarying changes, pushing out new releases without interrupting services and rolling back features that demonstrate problems. The chapter does not use the word 'incubation'. Also: releases branch from the mainline at a specific revision and never merge back; older releases are rebuilt at the same revision; bug fixes reach a release as cherry picks, each approved or rejected for inclusion; the release system produces a report of all changes in a release and re-runs unit tests on the release branch, creating an audit trail that they passed. ↩ ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. SAFe names the same altitudes Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team and is cited as one framework that uses them, not as the source of the labels. coined Agile Release Train (ART) SAFe's name for the train level: "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream". Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc.; this site uses "train" as the generic label for the same altitude. adopted safe-art Planning Interval (PI) SAFe's name for the planning cycle of a train: "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives". SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox, and calls the pattern of PI Planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule. Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
rule-registry.html: Rule registry The single list of the rules a team relies on, each with a stable identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and its known gaps, which validators, skills and evidence records refer to by identifier. Definition A rule registry is the one place where a team lists the rules its software must keep, one entry per rule. Each entry carries a stable identifier, a statement of the rule in a sentence or two, a route that says how the rule is enforced (a gate, a judgment or guidance), a named owner, and the known gaps in that enforcement. Other parts of the engineering environment point at entries by identifier: a validator names the rules it enforces, a skill names the rules it supports, and an evidence record names the rule checks that ran. "Rule registry" is a working name coined by this site, not an industry term; it is one of the five parts of the Engineering Kit . Why it matters In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), coding agents produce more changes than people can read line by line, and every change is expected to respect the same rules: who may see which data, which layers may depend on which, how large an operation may be. Those rules usually start out scattered across agent instruction files, review comments, wiki pages and the memory of a few senior engineers. A rule held only as a sentence in an agent's instructions is kept whenever the agent happens to keep it. Nothing refuses the change that breaks it, and nobody can say afterwards whether it held. A registry fixes three things that scattered rules cannot. First, identity: once a rule has an identifier, a check, a skill and a run record can all say which rule they concern, and the team can ask which rules have no check at all. Second, strength: the route makes explicit whether a rule is enforced by a machine, by a named person's call, or only by the agent's good behaviour, so a passing build is not mistaken for proof that every rule held. Third, responsibility: an owner per rule means a failing or noisy rule is somebody's problem to fix rather than everybody's reason to ignore it. The idea is familiar from security practice. Requirement and control catalogues give every item an identifier so that other documents and tools can refer to it precisely 10 6 , and NIST publishes its control catalogue as structured data that tools can read 7 . Security policy as code applies the same thinking to a team's own policies: they are written as files, kept under version control and validated automatically in the pipeline 14 . A rule registry brings that discipline to the engineering rules a team and its agents work under. How it works What an entry holds Every entry has the same fields. The table shows them for the access rule in the site's running example, a feature that lets users export customer records. Field What it holds Example: R-042 Identifier A short code that never changes and is never reused R-042 Statement The rule in one or two plain sentences An identity may export only the customer records it may read Route Gate, judgment or guidance, and for a split rule which part takes which route Gate Owner The named person or role who answers for the rule The security owner Known gaps What the enforcement does not cover, and gaps since closed None open. The background worker's broader query was recorded here as a gap and closed when the validator was extended to cover it External reference An outside control or standard the rule implements, if any SEC-004, the security-standard entry it serves Status Active, superseded or retired, with a pointer to any replacement Active Two further fields earn their place once the registry is in use. A gated rule records its rollout stage, report-only or required, and the date by which it is planned to become required; the Validators page describes that path. And each entry links to the record of why the rule exists and how it has changed, in the manner of an architecture decision record : Michael Nygard's short, numbered records of a decision's context, the decision itself, its status and its consequences 8 . The registry is held as data in the repository, next to the code it governs, so that tools can read it and every change to it is reviewed and versioned like any other change. The Thoughtworks Technology Radar makes the same argument for decision records: kept in source control rather than a wiki, they stay in step with the code 13 . Identifiers that stay put An identifier is useful only if it keeps meaning the same rule. Codes that encode a position in a document tend not to. OWASP's Application Security Verification Standard numbers each requirement by chapter, section and requirement, and asks other documents and tools to cite the standard's version alongside the number, because the numbers may change between versions 10 . When the standard was restructured for version 5.0, even requirements whose meaning had not changed received new numbers, and OWASP published mappings between the old and new schemes 11 . The recommended practice for a registry is therefore an identifier that carries no position: R-042 says nothing about where the rule sits, so the registry can be reorganised without renumbering it. A rule that is no longer needed is retired, not deleted, and its identifier is never given to another rule, so that an old run record or review comment still resolves to what it meant at the time. Public catalogues handle withdrawal in a similar way. NIST SP 800-53 keeps withdrawn controls in its catalogue under their identifiers, with a note of where their content went 6 . MITRE's weakness list keeps deprecated entries, grouped in a view of their own, each expected to point to its replacement 3 . Nygard's decision records are numbered in sequence, the numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded 8 . Choosing a route The route is set when a rule enters the registry, and it turns on one question: could a program tell, from the code, the configuration or the running system, that the rule has been broken, and give the same answer every time without a stream of false alarms that people learn to ignore? A rule for which the answer is yes is routed to a gate , a deterministic check that runs locally and in the pipeline and can block a merge. A rule whose breach only a person with context can recognise is routed to judgment: a named person decides against written criteria, and the decision is recorded. Either way, the agent can also be told why the rule exists, through a skill or its instructions, and that helps it get the change right first time. It is still not enforcement. An instruction asks; a gate refuses. A rule routed to guidance alone is one that no tool can check and nobody needs to sign off, such as a naming preference with no effect on correctness. It is the weakest route, and the registry makes that visible. Judgment suits rules whose breach depends on meaning rather than form. A program can list the columns a customer-record export returns, but whether a newly added column counts as personal data depends on what it holds and why the requester needs it, and a person decides that. Where a rule about structure can be written as an executable test, as many architecture goals can 4 , it belongs with a gate instead. A single rule can take two routes. R-017 limits the size of a customer-record export: the limit itself is a gate, because a check can count rows, while a request to exceed it goes to judgment, because only a person with the context can weigh a one-off business need against the risk. The route is a different axis from Birgitta Böckeler's regulation categories, which group what a harness regulates into maintainability, architecture fitness and behaviour 1 . A category says what a control is about; the route says how strongly it is enforced. The pairing is this site's own reading, not Böckeler's. How the rest of the kit refers to rules The registry is the kit's connecting structure because every other part cites it by identifier. A validator declares the rule identifiers it enforces, and its result names them. A skill declares the rules it helps the agent keep. A review skill , an agent that reads a change against the applicable rules and proposes findings, tags each finding with a rule identifier. In Böckeler's vocabulary validators are computational sensors and review skills are inferential ones 2 ; as this site's recommended practice, a review skill proposes and does not block. An evidence record lists which rule checks ran on a change and what each returned. With those references in place, questions that are otherwise guesswork have answers read straight from data: which validator enforces R-042, which gated rules have no validator yet, which skills still cite a retired rule. The Evidence schema and Skills with evals pages describe the other end of each reference. Entering, changing and retiring rules Entering. A rule enters when someone writes its entry and the owner accepts it. Agent instruction files are a good first place to look, because they often hold rules in passing: a line such as "the export job never writes customer email addresses to its logs" is a rule without an identifier. As recommended practice, each such line becomes an entry with a route and an owner, and the instruction stays where it is but cites the identifier, so the agent, a check and a reviewer all refer to the same rule. Promoting. The usual change of route is upward. A rule starts as guidance or judgment and moves to a gate once a tool can check it and it keeps being broken or keeps coming up in review. This is one step of the feedback path , in which a recurring review comment becomes a rule and a rule that keeps being violated becomes a gate. In the export example, reviewers keep writing that exports should leave out the internal notes fields. The comment enters the registry as a guidance rule with its own identifier. When the same miss appears in change after change, a validator is written, the route becomes gate, and the guidance stays behind only to explain why. One published account of harness engineering reports the same move: review comments and bugs are turned into documentation or tooling, and a rule is promoted into code when documentation is not enough 9 . The recommended practice is to write a gate for a miss that has already happened, rather than for one that might. Demoting. The route can also go down. A check found to be unreliable is treated as judgment until it is fixed, because a gate that raises false alarms trains people to override it. Checks that block need to be trusted: one large program-analysis platform put an analyser on probation once its not-useful rate, measured from developer feedback on its findings, reached 10 per cent, and could switch it off above 25 per cent 12 . Changing. A change to a rule is a reviewed change to the registry, made the way a change to code is made. The pull request shows the old and new statement and the reason, lists the validators and skills it affects, and is approved by the rule's owner. Because the registry lives in the repository, the revision an evidence record names also fixes the version of every rule the checks ran against, so a result is always read against the rule as it stood when the check ran. Exceptions. An exception lets one change depart from a rule without changing the rule. It is logged against the rule's identifier, with who allowed it and when it lapses. Several live exceptions against the same rule suggest that the rule, or its route, needs another look. A team may also mark some rules as never open to exception; an access rule such as R-042 is the obvious case. Who may grant an exception is a question of decision rights, which the map places in the operating model box of its enablement band; the registry records that an exception was granted. Retiring. A rule that is no longer needed is marked retired, with the recorded reason and a pointer to any rule that replaces it. It stays in force until that decision is recorded. Its identifier remains in the registry and is never reused. Owners and known gaps NIST's Risk Management Framework allocates each security control to the system, a part of it or its environment, so that it is clear where the control is provided 5 . The registry applies a similar idea to people at the level of a single rule, and as recommended practice gives each rule one accountable owner. In the entry this is a single name or role that can be reached, such as the security owner for R-042, never a list or a shared alias. The owner approves changes to the entry and is the person to ask when its check fails or is noisy. The known-gaps field records what the enforcement does not see. A gate proves only what its check inspects, so a passing result is read together with the gaps listed against the rule. When R-042's validator covered only the export request itself, the background worker's broader query was written down as a gap; extending the validator closed it, and the entry keeps the note. One simple measure, recommended by this site, shows whether the registry's routes are real: the number of active rules routed to a gate that no required validator cites. It can be read straight from the registry and the validators' declarations, and it falls to zero only when every gated rule is actually enforced. Which rules go in first No public study says how many rules a registry should start with. As recommended practice, the first entries come from the team's own recent history: the incidents and review comments of the last few months show which rules actually get broken, and a handful of those is enough to begin. A long first list tends to produce noise, and a check switched off for noise is hard to switch back on. These first rules and their validators, with the kit's verify command, which runs the same checks in the same way on a developer's machine and in the pipeline, and an evidence schema, make up the kit's deterministic floor . The registry then grows one rule at a time, as each new check earns the team's trust. Where it sits on the map The rule registry sits in the core band of the map, the band that does the work, as one of the five parts of the Engineering Kit box: rule registry, Validators , Skills with evals , Evidence schema and Adapters . It is the part the other four refer to. In the band's row, Harness engineering comes before the kit: it is the discipline that decides what belongs in the registry at all. Workflows come after it: they run the checks and skills that cite the registry, and their records carry rule identifiers onward. Rules flow into the registry from specifications and their access rules, recurring review comments, incidents, and the outside standards a team must meet, which an entry can reference as SEC-004 is referenced by R-042. Tracing a rule through the checks that ran to the decisions they informed is a matter for audit and traceability, which reads the registry but is not part of it. Pitfalls A registry nobody reads. The list exists as a document, but validators and skills do not cite it. Sign: checks whose results name no rule identifier, or rules that appear only in agent instruction files. Gates in name only. An entry says gate, but its validator is missing or has stayed report-only past its planned date. Sign: gated rules that no required validator cites. Speculative gates. Checks are added for rules nobody has seen broken, and the first set is too large. Sign: gates that are routinely overridden or switched off, and complaints about noise. Rules without a reason. Entries carry no link to why the rule exists. Sign: nobody can say whether a rule is still needed, so nothing is ever retired. Green read as full assurance. Known gaps are left empty. Sign: a rule whose check covers only the place where an operation is triggered, with nothing recorded about other code that reaches the same data. Reused or renumbered identifiers. An identifier is given to a new rule or recomputed after a reorganisation. Sign: old run records or review comments that point at a rule they never meant. Exceptions in place of change. The same departure is approved again and again. Sign: several live exceptions against one rule identifier. No real owner. An entry names a team alias or no one. Sign: a failing or noisy rule that stays unchanged for weeks. Related Engineering Kit : the package the registry belongs to, and its other parts. Validators : the deterministic checks that enforce gated rules, and the path from report-only to required. Skills with evals : packaged guidance for the agent, and how skills cite the rules they support. Evidence schema : the record of which rule checks ran on a change. Harness engineering : the discipline of deciding what the agent reads, what a machine checks and what a person decides. Workflows : the unit of delivery that runs the checks the registry defines. Terminology : the rule registry, rule routes and the terms above. Workflow catalog : every workflow, with the checks and decisions it holds.
