On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
safe-reference-model.html: SAFe reference model A mapping from the levels, events and Continuous Delivery Pipeline of Core SAFe to the lifecycle pages of this site, for readers who plan in SAFe terms and want to see where each delivery decision falls. Definition A reference model , in the sense OASIS gives the term, is "an abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment" 4 . OASIS wrote that definition for service-oriented architecture; this page borrows the sense and not the subject. Here the environment is delivery work in an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work). The entities are the levels, events and pipeline aspects of the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe), published by Scaled Agile, Inc., on one side, and the lifecycle pages of this site on the other. The page is "a reference model" in that sense: a mapping that shows which SAFe item lines up with which page of this site, and why. The mapping is this site's recommended practice. SAFe prints no such mapping, and no public study known to this site maps SAFe to agent-assisted delivery. The SAFe side rests on Core SAFe, the label SAFe's home page uses for the framework that AI-Native SAFe builds on 19 , as published at framework.scaledagile.com and read on 20 November 2026. The Core SAFe articles used here print no version number, and this page claims none. SAFe's configurations page is titled "SAFe 6.0 Configurations" and describes its contents as the latest version of SAFe 11 . One note on AI-Native SAFe. AI-Native SAFe builds on Core SAFe, which continues alongside it 19 . In AI-Native SAFe, a two-hour Sense and Respond event at the boundary of every iteration replaces the Core SAFe event Inspect and Adapt , and also includes the activities that were in the System Demo 6 . Both events are described below. Every other statement on this page rests on Core SAFe. The page is not SAFe guidance, not a prescription and not a description of any organisation. It does not say how any organisation plans, staffs or runs its delivery. Three SAFe levels are used, each defined here in SAFe's words so that the page reads without SAFe's own site: Portfolio is "a set of value streams that delivers a continuous flow of valuable solutions to customers within a common funding and governance model" 29 . Agile Release Train (ART) is "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream" 7 . Agile Team is "a cross-functional group of typically ten or fewer individuals with all the skills necessary to define, build, test, and deliver value to their customer" 5 . SAFe also names Large Solution SAFe, "for enterprises building large and complex solutions that do not require portfolio concerns" 25 , and the Solution Train, "the organizational construct used to build large solutions that requires the coordination of multiple ARTs and suppliers" 33 . This model maps neither. Why it matters A reader whose organisation plans in SAFe terms meets two vocabularies, the framework's and this site's, and the delivery decisions that matter run across both. Without a mapping, two things go wrong. A decision is placed at the wrong level, because a level name does not say which question belongs to it: a readiness question that one team should settle before it takes the work on is carried to an event for the whole train, or a funding question is settled inside a team. And events are copied without the decisions they serve, so a planning or review meeting is held on schedule while nobody can say which question it answers, which record it draws on or where its outcome is written down. The mapping below keeps each event tied to the decisions (see workflows ) and records it touches. This is recommended-practice reasoning from the structure of the two vocabularies, not a finding. The site keeps its own generic level labels, Portfolio, Train and Team, so that its pages do not depend on one framework's vocabulary. SAFe is cited as one framework whose levels sit at the same altitudes under its own names: Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team. This page is where the two sets of names are joined, so a reader can start from either. The join matters more once agents do part of the work. DORA's announcement of its 2025 report puts the risk plainly: "AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there" 3 . A team's levels, events and the decisions that belong to each are part of what is already there. If they are clear, agent assistance speeds them up; if they are blurred, it speeds up the blur. No public study known to this site maps SAFe to agent-assisted delivery, so the mapping below is this site's recommended practice, stated as such wherever it makes a join. How it works What the model takes from SAFe The model takes three levels (Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team), a set of SAFe events and timeboxes, and the four aspects of SAFe's Continuous Delivery Pipeline . It takes the work items that sit at each level only as far as the levels need them. SAFe's Planning Interval (PI) is "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives" 18 . The three Core SAFe cadence figures below are typical; none is a default or a requirement. A Planning Interval is typically 8 to 12 weeks. SAFe calls 8 to 12 weeks a good starting point and describes the pattern it gives for a PI as a suggestion rather than a strict rule 18 . PI Planning is typically two days 28 . Iteration Planning is about 90 minutes for a two-week iteration 23 . One sequence is enough for the mapping. A PI begins with PI Planning 18 . Inspect and Adapt is a significant event held at the end of each PI, and its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event 22 . The model says nothing about the order of events inside an iteration. Levels The table sets each SAFe level against the generic label this site gives the same altitude and the decision on this site that lines up with it. The labels link to the sections of the lifecycle levels page. Each decision is named as in the workflow catalog , and its identifier links to its row there. SAFe level Label on this site What SAFe places at the level Decision on this site that lines up with it Portfolio, a set of value streams under "a common funding and governance model" 29 Portfolio : initiatives, prioritisation, budgets Funding and prioritisation: Lean budgets and their guardrails, Strategic Themes, the Portfolio Backlog of epics, and WSJF 26 21 35 30 39 Intake and classification ( W01 ) Agile Release Train, a "long-lived team of Agile teams" 7 Train : features, planning cycle, integrated demo Features delivered within a Planning Interval, with PI Planning, PI Objectives, the ART backlog, the System Demo and Inspect and Adapt 17 18 27 8 36 22 Specification readiness ( W04 ); plan and architecture conformance ( W08 ) Agile Team, a cross-functional group with the skills to define, build, test and deliver value 5 Team : stories, iterations, readiness and done Stories, the Team Backlog, the iteration, Iteration Planning and Team Backlog Refinement 34 37 23 Task traceability and test planning ( W12 ) The decision in the last column sits beside the level's work. The site does not assign workflows to levels, as the lifecycle levels page states, so the column says which decision a level's events and work items line up with and not which altitude runs it. The paragraphs below give SAFe's own wording for each level's work items. Portfolio. In SAFe the portfolio level holds funding and prioritisation. Lean budgets are "a financial governance approach that funds value streams instead of projects" 26 , and Lean budget guardrails "describe the policies and practices for budgeting, spending, and governance for a specific portfolio" 21 . Strategic Themes are portfolio-level business objectives that connect the enterprise strategy to a portfolio 35 . The Portfolio Backlog is "a Kanban system that is used to capture and manage the business and enabler epics intended to create and evolve the portfolio's products, services, and solutions" 30 , and an Epic is "a significant solution development initiative" 16 . In SAFe, WSJF (weighted shortest job first) is estimated as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size 39 . Cost of Delay is the money or value lost by delaying or not doing a job for a time period, relative to other jobs 15 . SAFe's WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen's The Principles of Product Development Flow 39 , and this site credits WSJF to SAFe. On this site's side, the decision that lines up with this level is intake and classification ( W01 ). The join is recommended practice. Both the SAFe items and the intake decision concern which work is taken up and how it is classified, and the map labels the level "initiatives · prioritisation · budgets". Agile Release Train. A Feature is "solution functionality that delivers business value, fulfills a stakeholder need, and is sized to be delivered by an Agile Release Train within a PI" 17 . PI Planning is "a cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision" 28 , and PI Objectives "summarize the business and technical goals that teams and trains intend to achieve in the upcoming PI and are either committed or uncommitted" 27 . The ART backlog is "a Kanban system used to capture and manage the features and enablers that enhance the solution" 8 . The System Demo and Inspect and Adapt are set against pages of this site in the events table below. On this site's side, the decisions that line up with this level are specification readiness ( W04 ) and plan and architecture conformance ( W08 ). Their pages are Specification and Design . The join is recommended practice and is stated only for the records these decisions leave, which the site offers to a planning event. Agile Team. A Story is a short description of a small piece of desired functionality written from the user's perspective, and keeping stories small ensures they can be completed in a single iteration 34 . The Team Backlog is "a Kanban system that is used to capture and manage the user stories and enablers intended to enhance the solution" 37 . The team level is where stories are taken from that backlog into an iteration: in Iteration Planning "the team defines, organizes, and commits to the work for the next iteration" 23 . On this site's side, the decision that lines up with this level is task traceability and test planning ( W12 ). The map labels the level "stories · iterations · DoR / DoD". The join is recommended practice. The model maps decisions, not roles. SAFe defines roles of its own 7 . This site names the role accountable for each decision in the workflow catalog, so no row on this page maps one SAFe role to one role of this site. Events and cadence The table sets each SAFe event the model uses against the page and workflow catalog row it lines up with on this site. Apart from the sequence given above, in which a PI begins with PI Planning 18 , the order of the rows implies no order of events. Each join is this site's recommended mapping: the column of SAFe's words quotes what SAFe's pages say an event is or produces, and none of the SAFe pages cited here says that an event reads a record of this site. SAFe event In SAFe's words Lines up with on this site Why the join holds System Demo "provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART" 36 Release ; release readiness ( W25 ) Both bring the results of several changes together before a decision. The join is loose: the demo shows working features to stakeholders. Iteration "a standard, fixed-duration timebox during which Agile Teams and ARTs individually and collectively deliver incremental customer value while working towards the PI objectives" 24 Develop, Build and QA The iteration is the container and the three phases are the path one change takes inside it. The site draws one workflow, pull-request verification ( W23 ), across the three phases. Inspect and Adapt "a significant event held at the end of each PI", "structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop" 22 . The workshop is "a structured approach to identifying the root cause and actions to address systemic problems" 31 . Its output is "improvement backlog items that go into the ART Backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event" 22 , and the ART backlog is a Kanban system for the features and enablers that enhance the solution 8 Inspect and Adapt ; incident-to-development feedback ( W28 ) Both turn what was learned into changes to a backlog: SAFe's improvement backlog items on one side, and on this site's side a decision on which workflow to add or tighten next. Team Backlog Refinement "an event that helps Agile Teams clarify and prepare upcoming stories and features" 38 Specification ; specification readiness ( W04 ) The clarifying and preparing that SAFe's sentence names is the work that answers the specification readiness decision. PI Planning "a cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision", typically two days long, with outputs of "committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies" 28 . PI Objectives "summarize the business and technical goals that teams and trains intend to achieve in the upcoming PI and are either committed or uncommitted" 27 Specification ; specification readiness ( W04 ); Design ; plan and architecture conformance ( W08 ) PI Planning ends in commitments, and specification readiness and plan and architecture conformance are the decisions on this site that come before work is committed to. Iteration Planning "the team defines, organizes, and commits to the work for the next iteration", in about 90 minutes for a two-week iteration 23 . Iteration Goals are "a high-level summary of the business and technical goals that an Agile Team agrees to accomplish in an Iteration" 20 Definition of Ready and Done ; task traceability and test planning ( W12 ) Both concern which work a team takes on. The lengths in the table are SAFe's typical figures and not defaults; the Pitfalls section returns to this. The Continuous Delivery Pipeline against the phases SAFe describes its Continuous Delivery Pipeline as "the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value", with four aspects in this order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand 10 . This site draws nine phases, in order: Idea, Specification, Design, Develop, Build, QA, Deploy, Release and Operate. SAFe aspect In SAFe's words Phases on this site Decision that lines up with it Continuous exploration "continually exploring the market and customer needs, defining a vision, roadmap, and set of features for a solution" 13 Idea , Specification Intake and classification ( W01 ) and specification readiness ( W04 ) Continuous integration "new functionality is developed, tested, integrated, and validated in preparation for deployment and release" 14 Develop, Build and QA Pull-request verification ( W23 ) Continuous deployment "automates the migration of new functionality from a staging environment to production, where it is made available for release" 12 Deploy Deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ) Release on demand "releases new functionality immediately or incrementally based on business and customer needs" 32 Release Release readiness ( W25 ) Two phases have no row. SAFe's four aspects include none named for design or for operation, and the table does not force a row for either. On this site's side, Design sits between the first two aspects, and Operate follows the last. SAFe separates deployment from release. It states that "it's optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing" 12 and that releases are "decoupled from the work to deploy the functionality" 32 . This site draws the same line: Deploy and Release are separate phases with separate decisions, deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ) and release readiness ( W25 ), and the Deploy page sets out the difference between deploying a build and releasing a change. The join of aspects to phases is this site's recommended mapping. Ready, done and quality SAFe's glossary defines the Definition of Done as something that "specifies the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value" 20 . The Scrum Guide describes it as a formal description of the state of the increment 40 . Both treat done as a defined state that work either meets or does not. The site's Definition of Done, which it takes from the Scrum Guide, applies that state at three points: a story, an increment and a release. The map places its tag at Release, and the Definition of Ready and Done page sets out each point. Built-in quality is, in SAFe's words, "a set of practices to help ensure that the outputs of Agile teams in business and technology domains meet appropriate quality standards throughout the process of creating customer value" 9 . The counterpart on this site, as recommended practice, is the set of validators 2 that run in Develop, Build and QA , each leaving an evidence record . The entrance to the work is set out on this site's side by the Definition of Ready . The export feature through the model The customer-record export is a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records. It is the site's running example . The linked page follows the export through each workflow, and this page adds only where those workflows sit against SAFe: the export's open readiness question, which roles may export which records, is settled at specification readiness ( W04 ), the decision the events table sets beside Team Backlog Refinement and PI Planning. That placement is this site's recommended mapping, not a statement from SAFe. Where it sits on the map The page has no box on the map. A reader reaches it from the Portfolio, Train and Team labels in the lifecycle band, whose page, lifecycle levels , names SAFe as one framework that uses those altitudes. A reader also reaches it from the lifecycle section's navigation and from the terminology entries for the SAFe terms used here, such as the Agile Release Train, the Planning Interval, WSJF and Inspect and Adapt. Within the lifecycle band the page connects to the lifecycle levels page, to the phase pages named in the pipeline table, to Definition of Ready and Done , to the traceability spine that ties requirement to incident by identifier, and to Inspect and Adapt . In the core band it connects to Workflows , the Software factory , Harness engineering 1 , the Evidence schema and the Rule registry . Some labels outside the lifecycle band still carry SAFe's own words. The operating model box in the enablement band mentions an Agile Release Train, a PI cadence, a system demo and Inspect and Adapt, while the lifecycle band uses the generic labels Portfolio, Train and Team. A reader moving between bands therefore meets both vocabularies on the map, and this page is the join between them. Pitfalls Reading the mapping as SAFe's own, or as a requirement. The joins on this page are this site's recommended practice and carry no authority from SAFe. A reference model, in the OASIS sense, is a framework for understanding relationships. Sign: a plan or a standard cites this page as the framework's rule, or attributes one of its joins to Scaled Agile. Treating typical cadence figures as defaults. SAFe calls 8 to 12 weeks a good starting point for a Planning Interval and describes its pattern for a PI as a suggestion rather than a strict rule 18 . Sign: a calendar is fixed at the typical length of a PI, a planning event or an iteration planning meeting, with no reason recorded for the choice. Forcing one workflow per SAFe event. SAFe defines events by their purpose and timebox, for example PI Planning as "a cadence-based event for the entire ART" 28 and Inspect and Adapt as "a significant event held at the end of each PI" 22 . One event can line up with several decisions (see Workflows ), as PI Planning does with specification readiness ( W04 ) and plan and architecture conformance ( W08 ) in the events table, and decisions such as pull-request verification ( W23 ) and deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ) line up with a pipeline aspect and with no event. Sign: a workflow is named after a meeting, or a decision with no meeting has no workflow. Reading "done" as "released". The Scrum Guide says an item that does not meet the Definition of Done "cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review" 40 . Meeting it is a condition for a release decision, not the decision, and SAFe keeps deployment and release apart for the same reason 12 32 . Sign: stories are counted as delivered before any release decision has been made on them. Related Lifecycle levels : the three altitudes this page maps, with the decisions each one holds. Definition of Ready and Done : the readiness and done conditions the events and quality rows refer to. Traceability spine : the identifier chain from requirement to incident. Inspect and Adapt : the checkpoint this page lines up with SAFe's event of the same name. Idea , Specification , Design , Develop, Build and QA , Deploy , Release and Operate : the phases set against the pipeline aspects. Workflows . Software factory . Harness engineering , Evidence schema and Rule registry . Workflow catalog : rows intake and classification ( W01 ), specification readiness ( W04 ), plan and architecture conformance ( W08 ), task traceability and test planning ( W12 ), pull-request verification ( W23 ), release readiness ( W25 ), deployment and post-deploy verification ( W26 ) and incident-to-development feedback ( W28 ). Terminology : the reference model, the SAFe terms and their credits. Sources The mapping of SAFe items to the pages of this site, and the statement that no public study known to this site maps SAFe to agent-assisted delivery, are this site's recommended practice and carry no source. The sources below support the SAFe-side wording and the two outside definitions. The reference-model definition: OASIS 4 . Core SAFe as a label, the configurations page title, and the AI-Native note: 19 , 11 , 6 . Levels and their work items: 29 , 7 , 5 , 25 , 33 , 26 , 21 , 35 , 30 , 16 , 39 , 15 , 17 , 34 , 37 . Events, timeboxes and cadence figures: 18 , 28 , 27 , 36 , 22 , 31 , 8 , 23 , 38 , 24 , 20 . The Continuous Delivery Pipeline: 10 , 13 , 14 , 12 , 32 . Done and quality: 20 , 9 , 40 . AI and delivery: 3 . Defines the Definition of Done as a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product, and as the Increment's commitment, as the Product Goal and the Sprint Goal are the commitments of the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Says the moment a Product Backlog item meets it an Increment is born, and an item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review; an organisational Definition of Done is followed by all Scrum Teams as a minimum, otherwise the Scrum Team creates one appropriate for the product, and teams on one product must mutually define and comply with the same one; the Developers are accountable for instilling quality by adhering to it and are required to conform to it. Does not use the term Definition of Ready; says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event. Describes refinement as an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order and size, with the Developers who will be doing the work responsible for the sizing, and makes the Product Owner accountable for effective Product Backlog management, including creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items and ordering them. Names transparency, inspection and adaptation as the empirical Scrum pillars and says inspection without adaptation is considered pointless. The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to increase quality and effectiveness and inspects individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the Definition of Done; impactful improvements may be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint. An Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint, and the Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value. Describes Product Backlog refinement as the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items; counts ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood among the Product Owner's accountabilities; says the Product Owner may delegate the responsibility to others but remains accountable, and that the entire organization must respect the Product Owner's decisions, which are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog. Says the emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work, and that low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk. ↩ ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
skills-and-evals.html: Skills with evals A skill is packaged guidance a coding agent loads when a task calls for it; because it shapes behaviour without guaranteeing it, it ships with a record of scenario evaluations rather than on one passing run. Definition A skill is a packaged piece of guidance that a coding agent loads only when the task in hand calls for it: a short name and description the agent scans, a body of instructions it reads once it decides the skill applies, and, optionally, scripts and reference files it can use along the way. 4 3 The folder-and-file format is published as an open specification that a range of AI systems use. 8 3 In Birgitta Böckeler's vocabulary a skill is a guide, a control that steers the agent before it acts, as opposed to a sensor, which observes the result afterwards. 5 On this site a skill also names the rules it supports, and it ships with evals: a set of scenarios that test whether an agent working with the skill behaves as intended, run repeatedly and recorded across versions. A review skill is the sensor counterpart. It reads a change against the applicable rules and reports findings, which is what Böckeler calls an inferential sensor. 6 Why it matters In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), much of what a team knows about doing the work well has to reach the agent somehow: which records an export may return, which fields never leave the system, when to stop and ask. Written once as a skill, that know-how reaches every task that needs it without filling the agent's context on tasks that do not. 4 The risk is that a team starts treating the skill as a guarantee. Böckeler warns that as long as a language model is involved, the outcome remains a matter of probability. 4 One vendor's skill-authoring guidance uses exactly that failure as its worked example: an agent writes a query and leaves out a filter that the loaded skill tells it to apply. 7 The same prompt can also produce different code from one request to the next, and setting temperature to zero reduces that variation without removing it. 11 Two things follow. A skill cannot be the thing that enforces a rule, because nothing about loading it makes the agent comply. And a skill cannot be accepted the way a deterministic check is, on one green run, because the next run may differ. Without evals, a team cannot tell whether a skill helps, does nothing, or quietly makes the agent worse, and it cannot tell whether a model upgrade has changed any of that. 2 How it works Route the rule first. Every rule in the rule registry carries a route: gate, judgment or guidance. A skill serves the guidance route, and it may also help the agent meet a rule that a gate enforces. This site recommends a clear division of labour between validators and skills. When a validator can decide a rule, the validator carries it. A skill that touches the same rule can show the agent what a compliant change looks like, through examples and a loop of validating and fixing, 7 and this site recommends that it also explain why the rule exists, so the validator seldom has to fail. A skill earns its place in work that turns on interpretation, where no deterministic check reaches. Write the skill for on-demand loading. Until the agent decides the skill applies, it sees only the name and description, so the description states plainly which tasks the skill is for. The main file carries what nearly every use of the skill needs. Material that only some uses need goes in separate files that the main file points to. Any step that must give an identical result every time is a script the agent executes, not prose it interprets. 3 7 The skill cites the identifiers of the rules it supports, so the registry can list every skill that touches a rule. That link is this site's recommended practice; no public source describes it. Build the eval set before trusting the skill. An eval gives the agent an input, lets it work, and applies grading logic to the result. Each case pairs a realistic request with a description of success and one or more graders, and a set tests both the cases where a behaviour should occur and the cases where it should not. 2 1 Skill evals also check activation: some cases name the skill, others are ordinary requests that never mention it, to see whether the agent picks it up unprompted. 10 Practitioner guidance suggests that a small set of tasks drawn from real failures is enough to start. 2 The expected behaviour comes from the specification and the rule, not from the skill's own text, so that the eval has an independent basis . For the customer-record export , an access-rule skill supports R-042: it guides the agent to return only the records the caller may read, and to stop and ask when the specification leaves the access rule open. Its eval set might hold these cases. Case Input Passes when Access rule left open A specification for the export that does not say who may read which records The agent stops and asks instead of choosing a rule Unprompted activation A plain request to speed up the export, with no mention of access The agent still loads the skill and keeps the filter Already correct An export whose access rule is settled and implemented The agent leaves the filtering as it is Excluded field A request to add a field the specification leaves out of the export The agent points out the conflict with the specification Review skill A change whose background worker runs a broader query than the request path The review skill reports the broader query against R-042 The skill does not enforce R-042; its validator is what fails a change that returns records the caller may not read. The skill makes that failure less likely, and the evals show by how much. Run each case more than once. Because output varies between runs, each case runs as several trials. 2 Two summaries matter. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k trials succeeds; pass^k, proposed in agent-benchmark research, is the chance that all k succeed, and it falls as k rises, which makes it the stricter measure of reliability. 12 2 A case that passes on some runs and fails on others is flaky and needs investigating, not re-running until it passes. 1 Choose the grader to fit the check. Code-based graders are fast, cheap and reproducible but brittle to valid variation; model-based graders handle nuance but are themselves non-deterministic and need calibrating against people; human graders are the most trustworthy and the slowest. Mechanical checks, such as whether the query filters by caller, belong in code. 2 1 A model used as a grader is the practice Zheng and colleagues studied as LLM-as-a-judge . In their study the strongest judge agreed with human preferences more than 80% of the time, about as often as people agree with each other, and it showed position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. 13 Agreement with human grading is checked at the start and again from time to time. 2 9 Keep an evaluation history. Each run of the set compares the skill against a baseline: the same prompts without the skill, or the previous version of the skill. 1 Guidance on testing skills treats the aim as a score that can be compared over time. 10 This site recommends that the history record, for each skill version, the version of the eval set, the model and tool versions, the number of trials and the results, and that a skill ships only with such a history. That bar is recommended practice, not a published finding. Re-run when anything that shapes behaviour changes. Practitioner guidance runs evals on each change to the agent and on each model upgrade, and vendor guidance advises testing a skill with every model it will be used with. 2 7 After a change to the skill, every case runs again, not only the one that prompted the change. 1 This site adds two triggers as recommended practice: a change to a tool the skill relies on, and a change to any rule the skill cites, which also means revising the skill before its evals run. Once a skill is reliable, its cases become a regression suite that is expected to pass almost every time. 2 Keep the review skill advisory. A review skill reads a diff against the rules and reports findings tagged to rule identifiers. Böckeler notes that inferential sensors can address concerns such as semantic duplication only partially. 5 So, as this site's recommended practice, the review skill proposes and a validator or a named person decides. It is evaluated like any other skill, with cases where it should raise a finding and cases where it should stay quiet. Until those results show how often it is right and how often it raises a false alarm, its findings inform reviewers and nothing more; what weight they carry after that is set in the assurance band of the map. Every finding costs a human reviewer some attention, so a noisy review skill is expensive. These are recommended practice. Decide when a practice becomes a skill. The usual trigger is repetition: the team finds itself typing the same guidance into agent sessions again and again. 7 Vendor guidance suggests starting from where the agent struggles on representative tasks 3 , and writing the evaluation cases first, from failures already seen, and the skill text after them. 7 Guidance that turns out to be a checkable rule goes to a validator, as described under routing above. This site recommends that someone answers for each skill: that person keeps its eval set current and removes the skill once nothing depends on it. Where it sits on the map Skills with evals is one of the five parts of the Engineering Kit , in the core band, the band that does the work. The kit is the versioned, installable package that carries a team's reusable harness. Next to skills sit the rule registry, which gives each skill the rules it supports; the validators, which enforce what a skill only encourages; the evidence schema , which fixes the shape of what a run records; and the adapters that bind the kit to the team's tools. In the map's core row, Harness engineering comes before the kit and supplies the split between guides and sensors; Workflows come after it and use skills inside their agent tasks and the review skill inside their checks. The feedback path feeds all of this: a procedure the agent keeps needing becomes a skill, and a failure in production becomes a new eval case. 5 Pitfalls A skill carrying a rule that must always hold. The only defence for the access rule is a paragraph in a skill. Sign: a rule routed to a gate in the registry has skills citing it but no validator. Shipping on one good run. The skill passed once, on one model, and nobody kept the result. Sign: no baseline comparison, a single trial per case, and no model version in the record. Evals that grade the skill against itself. Expected behaviour is copied from the skill's text, so the eval can only confirm what the skill already says. Sign: case descriptions that paraphrase the skill rather than the specification or the rule. Only happy-path cases. Every case expects the skill to produce a change. Sign: no case in which the skill should stay out of the way, and the skill starts rewriting exports that were already correct. An unchecked model grader. The model-based grader's scores are accepted without anyone reading transcripts. 2 Sign: no record of how often the grader and a person agree. Stale history. The model or a cited rule changed and the evals did not run again. Sign: the last recorded run names an older model, tool or rule version than the one in use. Re-running a flaky case until it passes. Sign: the same case alternates between pass and fail across runs, and the recorded result is only the last one. 1 Skills without a failure behind them. Skills written on speculation pile up, each one more thing to maintain. Sign: nobody can name the repeated miss a skill fixes, who answers for it, or when its evals last ran. Outside skills installed unread. A skill from another team or a public collection is someone else's instructions and code, acting with the agent's access. Sign: a skill in use that nobody on the team has read, or whose scripts nobody has checked for what they send or fetch. Putting it through the team's usual supply-chain review is recommended practice. Treating review findings as verdicts. The review skill's output decides merges, or reviewers dismiss it wholesale. Sign: merges approved or held on a finding alone, or findings closed without a reason. Related Validators : the deterministic checks that enforce what a skill only encourages. Rule registry : where each rule's identifier, route and owner live, and which skills cite it. Engineering Kit : the package that carries skills, evals and the other parts. Harness engineering : the discipline, including guides, sensors and the two kinds of control. Evidence schema : the fixed shape of what a run records. Workflows : where skills and the review skill are used in delivery. Terminology and the workflow catalog .
