Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. On this site, an architecture rule expressed as a fitness function that runs with the build is a validator, and an architecture gate once it blocks. adopted ford-evolutionary-architectures Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a verify command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a few validators for rules the team has broken before, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency rules, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Flexible and scalable, but itself non-deterministic and subject to position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so its grades are checked against human judgement before they are relied on. In an eval set it is one kind of grader, alongside code-based checks and human review. adopted zheng-llm-judge Evidence record What a run records in one fixed shape, as a by-product of the run rather than a report written afterwards: schema version, change and configuration revisions, kit version, the checks expected before the run, each check's result with its rule ID, status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending and taken, and an overall status derived from the rest. Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable), it timed out again after one retry, or the tool itself crashed. It is never reported as passed or skipped; what it means for a merge or release is decided in assurance. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. The name is this site's; the distinction is established, for example in SARIF's record of whether a tool's execution succeeded, and in test frameworks that report errors apart from failures. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives), a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended), a work tracker, or a tool server the agent calls. It translates; it holds no rules, validator logic or schema. The test of an adapter is how little is in it. Adapted from Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters pattern (see that entry): his adapters sit at an application's ports, and this site applies the idea to the one layer of a kit that talks to outside tools. adapted cockburn-hexagonal Ports and adapters Alistair Cockburn's architecture pattern, also called hexagonal architecture: an application talks to the outside world only through ports, and a technology-specific adapter at each port translates between the outside device and the application, so the application can be driven by people, programs or tests and developed apart from the devices and databases it runs against. The Engineering Kit's tool adapters apply the same idea to the tools a kit runs against. adopted cockburn-hexagonal Anticorruption layer Eric Evans's domain-driven design pattern: an isolating layer that talks to another system through its existing interface and translates between the two models, so the other system's concepts do not reshape the model that uses it. A kit's adapters play this part between the kit's core and a tool's own vocabulary. adopted evans-ddd-reference Contract test Martin Fowler's name for a test that checks a test double still behaves like the real outside service it stands in for. It runs apart from the main build, at the pace the outside service changes. On this site, the contract suite a kit's core defines for each kind of adapter is the same idea pointed at the kit's own interface. adopted fowler-contract-test Consumer-driven contract Ian Robinson's service-evolution pattern: the consumers of a service state their expectations as tests, and the provider is checked against all of them, so it can change without breaking any consumer. adopted robinson-cdc Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. The idea of scaling test effort to risk comes from risk-based testing. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating state that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. Coined in this sense. Earlier uses of the phrase mean something else: Cusumano (1991) for Japanese firms that applied production-management discipline to large-scale software development, and Greenfield and Short (2004) for model-driven production of variants of a standard product. Recent writing on the "dark software factory", where agents produce software that no person reviews, is not what is meant either, nor is the industrial sense of identical outputs from a fixed process. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, plan and tasks, with clarification added where the specification leaves questions open. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. The law does not say fewer controls are better. This site's recommendation follows from shrinking what is governed: narrow what the agent may produce first, on a few well-defined execution surfaces, then start with a small set of controls fitted to failures actually seen. adopted ashby Portfolio, train and team levels One delivery lifecycle seen at three altitudes: portfolio, train and team. A portfolio decides which initiatives to fund, in what order and with what budget. A train decides which features enter a planning cycle and what an integrated demonstration shows. A team decides which stories to build in an iteration and when work counts as ready and as done. Intent and rules flow down the levels; evidence and lessons flow up. The three labels are generic names introduced by this site. SAFe names the same altitudes Portfolio, Agile Release Train and Agile Team and is cited as one framework that uses them, not as the source of the labels. coined Agile Release Train (ART) SAFe's name for the train level: "a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers, and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream". Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc.; this site uses "train" as the generic label for the same altitude. adopted safe-art Planning Interval (PI) SAFe's name for the planning cycle of a train: "a cadence-based timebox in which Agile Release Trains deliver continuous value to customers in alignment with PI Objectives". SAFe describes it as typically an 8 to 12-week timebox, and calls the pattern of PI Planning and iterations a suggestion rather than a strict rule. Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
software-factory.html: Software factory The operating state that appears when delivery workflows share one set of rules, one evidence format and one feedback path, so that what production teaches changes what the next specification asks. Definition A software factory , in the sense this site uses, is the operating state that appears when enough delivery workflows share one set of rules, one format for evidence and one path for feedback, so that what production teaches changes what the next specification asks. It is not a product, a platform or a team that can be bought or set up on a given day. It is a property of how workflows that already run are connected. In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the factory keeps people at every decision point: what makes it a factory is the shared thread of rule identifiers, evidence and recorded decisions, not unattended output. The sense is coined by this site, and the phrase has older meanings that are not intended here. Cusumano used it for Japanese firms that applied engineering and production-management discipline to large-scale software development 5 . Greenfield and Short used it for a configuration of languages, patterns, frameworks and tools that produces variants of a standard product from models 12 . Both describe standardised, repeatable production. Recent practitioner writing uses "dark software factory" for the far end of agent-assisted development, named after a factory run by robots with the lights out 17 , and one publicly described team works to the principles that code is neither written nor reviewed by people, with validation against scenarios in place of code review 20 . This site means neither identical outputs nor removed human review. Why it matters A single workflow improves one delivery decision. Several workflows that share nothing improve several decisions separately, and each lesson stays where it was learned. An incident is fixed in code, and the next specification repeats the gap that let it through. Each workflow keeps its own copy of the rules, and the copies drift until two workflows enforce different versions of the same rule. Evidence written in one format cannot be read by the next workflow unless someone copies it across by hand. Research on AI adoption suggests why the connections matter more as agents do more of the work. DORA's 2025 research describes AI's primary role as an amplifier that magnifies an organisation's existing strengths and weaknesses 8 . DORA's announcement of that report observes a positive relationship between AI adoption and software delivery throughput, and a continuing negative relationship with software delivery stability 7 . Its 2024 research found that AI adoption negatively affects software delivery stability and throughput, and reminded teams that fundamentals such as small batch sizes and robust testing remain crucial 6 . DORA also groups customer feedback with value-stream visibility, small batches and team experimentation as capabilities that help predict delivery and organisational performance 10 . None of this is a finding about software factories: no public study shows that connecting agent workflows through shared rules, evidence and feedback improves outcomes. What follows is recommended practice, built on that adjacent evidence. How it works It emerges from workflows that already run No team starts by building a factory. It starts with one workflow that runs on real changes, such as pull-request verification , and adds another once the first is trusted. Shared parts appear when a second workflow needs something the first already has: it reads the access rule from the registry instead of keeping its own copy, and it reads check results in the format the first workflow already writes. Nothing moves into the shared layer until a workflow in use has needed it. Guidance on internal platforms points the same way. The Thoughtworks Technology Radar observes that teams often aim for too much of a platform vision too fast, and recommends growing a platform in increments 19 from what Team Topologies calls the thinnest viable platform: a platform kept no thicker than its users need, which can start as little more than a wiki page 18 . DORA lists quality internal platforms among the capabilities that amplify the benefits of AI 9 , so the risk lies in building shared parts ahead of the workflows that show what they must hold, not in having them. Growing the shared layer only from workflows that already run is this site's recommended practice. Three things are shared Rules. One rule registry holds the rules that apply across changes, each with an identifier, a route (a gate that blocks, a named person's judgment, or guidance) and an owner, and every workflow reads that registry rather than a copy of it. Material about a single change, such as its specification, plan and evidence, stays in version control with that change's code and is reviewed alongside it. Keeping it out of the registry keeps the registry small enough for its owners to keep current. Evidence. Every workflow writes its results in the one shape the evidence schema fixes, and the next workflow reads that record instead of asking the same questions again. A check that produced no verdict is recorded as could_not_run with its cause, and each human decision carries a reason code from a fixed list rather than free text. Because the codes are shared, a later workflow can act on a decision without interpreting prose, and a team can count how often each reason recurs across all its workflows. Keeping one list of reason codes for every workflow is recommended practice. Feedback. One feedback path decides where each lesson goes, and the change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. Böckeler calls the same practice the steering loop, in which people improve the harness (the context, tools, permissions and checks around an agent) based on recurring failures 2 . She also proposes harness templates, bundles of guides and sensors for a common type of service, which carry one team's controls to the next service of the same kind 2 . The Engineering Kit is the artefact that carries the shared rules, the deterministic checks (what Böckeler's sensors writing treats as computational sensors 3 ) and the evidence schema from one workflow and one team to the next. Production feedback reaches specification An incident review asks where the gap first became possible, not only where it showed. If nobody asked the question that would have exposed it, the action lands in specification readiness ; if a rule existed but nothing checked it, the action becomes a check tied to that rule's identifier. The site reliability engineering workbook notes that postmortem action items with little or no ownership are less likely to be resolved 11 , so each action names one owner and the stage it changes. Because every workflow reads the same registry and writes the same record, one change upstream reaches every later change of that kind. A new check or a tighter threshold does not start as a gate. It runs report-only first, recording what it would have blocked, and becomes required once its failures prove to be real problems rather than noise, since a gate that raises false alarms teaches people to override it. Repeated exceptions travel the same path: when one rule collects the same exception change after change, the pattern goes back to the rule's owner as a question about the rule or its route, instead of being granted once more. Both are this site's recommended practice. The running example across workflows In the customer-record export , a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records, the specification readiness workflow finds that the specification does not yet say which roles may export which records, the question the access rule R-042 turns on. The product owner answers it before planning, because it concerns what the feature is for; the security owner, who owns R-042, confirms that the answer stays within the rule. The pull-request verification workflow reads that readiness record and runs the R-042 validator and the 50k-row load scenario tied to the volume-limit rule R-017. On the first pull request the validator fails on the background worker's broader query, and the load scenario reports could_not_run because the load-test tool is missing from the runner image. The worker's query is narrowed, the runner image gains the tool, and the checks run again. The release readiness workflow reads the resulting evidence record instead of asking the same questions again. In production, a scheduled full export, within R-017's limit but far larger than the 50k-row scenario, times out. The incident review traces the miss to specification: nobody asked what the largest export would be, so the scenario was sized for ordinary requests. Three changes follow. A larger load scenario joins the checks tied to R-017, the agent's evaluation set gains a case for the long-running export, and the readiness workflow now asks every export-like specification for the largest export it expects. The next export-like feature meets that question before planning starts. The identifiers R-042 and R-017 run through every record in the story; that shared thread, not any tool, is the factory. People keep the decisions In each workflow the agent does the drafting: open questions on a specification, plans, code and first reviews. Deterministic checks settle whatever can be settled mechanically, and named people decide what needs context no workflow holds, such as which roles may export which records. The agent never fills a decision field in the evidence record. Morris describes the human role as working on the loop: people build and adjust the loop that produces the work, rather than inspecting every output or leaving the agents to it 14 . Autonomy widens in that direction. When the same human correction keeps recurring, it becomes a rule and a check, and the person's review narrows to what the checks cannot decide; the decision point stays, while the mechanical part of it moves to a gate. Widening autonomy only by turning repeated judgments into checks, never by dropping an approval, is this site's recommended practice. Where it sits on the map The software factory is the fourth box of the core band (band 3, "what does the work"). The row reads Harness engineering, then the Engineering Kit , then Workflows, then the software factory: it comes after the discipline, the artefact and the unit of work. The map labels it the operating state and draws it with a dashed border, because it emerges from the other three rather than being built beside them. It is distinct from the operating model box in the enablement band, which covers team cadence and decision rights. In the lifecycle band, the map places each workflow in its phase, draws the loop by which incident feedback changes what specification asks, and runs a traceability spine from requirement to incident, linked by rule identifiers. The spine and the periodic review of delivery evidence are covered on the Traceability spine and Inspect and Adapt 15 pages. The enablement band holds the runtime and tools, the people and roles, and that operating model, all of which the factory depends on. The assurance band holds the evidence record on every run and the measurement that shows whether the connections help. The adoption path's final stage, "Factory emerges", is where a team tests whether it has reached this state; that stage sets the criteria. Pitfalls Skill erosion. Bainbridge argued that when automation does most of a task, people are left monitoring it, and manual skills they no longer practise deteriorate, which makes taking over harder 1 . A survey of knowledge workers found that higher confidence in generative AI went with less critical thinking, on self-reported data 13 . The factory relies on human judgment at every decision point, so as recommended practice the people who hold those decisions still do some of the work unaided. The sign is people who struggle to take over when the agent or its checks are unavailable. Unowned or over-concentrated connections. The rules, evidence format and feedback path between workflows belong to no single workflow. Conway observed that organisations design systems that copy their communication structures 4 , so without an owner the connections tend to split along team lines. As recommended practice, the shared rules have one accountable owner, recorded by name, and ownership is confirmed again whenever people or teams change, not only when something goes wrong. The signs are rule changes queued behind one person, the same exception granted repeatedly for one rule, or nobody able to say who approves a change to the shared rules. Reading the factory as unattended throughput. Treating human decision points as the bottleneck to remove turns the factory into the lights-out sense this site does not mean, and DORA's 2024 research, which found that AI adoption negatively affects delivery stability, reminds teams that small batch sizes and robust testing remain crucial 6 . The sign is a proposal to waive a check or drop an approval to keep up with agent output. Lessons that never close. Incident reviews write actions that never reach the stage that owns the gap. The sign is the same kind of miss recurring after it has been reviewed, or actions with no single owner 11 . Related Workflows : the unit of work the factory connects, with its trigger, checks, human decision, evidence and owner. Harness engineering : the discipline behind the controls the factory shares. Engineering Kit : the versioned package that carries the shared rules, checks and evidence schema between workflows and teams. Rule registry : the shared rules, each with an identifier, a route and an owner. Evidence schema : the fixed shape of the record every workflow writes and the next one reads. Validators , Skills with evals and Adapters : the kit's other parts. Workflow catalog : the list of workflows the factory draws on. Pull-request verification : whether one revision of a change may join the mainline. Incident feedback : which earlier control changes after an incident. Traceability spine : the chain of linked artefacts from requirement to incident. Inspect and Adapt : the periodic checkpoint at which delivery evidence is read together. Lifecycle levels : the portfolio, train and team levels at which the lifecycle runs. Definition of Ready and Definition of Done : the entry and exit criteria for an item of work, including the Definition of Done from the Scrum Guide 16 . Terminology : the glossary entry and the credit for each term. Sources Cusumano, Japan's Software Factories : an earlier, production-management sense of the term 5 . Greenfield and Short, Software Factories : the model-driven sense of the term 12 . Shapiro, the five levels of AI-assisted programming, and Willison's account of a team whose code no person writes or reviews: recent senses of the term that differ from this site's 17 20 . Morris on people working on the loop 14 ; Böckeler on the steering loop, harness templates and sensors 2 3 . DORA's 2024 and 2025 research on AI adoption, its announcement of the 2025 report, its AI capabilities model and its customer feedback capability 6 8 7 9 10 . Thoughtworks on incremental developer platforms, and Team Topologies on the thinnest viable platform 19 18 . Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
spec-readiness.html: Specification readiness The workflow that decides whether a team can start planning from one revision of a specification, with every open question recorded and either settled or accepted as open by the person accountable for it, and leaves a readiness record. Decision Can a team begin planning from this revision of the specification now, knowing exactly which questions remain open? The workflow answers that once for each revision. Its catalog entry is W04 , and the phase it closes is described on Specification . "Ready" has a public anchor. The 2020 Scrum Guide says that Product Backlog items the Scrum Team can complete within one Sprint "are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event"; the Guide does not use the term Definition of Ready 12 , which is a team practice described under Definition of Ready . In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the decision carries more weight, because an agent given a specification that is silent on a point still produces something. One open-source spec-driven toolkit 13 gives this as the reason its templates mark a gap instead of filling it: doing so "prevents the common LLM behavior of making plausible but potentially incorrect assumptions" 14 . Settling such questions before planning, rather than in code, is this site's recommended practice. Trigger A run starts when someone asks for planning to begin on a named revision of a specification. The request has to name the revision, because the record the run leaves speaks for that revision and no other. Two later events start a fresh run, and both are recommended practice. The first is a new revision after acceptance. The earlier record stays attached to the earlier revision, as every evidence record does (see Evidence schema ), and the new revision is not ready until its own run decides. The second is a lesson that adds a question for a kind of specification: every specification of that kind that has not yet been planned is opened again so the new question can be asked. A run does not replace refinement. The Scrum Guide calls refinement "the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items" and treats it as ongoing 12 . A run records where refinement has reached at the moment planning is requested. Inputs The run reads the change itself, earlier records and parts of the project's kit. The specification revision and its acceptance criteria. ISTQB defines acceptance criteria as "the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders" 6 . The intake record. What was recorded when the work was taken in, by Intake and triage (catalog W01 ). The rule entries. The rule registry entry for every rule the specification touches. For the customer-record export , the site's hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records, these are R-042, the access rule on who may export which records, and R-017, the volume limit for large exports. The team's Definition of Ready. No source cited on this site prescribes its contents; see Definition of Ready . Questions added by earlier lessons. Questions that past misses added for specifications of this kind. They arrive by the feedback path described on Harness engineering 2 . The security requirements that apply. NIST's Secure Software Development Framework, practice PO.1, asks that security requirements for software development be known at all times, so they can be taken into account throughout development and collected once and shared; task PO.1.2 asks an organisation to identify and document all security requirements for the software it develops and to maintain them over time 8 . The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard is one public catalogue of such requirements for web applications and services. It can be filtered to the chapters that apply, and an organisation chooses its level from its own analysis of risk 9 . Agent task What the agent looks for is set out in the catalog row W04 and is not repeated here. How it works is this site's recommended practice, as Specification states it: the agent reads the specification while it is still being written and raises questions, and a person answers them. Public evidence on the reading is narrow. An industrial study presented at ICSME 2025 examined language models detecting and explaining ambiguity in real-world industrial requirements. Giving the model ten examples in the prompt classified ambiguous requirements better than giving none, and eight industry experts evaluated what the models wrote 10 . The study does not show that the practice improves delivery. The toolkit cited above builds the same caution into its templates: wherever the prompt leaves something unspecified, they require a marker of the form [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: specific question] in place of a guess ("Don't guess") 14 . Two points of the agent's work matter most for this decision, both recommended practice. It marks a question and leaves the answer to a person. It can find that something is open; it cannot know what the business wants. Given a specification with a question still open, it stops and asks. For the export, the evaluation case "Access rule left open" on Skills with evals passes only when the agent asks instead of choosing an access rule itself. Checks A check here decides what a tool can settle from the document alone. Checks confirm form; they never confirm that the specification asks for the right thing ( Specification ). Which checks the workflow requires is set in its catalog row; this section describes the properties that make a check usable in this decision. A marker can be found. The toolkit's specification checklist, which it says acts as "unit tests" for the specification, asks under requirement completeness, in this order, that no clarification markers remain, that requirements are testable and unambiguous, and that success criteria are measurable 14 . Only the first can be decided by searching the text. As recommended practice, it becomes a check, and the other two stay with people. A criterion has a checkable shape; whether it is testable stays a judgment. ISTQB defines testability as "the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met" 7 . That degree is a judgment, so a tool looks only at form. Given, when, then is one such form: Martin Fowler describes it as a style of representing tests in three parts (the state before the behaviour, the behaviour being specified and the changes expected), developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development 5 . Checking the shape is recommended practice; whether the criterion is the right one is a person's call. Every result is one of four. Each check ends passed, failed, skipped or could_not_run , the results defined under The could_not_run result . Could_not_run, like failed, prevents a positive status. As an example, and as recommended practice: if the rule registry cannot be read, the run cannot list the rules the specification touches, so a check that depends on that list reports could_not_run, not passed. Guardrails How a workflow 's agent is limited is described on Workflows . Two stop conditions are particular to this decision. A rule the registry does not hold. When the specification cites a rule with no registry entry, the run stops and the gap goes to whoever maintains the registry. This is recommended practice: a rule exists for the kit only once its entry is written and its owner accepts it ( Rule registry ). An item too large to plan as one unit. The run stops and the item goes back for splitting. Two public sources point the same way. The Scrum Guide ties readiness to what can be completed within one Sprint 12 , and DORA advises breaking work into units "that can be completed independently and in short timeframes" 4 . This page sets no size limit; a team states its own in its Definition of Ready. Human decision Who decides is set in the catalog row W04 . What public sources and this site's Core pages add is a set of accountabilities, each with its own basis. The Scrum Guide makes the Product Owner accountable for creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items and for ensuring that the backlog is transparent, visible and understood. The Product Owner may delegate that work and remains accountable for it 12 . A question about what the specification is for therefore goes to whoever holds that accountability. The same Guide makes the Developers who will be doing the work responsible for sizing it 12 . Whether an item is small enough to plan as one unit is their call, not the agent's. Each rule in the Rule registry has one accountable owner, the person to ask about that rule. When an answer would depart from a rule, an exception, where the rule allows one, is logged against the rule with who allowed it and when it lapses; some rules, such as the access rule R-042, are never open to exception ( Rule registry ). When the decider rejects a question the agent raised, the rejection is recorded with a reason chosen from a fixed list ( Evidence schema ), and those rejections feed the evaluation of the skill behind the agent ( Skills with evals ). The decider may not accept while a required check has failed or reported could_not_run, and may not accept an answer about R-042 that the rule does not allow: a readiness criterion tied to R-042 is met only as written ( The export example ). Both limits are recommended practice. The team, for its part, has a public basis for refusing an item: the Agile Alliance lists among the benefits of a Definition of Ready an explicit agreement that allows a team to push back on accepting ill-defined features 1 . Outputs and evidence The run leaves a readiness record in the shape fixed by the Evidence schema . Later workflows read the record instead of asking the same questions again, which is the evidence hand-off . Open questions go into the record, not a conversation, for a reason the Scrum Guide gives: transparency means the work is visible to those performing it and to those receiving it, and low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk 12 . SSDF PO.1 gives a similar reason for security requirements: collected once and shared, they spare the duplicated effort of gathering them again 8 . The record has six readers. Design conformance (catalog W08 ) plans from the accepted specification. Pull-request verification (catalog W23 ) takes the criteria and rules as part of the independent basis it judges code against. Task traceability and test planning (catalog W12 ) builds its tasks and tests from the criteria. The Traceability spine keys its link from requirement to specification by the criterion identifiers the record holds. Incident feedback (catalog W28 ) reads it when a miss in production traces back to a question nobody asked. Inspect and Adapt 11 , the periodic checkpoint, may change what readiness asks of a kind of specification. In the export example, the first run's record shows the question the access rule turns on, which roles may export which records, as open, and the specification as not ready. Once the answer is written into the specification within R-042, the run on that new revision records the question as settled before planning starts; Software factory follows the item from there. Later, after a scheduled full export within R-017's limit times out in production, readiness asks every export-like specification for the largest export it expects ( The export example ). The record of the next run on such a specification shows that question asked and answered before planning, where before the incident it would not have appeared. The export's other open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure and audit) are not answered on this page. Failure paths The general failure paths every workflow shares are on Workflows and are not repeated here. For this decision, as recommended practice, two cases need stating. When a required check fails, for example because a clarification marker is still in the text, the specification is not ready. The question goes back to whoever is accountable for the item, as described under Human decision, and a later revision gets its own run. When a check reports could_not_run, for example because the rule registry cannot be read, the run cannot show a positive status either. The fix belongs to whoever maintains the registry or the tool, not to the specification's author. In both cases the record names the check that stopped the run. Measures No public study measures this workflow. Every measure below is recommended practice, each is read against a baseline, and none carries a target value. The baseline principle is borrowed by analogy: DORA advises setting a baseline for an application's current performance and improving over time, rather than competing against other teams 3 . DORA says this of its own delivery metrics, not of specification readiness. Agent questions accepted and rejected. The share of each. Baseline: the skill's results on its evaluation cases for its current version ( Skills with evals ). It is an input to those evaluations, never a target. Open questions carried into planning. How many were accepted as open, and how many of those later changed the code. Baseline: the same counts over the first period in which the workflow runs. Owner One accountable owner answers for the workflow itself, keeping its question sets and required checks current, and is distinct from the people who decide each run ( Workflows ). The Definition of Ready it applies has one named owner, a person and never the agent whose work it judges, and owning it means keeping it current ( Who owns each ). As recommended practice, the workflow's owner adds a question for a kind of specification when a lesson arrives and decides which checks are required. Who decides in a given run stays as the catalog row sets it. Related Intake and triage : the workflow whose record this one reads. Incident feedback : the workflow through which a production miss adds a question to readiness. Design conformance : the workflow that plans from the accepted specification. Pull-request verification : the workflow that judges code against the accepted criteria and rules. Specification : the phase this workflow closes. Definition of Ready : the team practice the workflow applies. Traceability spine : the chain of identifiers that starts with the acceptance criteria. Inspect and Adapt : the checkpoint that may change what readiness asks. Core: Workflows , Skills with evals , Rule registry , Evidence schema and Engineering Kit . Workflow catalog: Specification readiness , Design-to-specification handoff , Threat modeling , Spike and Task traceability and test planning .
