Credited to Scaled Agile, Inc. adopted safe-framework WSJF (weighted shortest job first) A prioritisation measure that SAFe estimates as the relative cost of delay divided by the relative job duration, from relative user and business value, time criticality, risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement, and job size. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.), whose WSJF page opens with an epigraph attributed to Don Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow. This site credits WSJF to SAFe and does not cite the book. adopted safe-wsjf Reference model "An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of some environment", in the words of the OASIS Reference Model for Service Oriented Architecture, where the term is defined for service-oriented environments. This site borrows the sense, not the subject: its SAFe reference model is a mapping that shows which item of Core SAFe lines up with which page of this site, and why. It is the site's recommended practice, not SAFe guidance and not a description of any organisation. adopted oasis-soa-rm PI Planning SAFe's cadence-based event for the entire ART that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. Its outputs are committed PI objectives from the Agile Teams and an ART planning board that reflects feature delivery dates and dependencies. SAFe describes it as typically a two-day event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). adopted safe-pi-planning Inspect and Adapt SAFe's name for a significant event held at the end of each PI. It is structured into three parts: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. Its improvement backlog items go into the ART backlog for consideration in the next PI Planning event. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). The site's own Inspect and Adapt page uses the name for its checkpoint where evidence is reviewed and a workflow is added or tightened; the earlier use of the phrase outside SAFe is not claimed here. adopted safe-inspect-and-adapt System Demo SAFe's event that provides stakeholders an integrated view of new features for the most recent iteration delivered by all the teams on the ART. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). On this site it lines up loosely with the release readiness decision, which also brings the results of several changes together. adopted safe-system-demo Continuous Delivery Pipeline SAFe's name for the workflows, activities, and automation needed to guide new functionality from ideation to an on-demand release of value. It has four aspects, in order: continuous exploration, continuous integration, continuous deployment and release on demand. Credited to the Scaled Agile Framework (Scaled Agile, Inc.). Not to be confused with a deployment pipeline as Fowler describes it, a build broken into stages. adopted safe-cdp INVEST Bill Wake's acronym, published in 2003, for the qualities of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. The Agile Alliance glossary notes that a team's Definition of Ready is generally based on it. This site uses it as one public test of whether an item is ready, not as the contents of any team's definition. adopted wake-invest Acceptance criteria In the ISTQB glossary's current wording, the criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders. On this site they are written during Specification, carry identifiers so that later tasks and tests can point back to them, and form part of the independent basis for verification. adopted istqb-acceptance-criteria Testability In the ISTQB glossary, the degree to which test conditions can be established for a component or system, and tests can be performed to determine whether those test conditions have been met. An acceptance criterion with no test condition to establish cannot settle whether the work is accepted. adopted istqb-testability Given, when, then A form for writing a requirement as a concrete example: a starting state, an action, and the expected outcome. Developed by Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts as part of Behavior-Driven Development, as described by Martin Fowler. adopted fowler-given-when-then Spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source Birgitta Böckeler's three degrees of commitment to a specification in spec-driven development. Spec-first: a specification is written before the code and used for the task at hand. Spec-anchored: the specification is kept after the task and used as the feature evolves. Spec-as-source: the specification is the main artefact a person edits, and the code follows from it. adopted bockeler-sdd Test pyramid The advice to have many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack tests running through a user interface, drawn as a pyramid. Martin Fowler's bliki entry credits Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile with spreading the name. On this site it is one of the traditional QA practices that still shapes what an agent's tests should look like. adopted fowler-test-pyramid Hermetic build A build that depends only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so that the same revision built on different machines gives identical results, as the release engineering chapter of Google's site reliability engineering book describes. With coding agents, the build stays hermetic and an agent proposes changes to its configuration rather than taking part in it. adopted sre-book-release-engineering Deploy versus release Deployment is the act of putting a revision into an environment; release is exposing its behaviour to users. The two coincide unless a toggle, a canary or a staged rollout separates them. Several public sources keep the words apart: SAFe says it is optimal to separate the deployment process from releasing; the Thoughtworks Technology Radar placed "Decoupling deployment from release" in Adopt (November 2015 and April 2016); and Pete Hodgson's article on feature toggles (9 October 2017) calls separating feature release from code deployment "the Continuous Delivery principle". No originator is credited here. On this site, a deployment's health is decided in the Deploy phase and exposure to users in Release. common Release toggle One of the four kinds of feature toggle Pete Hodgson distinguishes by lifespan (release, experiment, ops and permissioning). A release toggle lets incomplete or untested code paths ship to production as latent code that may never be turned on, so exposure to users can be decided apart from deployment. It is meant to be short-lived: Hodgson treats toggles as inventory with a carrying cost and says release toggles should generally not stay much longer than a week or two. adopted fowler-feature-toggles Dark launching Martin Fowler's description: taking a new or changed back-end behaviour and calling it from existing users without their being able to tell it is being called, to assess load and performance before the capability is announced. Fowler notes that the term has been subject to semantic diffusion, so other sources may use it more loosely. adopted fowler-dark-launching Definition of Ready The criteria a team makes explicit and visible that an item must meet before the team accepts it for work; the Agile Alliance glossary describes them for a user story and as generally based on the INVEST matrix. The Scrum Guide does not use the term; it says Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. common Definition of Done A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide). It is the Increment's commitment, and a Product Backlog item that does not meet it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. SAFe's glossary words it as the requirements for completeness of a work product or increment of value. This site applies it at story, increment and release, and treats the release level as recommended practice. adopted scrum-guide-2020 Traceability spine The map's name for the chain of seven kinds of artefact (requirement, spec, task, test, change, release, incident), each linked to the next by an identifier. Rule IDs tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name, and the extension of the chain to the incident, are this site's, built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) describe it: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement forwards and backwards. coined Pre-integration review Martin Fowler's name for the branching pattern in which every commit to the mainline is peer-reviewed before the mainline accepts it; he describes the pull request as a mechanism that combines feature branching with this kind of review. On this site it is the practice the pull-request verification workflow puts into a recorded decision for one revision. adopted fowler-branching-patterns Canary release (canarying) Danilo Sato's description on martinfowler.com: rolling out a change slowly to a small subset of users before the entire infrastructure, with rollback by rerouting users back to the old version. Google's Site Reliability Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation, in which the part that receives the change, the canary, is judged against the remainder, the control, and absolute measures such as service level objectives are used as well. adopted fowler-canary-release Service level objective (SLO) From Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by a service level indicator (SLI), where an SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided. The book calls SLIs and SLOs crucial elements in the control loops used to manage systems. adopted deployverif-sre-book-slo Postmortem A written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent it recurring, in the definition of Google's site reliability engineering (SRE) book. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
traceability-spine.html: Traceability spine The chain of seven artefacts from requirement to incident, each pair linked by an identifier and checked for orphans in both directions, with rule IDs as the keys that tie checks and findings, and through them decisions, to the chain. Definition Requirements traceability is, in Gotel and Finkelstein's definition, "the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement, in both a forwards and backwards direction (i.e., from its origins, through its development and specification, to its subsequent deployment and use ...)". 4 On the map of the AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the traceability spine is that idea drawn as one line under the phases. It is a chain of seven kinds of artefact: requirement, spec, task, test, change, release and incident. An identifier links each artefact to the next. Rule IDs, the stable codes that a rule registry gives each rule, tie checks and findings to the chain, and decisions are tied to it through the checks and findings they read. The name is this site's, coined for the map, and so is the extension of the chain past release to the incident that follows. Both are built on requirements traceability as Gotel and Finkelstein describe it. 4 Why it matters Each missing link has its own cost. Requirement without a test. The requirement ships on trust. Traceability can point out requirements that are not tested. 6 Test without a requirement. The test costs time to write, run and maintain, and nobody can say what it protects. The same source calls these extra tests. 6 Change without a task or criterion. The reviewer has no stated intent to judge the change against, so scope creep and unexplained edits pass as easily as intended ones. Incident without a path to the specification. The failure is fixed where it showed, and the gap that let it through stays open. The catalog workflow for this link is Incident-to-development feedback . Following a requirement in both directions is part of the definition: forwards to deployment and use, backwards to its origins. 4 A chain checked in one direction only leaves half of these failures invisible. Public evidence that links go missing when left to habit is limited but concrete. An analysis of six open-source projects found that on average only 60% of the commits were linked to specific issues, and its authors note that without these fundamental links the entire set of project-wide links will be incomplete. 11 The result concerns commit-to-issue links in six projects. It is from the authors' preprint, and it is not a measure of traceability practice in general. Some regulated work requires the practice. NASA's software engineering handbook, on requirement SWE-052, asks projects to "perform, record, and maintain bi-directional traceability" between listed pairs of products, and the requirement applies according to software class, not equally to all software. 6 It is one public example, not a rule for every project or organisation. Coding agents raise the stakes. They write tasks, tests and changes faster than people can read them, so more artefacts exist whose reason nobody has checked. No public study measures how agents affect traceability. Treating the chain as something the workflows write and checks verify, rather than something people reconstruct, is this site's recommended practice. How it works The seven artefacts, in the map's order Requirement. A need or constraint the product must meet, with a named origin. It enters at the idea stage. Spec. The specification that answers the requirement and states its acceptance criteria 5 . Task. A unit of planned work from the design stage, derived from the criteria. Test. A check that a criterion holds, together with its recorded result. Change. A revision of code or configuration made for a task, built and verified in Develop, Build and QA . Release. The candidate revision, with its records, that is approved in Release and put into an environment in Deploy . Incident. An event in operation where the software departs from what was expected, handled in Operate . The link between each adjacent pair The table gives, for each pair, the identifier that links it, the catalog workflow that writes the link and what a reader sees when the link is missing. Which identifier links which pair is this site's model, not a public standard. Each workflow's decision, checks and evidence are in its row of the workflow catalog , and the record fields that carry the links are on the evidence schema page. Pair Linking identifier Written by What a missing link looks like Requirement to spec The acceptance-criterion identifier. Each criterion in the spec has its own, and names the requirement it answers Specification readiness A requirement that no criterion answers, so nothing later in the chain can point back to it Spec to task The criterion identifier, carried on each task Task traceability and test planning Planned work whose purpose cannot be looked up in the spec, which is how scope creep enters Task to test The criterion identifier, carried on each test and on its recorded result Task traceability and test planning; Acceptance-test generation and execution A criterion that is built but never shown to hold, because no recorded result names it Test to change The change revision named on the evidence record that holds each result; the change in turn cites its task Task execution loop ; Pull-request verification A pass that cannot be tied to the code that merges, because it names another revision or none Change to release The revisions of the changes the release candidate contains Release readiness A release whose contents nobody can list by revision Release to incident The identifier of the release that was running, recorded on the incident record Deployment and post-deploy verification ; Incident remediation ; Incident-to-development feedback An incident that cannot be matched to a release, so the trail back to the requirement starts from guesswork Read down the table, the identifiers change class. The upper half is keyed by criterion and task identifiers, which exist before any code does. The lower half is keyed by revisions and release identifiers, which exist because a run or a build produced them, with rule IDs on every check result beside them. The criterion identifier on a recorded test result is the join between the two halves. Read up the table, the same identifiers lead from an incident back to the requirement. For the pair at the far end, supply-chain provenance is a public relative: "verifiable information about software artifacts describing where, when, and how something was produced". 14 It ties a built artefact back to how it was made. The spine asks a similar question of the whole chain: where did this artefact come from, and what did it lead to? Orphans in both directions An orphan is an artefact with no link on one side. Orphans point in two directions, and the chain is checked in both. A forward orphan is a requirement that no test reaches, so the requirement ships on trust. A backward orphan is a test, task or change that leads to no requirement, so it costs effort and protects nothing anyone can name. NASA's handbook describes the same two failures from the side of testing: traceability "can point out software requirements that are not tested (i.e., missing tests) and tests that do not serve to test requirements (i.e., extra tests)". 6 NASA's handbook lists six bi-directional pairs, among them higher-level and software requirements, requirements and design components, design components and code, and requirements and software verification. 6 That is a public example. This site's seven-artefact chain is its own, and the pairs are not the same. Checking is not a one-time act. The handbook describes the matrix as completed left to right early in the appropriate phase, with the forward trace extended to the next set of products as each column is completed, and as maintained throughout the life of the project. 6 A trace that is complete at planning and stale at release has not done its job. Rule IDs as link keys The criterion and task identifiers link the upstream half of the chain. Across the downstream half, rule IDs do the linking. The evidence schema puts the ID of the rule concerned on every expected check, result and finding, so results and findings about the same rule line up across runs and workflows. A decision carries no rule ID of its own. It is tied to the chain through the checks and findings it reads, which name the rules. Using rule IDs as the keys of the spine in this way is this site's recommended practice, and no public standard prescribes it. The rule registry page describes how the identifiers are defined and kept stable, and the results come from validators , deterministic checks this site adapts from what Böckeler calls computational sensors. 2 Public identifier schemes show the same discipline. OWASP's Application Security Verification Standard numbers its requirements by chapter, section and requirement, prefixes them with the version when cited ( v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement> ), and encourages organisation-specific forks provided they maintain traceability, so that passing a requirement means the same across all versions. 9 The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide, a community-created guide, gives each test scenario an identifier in the form WSTG-<category>-<number> , for example WSTG-INFO-02. 10 NIST's Secure Software Development Framework version 1.1 identifies each practice, for example PO.1.2, "Identify and document all security requirements for organization-developed software to meet, and maintain the requirements over time", and RV.3, "Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes". 8 These are cited as examples of stable identifiers, not as sources of a traceability requirement. They show how a requirement or practice stays the same thing across documents, tools and versions. Stable identifiers let each link be written at the moment its artefact is made. This site's recommended practice is that the workflow producing an artefact records the link in its evidence record as a by-product of the run, so the chain never has to be rebuilt afterwards; the "Written by" column of the table above names the catalog row for each pair. The commit-to-issue analysis cited under "Why it matters" shows how incomplete links left to habit can be, and it does not test this recommendation. The customer-record export, left to right and back The running example is a hypothetical feature that lets users export customer records. Its open decisions are which records, which fields, how large an export may be, what happens on failure, and how the feature is audited. The walk below names the artefact and the identifier at each step, using classes of artefact rather than invented identifiers, except the revision shown on the evidence schema page. Requirement to spec. The need that users export only the records they may read is answered by the spec's acceptance criterion on who may export which records, and that criterion's identifier, with the access rule R-042 it relies on, is the link. Spec to task, and task to test. Every task and test written for that criterion carries its identifier, and the two checks that guard the rules, the access validator and the 50k-row load scenario, carry R-042 and the volume-limit rule R-017. Test to change. The pull-request run's evidence record names the change revision 3f9c2e1 and records R-042 as failed and R-017 as could_not_run , so both results belong to that exact revision ( evidence schema ). Change to release. Once the background worker's query is narrowed and the checks run again, release readiness reads the record for the new revision, not the first one, so the release links to the change through the revision that ships. Release to incident, and back. When a scheduled full export, within R-017's limit but far larger than the 50k-row scenario, times out in production, the incident record names the running release, and the identifiers lead back through R-017's checks to the specification, where nobody had asked how large the largest export would be ( software factory ). Where it sits on the map The spine belongs to the lifecycle band, the second band of the map. It is drawn under the phases as a line of seven labelled nodes, captioned "traceability spine, linked by rule IDs". Above the phases, a dashed arrow reads "incident feedback changes what Specification asks". Each link is written in the phase of its workflow, from Specification through Deploy to Operate. The workflows page describes what a workflow is, and the workflow catalog lists each one with its phase. In the core band, the rule registry holds the identifiers and the evidence schema holds the fields of each record. The spine is the chain that reads both. Later workflows read the records of earlier ones, which the glossary calls the evidence hand-off , and the spine is that hand-off followed from requirement to incident. The software factory depends on the shared identifiers for the same reason. This page covers the release-to-incident link and the way the identifiers lead from an incident back to the requirement and the specification that answered it, which is the route the map's dashed arrow shows. The feedback path itself, this site's extension of Böckeler's steering loop, 1 is described in harness engineering and on the software factory page. The periodic review this site calls Inspect and Adapt , after SAFe's event of that name, 12 reads what has landed; see Inspect and Adapt . One public anchor for the return path is NIST's incident response profile, which feeds lessons learned from all activities back into the Improvement category of its framework. 7 The assurance band reads the records for audit and for their validity per revision, which this page does not cover. Pitfalls An identifier is reused or reassigned. A retired rule's code goes to a new rule, or numbers are recomputed after a reorganisation. Sign: the same identifier points at different content in different months. See rule registry . OWASP's ASVS shows why the discipline matters: its requirement numbers may change between versions, so other documents are asked to cite the version, and an organisation-specific fork is encouraged only if it maintains traceability, so that passing a requirement means the same across all versions. 9 Links are written afterwards by hand. The trace is assembled at the end, from memory and commit history. Sign: the trace is older than the change it describes. NASA's handbook asks for the matrix to be maintained throughout the life of the project, 6 and the commit-to-issue analysis cited above shows how incomplete links left to habit can be. 11 The recommended practice is to have the workflow that makes the artefact write the link. Only the forward direction is checked. Every requirement has a test, so the chain looks complete. Sign: tests nobody can tie to a requirement, the extra tests of the NASA statement. 6 The definition asks for both directions. 4 A change is traced to a branch, not a revision. A branch moves, so the link changes meaning. Sign: the record names a branch. See evidence schema . An incident closes with no link upstream. The review writes actions, but none reaches the stage that owns the gap. Sign: the same kind of miss recurs. Postmortem action items without clear ownership are less likely to be resolved, and the value of a postmortem is proportional to the learning it creates. 3 An agent's task-to-criterion mapping is accepted unchecked. A mapping that looks complete is not a verified one. The catalog workflow concerned is Task traceability and test planning . Sign: no orphan check ran, or a could_not_run result was read as a pass, which the workflows page rules out. Related Rule registry : where rule IDs are defined, kept stable and owned. Evidence schema : the fields of the record that carries rule IDs and revisions. Workflows : the unit of work that writes each link. Software factory : the operating state that shared identifiers make possible. Harness engineering : the discipline that decides what a machine checks and what a person decides. Specification , Design , Develop, Build and QA , Deploy , Release and Operate : the phases whose artefacts form the chain. Definition of Ready and Definition of Done : the two gates the map marks on the phases. The Definition of Done is the Scrum Guide's term. 13 Inspect and Adapt : the review of what landed. Validators : the deterministic checks whose results carry rule IDs. Workflow catalog : rows W04 , W12 , W13 , W17 , W23 , W25 , W26 , W27 and W28 , named in the table above. Terminology: traceability spine , rule registry , evidence record , evidence hand-off and feedback path . Sources The definition of requirements traceability: Gotel and Finkelstein. 4 Missing and extra tests, the six bi-directional pairs, how the matrix is built and maintained, and the class-based requirement: NASA's software engineering handbook. 6 Missing links in practice: the preprint of Rath and colleagues, on six open-source projects. 11 Stable, versioned identifiers: the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, 9 the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide 10 and the NIST Secure Software Development Framework. 8 Verifiable information about how an artefact was produced: SLSA provenance. 14 Learning from incidents: the site reliability engineering workbook on postmortems 3 and NIST's incident response profile. 7 Acceptance criteria: the ISTQB glossary. 5 The steering loop, which this site extends as the feedback path: Böckeler. 1 Computational sensors, from which this site adapts validators: Böckeler. 2 Inspect and Adapt as an event: Scaled Agile, Inc. 12 The Definition of Done: Schwaber and Sutherland, the 2020 Scrum Guide. 13 Which identifier links each pair, using rule IDs as the keys of the chain, writing each link as a by-product of the workflow that makes the artefact, the effect of agents on traceability, and checking both directions of the chain are this site's recommended practice; no public source states them. Defines the Definition of Done as a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product, and as the Increment's commitment, as the Product Goal and the Sprint Goal are the commitments of the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Identifies the format with the versioned predicate type https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1, requires consumers to ignore unrecognized fields, and keeps minor versions backwards compatible. ↩ ↩ AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; one model vendor's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating state (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Technology profile The Engineering Kit layer that packages what one supported stack needs: its validators, pinned tool versions, skills, scaffolds and default thresholds. It adds rules and checks for its stack; it does not change what the shared core's rules mean and carries no one project's choices. One concrete form of what Böckeler proposes as a harness template. coined Project configuration The Engineering Kit layer where one project supplies meaning, as a committed, reviewed file: which rules apply and which checks run for each kind of change, thresholds within the bounds the core or profile allows, exceptions with an owner and expiry, and the chosen profile and adapters. It cannot change the evidence schema, redefine a result state or waive a rule the core marks as never open to exception. coined Golden path The opinionated, supported way to build a kind of system that a platform offers its users, with templates and documentation, so that each team does not assemble its own tooling. Associated with Spotify's engineering writing and used in the CNCF platforms white paper and by DORA. An Engineering Kit's technology profiles play a similar part for the harness around a coding agent. adopted spotify-golden-paths Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills with evaluation scenarios, evidence schema and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration) and run through three commands: init (install), doctor (check prerequisites) and verify (run the declared checks and write the evidence record, the same way locally and in CI). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Architecture decision record Michael Nygard's short record of one architecturally significant decision: its title, context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Records are numbered in sequence, numbers are not reused, and a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded rather than edited. This site uses the same pattern for the history of each rule in the rule registry. adopted nygard-adr Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the kit's verify command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Fitness function (architectural) From evolutionary-architecture practice (Ford, Parsons and Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures), which borrows the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. On this site it proposes and cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to grade the output of another model or agent, as studied by Zheng et al. (2023). Each field has one kind of writer (the kit, a validator, an agent or a named person). A team has one when every qualifying change goes through it and leaves a record that the next decision reads. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. The SRE book and workbook describe it as blameless: it looks for contributing causes in the system without blaming any person or team. adopted incident-sre-book-postmortem Regression testing In the ISTQB glossary, a type of change-related testing that detects whether defects have been introduced or uncovered in unchanged areas of the software. The same glossary separates it from confirmation testing, which follows the fix of a defect and confirms that the failure it caused does not reoccur. adopted incident-istqb-regression-testing
validators.html: Validators A validator is a deterministic check, written as code and tied to rule identifiers, that runs the same way locally and in CI, reports passed, failed, skipped or could_not_run, and can block a merge once it has earned trust. Definition A validator is a deterministic check, written as code, that enforces one or more rules from a team's rule registry and names those rule identifiers in every result it reports. It behaves identically on a developer's machine, inside a coding agent's session and in continuous integration (CI). It returns one of four results: passed, failed, skipped or could_not_run . Once it has proved trustworthy, it can block a merge. The term is this site's adaptation of Birgitta Böckeler's computational sensor: a feedback control that is deterministic and fast, run by ordinary computation rather than by a model, in contrast to inferential controls such as AI code review. 1 2 A validator usually wraps an existing tool, such as a linter, a type checker, a test suite or a dependency-rule checker. What turns the tool into a validator is the contract around it: the rule it answers to, the result it reports, and the same behaviour wherever it runs. A validator differs from its neighbours in specific ways. A unit test checks that code does what its author intended, while a validator checks a rule the team has agreed on, and may use tests to do it. A linter is one possible engine inside a validator; on its own it has no rule identifier and no defined result for "could not run". A review skill , an agent that reads a diff against the rules and reports findings, is an inferential sensor; 2 as this site's recommended practice, it proposes and does not block. Why it matters In an AI SDLC (the software development lifecycle with AI agents doing part of the work), the volume of change rises faster than the capacity to review it. A rule that lives only in a guidance document or in a reviewer's memory is applied unevenly, and the unevenness grows with the volume. Böckeler separates computational controls, which are deterministic and fast, from inferential ones, which are slower, more expensive and less deterministic. 1 She describes computational sensors as cheap and fast enough to run on every change, with inferential review kept for what deterministic tools cannot judge. 1 One model vendor's published account of harness engineering on a large codebase describes the same move: architectural constraints enforced through automated checks rather than through reminders. 14 Every rule a machine can check the same way each time is one less thing a person has to remember to look for. The contract around the check is what makes this safe. Without it, familiar failures follow. A check that behaves differently locally and in CI sends developers and agents after failures they cannot reproduce, whereas continuous-integration practice expects any developer to be able to run the mainline build on their own machine. 5 A check that reports a missing tool as "no findings" quietly removes a gate. A check that blocks before anyone trusts it gets bypassed or switched off. A flaky check teaches people to re-run until the result turns green. How it works One rule, one identifier Each validator declares the rule identifiers it enforces, and each finding it reports carries the identifier of the rule it concerns. In the customer-record export , rule R-042 says that every query path serving an export filters by the records the caller is allowed to read. The access validator for R-042 reports each finding against R-042, with the file and query that break it. SARIF, the OASIS standard format for static-analysis output, keys results the same way: each result carries a ruleId , the stable identifier of the rule that was evaluated to produce it. 17 The site recommends the link for three reasons. A finding leads straight to the rule's text and its owner. The registry can show which rules are enforced by a validator and which still depend on judgment. When a rule retires, the validators that enforce it are easy to find and retire with it. Not every rule suits a validator. The test is whether a program can detect a violation and give the same verdict every time it runs on the same input. Rules about how code is arranged and what it may depend on usually pass: forbidden imports between modules, committed credentials, disallowed licences, interface schemas that must not break. Rules about purpose usually do not, and they stay with named people. In the export example, R-042 passes the test, because a program can find a query path that reads customer records without the caller's filter; whether the exported fields are the ones users actually need does not. A rule that passes the test is routed to a gate in the Rule registry , and its validator is built next. The same run everywhere A validator has one entry point, pinned tool versions and one configuration. The developer's machine, the agent's session and the CI pipeline all call that entry point; CI calls the check and never redefines it. The Engineering Kit 's verify command runs a project's validators this way. The kit supplies the mechanism (the entry point, the four results and the report format), and the project supplies the meaning: which of its rules have validators, and what their limits are. Continuous-integration practice asks for a fast build that any developer can reproduce locally, and a validator inherits both expectations: fast enough to run on every change, and reproducible off the shared build. 5 Reporting the result Every run ends in exactly one of four results, each tagged with the rule identifier: passed : the rule was evaluated against the change and no violation was found. failed : a violation was found. The result gives the rule, the location and what is wrong, and links to the full report. skipped : the rule does not apply to this change, for example because the change touches no export path. The validator decides this from a declared condition, never by guessing. could_not_run : the rule applies and the check was required, but no verdict was produced, because a tool was missing, an environment was unavailable, the run timed out or the tool crashed. Top row: three callers, the developer's machine, the agent's session and the CI (continuous integration) pipeline, all call the same validator through one entry point with pinned tool versions and one configuration; CI calls the check and never redefines it. The validator enforces rule R-042 from the rule registry, and every finding it reports carries that rule identifier. Below, a table: every run ends in exactly one of four results, tagged with the rule identifier. passed: the rule was evaluated and no violation was found. failed: a violation was found; the result gives the rule, the location, what is wrong and a link to the full report. skipped: the rule does not apply to this change, decided from a declared condition, never by guessing. could_not_run: the rule applies but no verdict was produced, because a tool was missing, an environment was unavailable, the run timed out after one retry, or the tool crashed. While the validator is report-only, it runs on every pull request and its findings are visible, but no result can stop a merge. Once it is required: passed does not block; failed blocks the merge; a change host may count skipped as satisfied, so it must mean only that the rule does not apply; could_not_run is no verdict, never a pass and never reported as skipped, and the assurance band of the map sets what it means for the merge. A footer notes that the validator only reports, and that the switch from report-only to required is itself a reviewed change, decided by the validator's owner from its record, not the calendar: where its failures pointed at real problems that people fixed, it becomes required; where they were mostly noise, it is corrected or retired. Real problems that people fixed make it required; mostly noise means it is corrected or retired. Validator: adapted from Böckeler’s computational sensors (martinfowler.com) Figure 1. A validator for rule R-042 runs through one entry point on every machine and ends each run in one of four results, none of which can stop a merge while it is report-only. SVG · PNG SARIF draws the same line between "did the tool run" and "what did it find". Each run records whether the tool's execution succeeded separately from its results, and the format has a result kind for a rule that was not evaluated because it does not apply. Its informative appendix warns that when the tool reports an execution error, its results cannot be assumed complete. 17 In SARIF's terms, passed corresponds to pass , failed to fail and skipped to notApplicable . Could_not_run is this site's own term; the nearest SARIF equivalent is an unsuccessful execution. A validator detects that it cannot run by checking its prerequisites before it evaluates anything: the tool is present at the expected version, the environment answers, and the test data exists. It reads the tool's actual output rather than trusting the exit code alone, since SARIF notes that not every program exits with 0 on success and non-zero on failure. 17 When the validator never starts at all, it cannot report anything, and SARIF expects the component that launched the tool to write the record instead. 17 In practice, the runner treats a required validator that produced no result as could_not_run. Could_not_run must never be reported as skipped. At least one change host counts a skipped required status check as satisfied, 9 so a missing environment reported as "skipped" lets the change through unchecked. In the export example, R-017, the volume-limit rule, states a row limit for a single export, and its check runs the 50k-row load scenario. On the first export pull request the load-test tool is missing from the runner image, so the check reports could_not_run and names the missing tool. It does not report failed, because the change is not at fault, and it does not report skipped, because the rule applies. The validator only reports. What each result means for a merge or release decision is set in the assurance band of the map, and the kit-wide definition of could_not_run is on the Engineering Kit page. From report-only to required A new validator first runs in report-only mode: it runs on every pull request and its findings are visible, but it cannot stop a merge. Policy engines ship modes for exactly this. One open-source cluster policy engine's dry-run mode lets new constraints be tested in a running cluster without enforcing them, and its warn mode also tells the requester why a request would have been denied. 7 A container orchestrator's built-in admission policies offer deny, warn and audit as separate actions. 12 CI platforms have a weaker counterpart: one platform's documentation describes a job allowed to fail, which shows a warning while the pipeline still counts as successful. 10 A finding that shows only as a warning on a passing job is easy to miss, so report-only results need a place where people actually read them. No public source says when a validator should start to block, so this is recommended practice. A validator enters report-only mode with an owner and a date by which the decision is due. The decision comes from its record, not the calendar. Where its failures pointed at real problems that people fixed in the code, it becomes a required check. Where they were mostly noise, the validator is corrected and the date moves, or the validator is retired. The switch to required is itself a reviewed change, so the evidence shows when the check began to block. In the export example, the access validator for R-042 is a required check that covers background workers as well as the request path. A background worker's broader query had been a recurring finding in human review, and that repeated finding is why the validator was extended to cover worker queries. On the first export pull request it reports failed, tagged R-042, and points to the worker's query, which reads more records than the caller may see. Timeouts Each validator sets its own time limit and does not rely on a runner's default, which may be far longer than the check needs. A timeout is never a pass. Check platforms keep "timed out" as a conclusion separate from success, 8 and one test runner's timeout plugin ends a hanging test by failing it or by stopping the process. 16 The site recommends one retry, to rule out a transient fault in the environment. If the retry also times out, the validator reports could_not_run, stating the limit and how far the run got. The exception is a rule that is itself a time budget, such as a response-time limit; there, running out of time is the violation, and the result is failed. Flaky checks A flaky check passes and fails on the same code, so a failure stops being a reliable signal: real failures get overlooked, and time goes on re-runs. 15 Martin Fowler argues that non-deterministic tests damage trust in the whole suite. He treats quarantine as a short-term measure that needs a limit on how many tests it holds or how long they stay there. 6 Google's testing team has described re-running failed tests and automatically quarantining the flakiest ones, with a bug filed for each. 11 One empirical study of fixes to flaky tests in open-source projects reports asynchronous waits, concurrency and test-order dependency as the most common causes. 13 How a workflow run treats a check that failed and then passed is on the Workflows page. Checks that depend on timing or shared environments, such as the 50k-row load scenario for R-017, are the most exposed, since asynchronous waits and concurrency are among the causes Luo and colleagues found most often. 13 Fitness functions for architecture rules Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua introduced the architectural fitness function in Building Evolutionary Architectures , borrowing the idea from evolutionary computing: an objective assessment of how well a system preserves an architectural characteristic, carried out through tests, metrics, monitoring and similar mechanisms. 4 18 Fitness function-driven development writes these checks first, in the manner of test-driven development, so that architectural conformance gets feedback during development rather than after it. 3 An architecture rule becomes a validator when it is expressed as a structural check that runs with the build, such as an architecture test in the application's own test suite or a dependency-rule checker's configuration. In the export example, such rules might say that the export feature reaches customer records only through the data-access layer, that the domain layer depends on nothing above it, and that no dependency cycles exist between modules. Böckeler's worked examples include dependency rules, written with the agent's help, that enforce a codebase's module layers. 2 The recommended practice is to begin with structural rules this codebase has already been seen to break, and to add them one at a time, so that each rule's failures are understood before the next rule arrives. A failure message that names the rule, the offending dependency and the permitted alternative lets a coding agent correct its own change without a person translating. Keeping the validator honest An agent asked to make a check pass may find it easier to change the check than the code. As recommended practice, a validator's code, configuration and limits sit outside what an agent may change unsupervised: a change that alters a validator and the code it checks at the same time goes to a person for review. Tests an agent writes to satisfy a validator are reviewed for what they actually establish, and a test that has never been seen to fail without the behaviour it checks is weak evidence. Ready to ship No public source sets a release bar for a check of this kind, so the following is this site's recommended practice. A validator is ready to ship in the kit, even in report-only mode, when: it gives the same result locally, in the agent's session and in CI; it has a known-bad example that must fail and a known-good example that must pass, both kept with the validator and run whenever it changes; it reports could_not_run for each prerequisite it depends on, and never reports passed or skipped when a prerequisite is missing; it has its own time limit and a named owner; each failure carries the rule identifier, the location, what is wrong and a link to the evidence. Where it sits on the map Validators sit in the core band, band 3 of the map ("what does the work"), as one of the five parts inside the Engineering Kit box. Before a validator comes its rule: a rule routed to a gate in the Rule registry becomes a validator here. Alongside are skills, which guide what an agent tries to do rather than checking the result, and so meet a different acceptance bar (see Skills with evals ). After the validator, each result lands in the evidence record , whose fields are fixed on the Evidence schema page. Adapters bind validators to a particular CI runner and change host without making them depend on either. In the vocabulary of Harness engineering , validators are the computational sensors, while skills and instructions are guides. 1 Every workflow calls validators at its checks step (see Workflows ). The assurance band of the map decides what their results mean for merge and release. Pitfalls Report-only with no end. Validators stay non-blocking long after their findings became actionable. Sign to watch: validators past their end date, and report-only findings that nobody acts on. Blocking before trust. A validator becomes required while it is still noisy. Sign to watch: requests to bypass it, or the check quietly switched off. A missing prerequisite reported as clean. A validator that could not run reports passed or skipped. Sign to watch: a required check that reports no findings on a run that scanned zero files or never reached its environment. Retry to green. Failures that pass on a second run are counted as passes. Sign to watch: rising re-run counts, and reports that show only the final pass of a check that failed first. Drift between local and CI. The pipeline runs its own version of the check. Sign to watch: "it passes on my machine" in pull-request threads, or a CI configuration that repeats the check's logic. Failures nobody can act on. A red status with no rule identifier, location or evidence link. Sign to watch: questions in the pull request about what failed and why. The check weakened by the change it checks. An agent relaxes a validator to get a pass. Sign to watch: a single change that edits both a validator or its limits and the code it checks. Orphaned validators. Checks keep running after their rule has changed or retired. Sign to watch: findings with no rule identifier, or identifiers the registry no longer holds. Related Rule registry : where each rule gets its identifier, route and owner. Engineering Kit : the package validators ship in, its verify command and the kit-wide could_not_run result. Evidence schema : the fields that record each validator's result. Skills with evals : the probabilistic counterpart to validators, and why its bar differs. Adapters : how validators bind to a CI runner and change host. Harness engineering : the discipline in which validators are the computational sensors. Workflows : where validators run as the checks step of each delivery decision. Workflow catalog , the Validator entry and the rest of the Terminology : the list of workflows, and where each term on this page comes from.
